Settling conflicts (option A) belongs to leading, and deciding what needs to be done (option B) belongs to planning and organizing. Enforcing rules (option D) is at most a small part of controlling, not its main purpose.

questions.question: Which of these is part of organizing?

options.d: deciding who will do which tasks

questions.explanation: Organizing is about arranging work, which includes deciding what tasks need doing and who will do them. Setting goals (option A) is planning. Settling conflicts and motivating people (options B and C) are part of leading.

questions.question: Under which management function would settling a conflict fall?
questions.explanation: Leading covers working with and through people, which includes motivating them, communicating and settling conflicts. Controlling (option A) is about monitoring and correcting performance, and planning (option B) is about setting goals and strategies. Organizing (option C) arranges tasks and reporting lines, but handling a disagreement between people is a leading job.

questions.question: A key part of the controlling function is ______.
questions.explanation: Controlling means checking how work is going, which involves evaluating actual performance against the goals that were set and correcting any gaps. Structuring (option B) belongs to organizing. Punishing (option D) is not the purpose of controlling, which focuses on keeping work on track.

questions.question: Who created a framework describing what managers do in terms of ten different but closely linked roles?
questions.explanation: Henry Mintzberg, after watching managers at work, grouped what they do into ten roles: three interpersonal, three informational and four decisional. Fayol (option A) is known for the management functions, and Katz (option B) for managerial skills. Henry Ford (option D) was an industrialist who did not create this framework.

questions.question: Under Mintzberg's categories, giving a speech at a company dinner would count as which type of role?
questions.explanation: Speaking at a company dinner is a ceremonial, symbolic duty, which is the figurehead role, and figurehead is one of Mintzberg's interpersonal roles. Option A is tempting because speeches can share information, as the spokesperson role does, but a dinner speech is mainly symbolic. Entrepreneur (option D) is a decisional role about starting new projects.

questions.question: How did Mintzberg arrive at his ten managerial roles?

options.a: by mailing questionnaires to thousands of managers
options.b: by watching hundreds of managers over several years
options.c: by closely studying the work activities of five chief executives
options.d: by applying common sense to the situation

questions.explanation: Mintzberg based his roles on detailed observation of the actual work of five chief executives. He did not use mass questionnaires (option A) or observe hundreds of managers (option B). Option D is wrong because his conclusions came from careful study, not common sense.

questions.question: In Mintzberg's framework, why is negotiator classed as a decisional role?

options.a: Negotiating involves taking a position and deciding how and when to compromise.
options.b: Negotiating requires a manager to handle money.
options.c: Only top managers, who make all decisions, negotiate.
options.d: Negotiating needs no interpersonal or informational skill.

questions.explanation: Negotiating is mainly about making choices: what position to take, what to give up and when to compromise. That is why it sits among the decisional roles. Option D is wrong because negotiating actually needs strong people and information skills. Options B and C are wrong because negotiation is not only about money and is not limited to top managers.

questions.question: A manager from a drug company who attends a meeting of university scientists is acting in which role?
questions.explanation: The liaison role means building and keeping contacts with people outside one's own unit or organization, and meeting outside scientists fits that well. Option B, figurehead, is about ceremonial duties, which this meeting is not. Options A and D name whole groups of roles that do not include liaison, which is an interpersonal role.

questions.question: A finance manager who regularly reads business newspapers to keep up with financial news is playing which role?
questions.explanation: In the monitor role, a manager seeks out and receives information about what is happening inside and outside the organization, and following financial news does exactly that. Option C, disseminator, means passing information on to members of the organization, which simply reading does not do. Liaison (option D) is about building outside contacts, and leader (option A) is about directing staff.

questions.question: Which finding from Mintzberg's study came as a surprise?

options.b: Managers were careful, reflective thinkers who planned strategies step by step.
options.c: Managers might spend hours on one activity in a normal day.
options.d: Managers spent only a short time on each activity.

questions.explanation: Mintzberg found that managers jumped between many short, varied, unplanned activities and rarely spent long on any one of them. This went against the common belief in option B, that managers were reflective planners working methodically. Option C is the opposite of what he found, and option A was not his conclusion.

questions.question: All of these are informational roles in Mintzberg's framework EXCEPT ______.
questions.explanation: Entrepreneur is a decisional role, because it involves spotting opportunities and starting projects to take advantage of them. Monitor, disseminator and spokesperson (options B, C and D) are Mintzberg's three informational roles, which deal with gathering, sharing and passing on information.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a decisional role in Mintzberg's framework?
questions.explanation: Spokesperson is an informational role, because it involves passing information to people outside the organization. Entrepreneur, disturbance handler and resource allocator (options B, C and D) are decisional roles, along with negotiator, because each requires the manager to make choices.

questions.question: Which of Mintzberg's roles has essentially the same name as one of the four management functions?
questions.explanation: The leader role is about directing and motivating people, which is exactly what the leading function covers, so the two match almost word for word. Monitor (option C) is tempting because it sounds like controlling, but it is an informational role about gathering information, not the controlling function itself. Resource allocator and negotiator (options B and D) are decisional roles that support planning rather than share a function's name.

questions.question: What is the main difference between non-profit and for-profit organizations?
questions.explanation: The big difference is how each "keeps score": for-profit firms judge success mainly by profit, while non-profits judge it by how well they serve their mission, such as helping a community. Decision making, motivation and hiring (options A, C and D) work in broadly similar ways in both types of organization.

questions.question: Which role matters more to managers of small organizations than to managers of large companies?
questions.explanation: In a small organization the manager is often the main face of the business, representing it to customers, bankers and the public, so the spokesperson role is especially important. Resource allocator (option D) matters more in large organizations, where managers spend much of their time deciding who gets what. Entrepreneur (option C) is important in small firms too, but spokesperson is the role singled out as most important there.

questions.question: Which of these is LEAST likely to describe a small organization?

options.a: Planning is not likely to be an elaborate, formal ritual.
options.c: Employees are likely to be tracked by computerised monitoring systems.
options.d: The organization's design is likely to be simpler and less structured.

questions.explanation: Small organizations usually rely on direct, personal supervision rather than formal, computerised systems to keep track of employees, so option C is the one that does not fit. Options A, B and D all describe typical features of small organizations: informal planning, informal relationships and a simple, loose structure.

questions.question: Why might a non-profit manager seem just as worried about money as a for-profit manager?

options.a: Non-profit managers are judged only on financial results.
options.b: Non-profit managers like to appear to care about the "bottom line".
options.c: Many non-profits run on tight budgets and must be very efficient.
options.d: Non-profits are required to make a profit.

questions.explanation: Many non-profits work with very limited funds, so their managers must manage money carefully and get the most out of every naira. Option A is wrong because non-profits are judged mainly on how well they serve their mission. Option D is wrong because non-profits do not exist to make a profit.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT counted as a political skill for a manager?
questions.explanation: Political skill involves reading social situations well, building networks, influencing others and coming across as sincere, so a dominant personality is not one of them. Networking ability, social astuteness and sincerity (options B, C and D) are all recognised parts of political skill.

questions.question: Compared with someone managing a large organization, a small business manager is more likely to be a(n) ______.
questions.explanation: A small business has few people, so its manager has to handle many different tasks that big firms would give to separate specialists, which makes the manager a generalist. Option A describes managers in large organizations, where work is divided into specialised jobs. Figurehead and monitor (options B and D) are roles every manager plays, not features that set small business managers apart.

questions.question: Unlike a small business manager, a manager in a large organization focuses mainly on ______.

options.b: internal matters, especially sharing out resources
options.d: planning ways to improve the structure

questions.explanation: In a large organization, deciding who gets which resources is a major and constant concern, so the manager's focus is mostly internal. Option A describes the small business manager, who looks outward and acts more as an entrepreneur and spokesperson. Setting goals and improving structure (options C and D) matter too, but they are not the main focus that separates the two kinds of manager.

questions.question: A business has only about 100 employees. What would stop it from being classed as a small business?

options.b: It has a major influence on its industry.
options.d: It has no influence on its industry.

questions.explanation: A small business is one that has relatively few employees, is independently owned and has no dominant influence on its industry, so a firm with a major impact on its industry would not count as small. Profit, whether low or high (options A and C), is not part of the definition. Option D actually fits a small business rather than ruling it out.

questions.question: Which of these is networking most likely to help a manager achieve?
questions.explanation: Networking means building relationships with people inside and outside the organization. Those connections give a manager allies and influence, which is what a power base is, and building one is the job of political skills. Efficiency (option A) is about using resources well and effectiveness (option B) is about reaching goals, while setting goals (option C) is part of planning.

questions.question: Almost every managerial task involves ______.
questions.explanation: Whatever managers are doing, whether planning, organizing, leading or controlling, they are constantly making choices, so decision making runs through nearly all managerial work. Technical skills, long-term planning and political skills (options B, C and D) are needed for some tasks but not for almost all of them.

questions.question: In the four-skill version of Katz's framework, the critical managerial skills are ______.
questions.explanation: The four skills are technical, interpersonal, conceptual and political. Options A and B include "empirical" skills, which are not part of the scheme. Option C includes "controlling", which is a management function, not a skill.

questions.question: For a building contractor, knowing the building codes would count as a(n) ______ skill.
questions.explanation: Technical skills are the job-specific knowledge and techniques needed to do a particular kind of work, and building codes are exactly that kind of specialised knowledge for a contractor. Interpersonal and political skills (options A and D) are about dealing with people. Conceptual skills (option C) involve analysing and thinking through complex situations, not knowing specific regulations.

questions.question: Being good at motivating subordinates belongs under which category of skills?
questions.explanation: Motivating others means working well with people, which is what interpersonal skills are about. Conceptual skills (option B) involve analysing complex situations, and technical skills (option C) are specialised job knowledge. Political skills (option D) concern building power and influence, rather than inspiring staff to do their best.

questions.question: Which of these could be a technical skill?
questions.explanation: Technical skills are specialised, job-specific abilities, and computer programming is a clear example. Speaking and writing well (options A and C) are general communication abilities that support interpersonal skills, and decision making (option D) is a broad ability that draws on conceptual skills.

questions.question: Strong political skills would matter most to a manager who ______.

options.b: wants fair pay for his or her level
options.c: wants to move up the organization

questions.explanation: Political skills help managers build a power base and the right connections, which is what helps people rise through the ranks. Job security, fair pay and a lighter workload (options A, B and D) do not depend nearly as much on building influence and allies.

questions.question: Which set of skills would a country's president be least likely to need?
questions.explanation: A president needs strong political, interpersonal and conceptual skills to lead, win support and think through complex national issues. Technical skills, meaning specialised, hands-on job knowledge, matter least at this top level, because experts and officials handle the technical details.

questions.question: Who would gain the least from studying management?
questions.explanation: A fan simply watches and supports, and is not responsible for running or working within the club, so studying management helps them least. The coach (option A) manages players directly, the owner (option C) runs the club as an organization, and the player (option D) works under managers, so all three can use management knowledge.

questions.question: Why should all of us care about how organizations are managed?

options.a: We all make money from organizational profits.
options.b: We deal with organizations every day of our lives.
options.c: We all rely on organizations for jobs.
options.d: Organizations control every part of our lives.

questions.explanation: Every day we deal with organizations, such as schools, banks, hospitals, shops and transport companies, so how well they are managed affects us all. Options A and C are not true for everyone, because some people do not earn from or work for organizations. Option D is an exaggeration.

questions.question: During hard economic times, well-managed companies can still prosper by relying on ______.
questions.explanation: Well-managed companies build strong customer loyalty, and loyal customers keep buying even when times are hard. Bailouts and bankruptcy (options A and B) are signs of trouble, not ways to prosper. Raising prices (option C) during a downturn is more likely to drive customers away.

questions.question: Which of these is the hardest ethical challenge facing managers in today's business climate?

options.a: being unable to hire new staff
options.b: having to dismiss staff who are not productive
options.c: having to downsize and lay off staff who are hardworking and productive
options.d: making employees pay more towards their health insurance

questions.explanation: Letting go of people who have worked hard and done nothing wrong is the toughest ethical position for a manager. Dismissing unproductive staff (option B) is easier to justify because it is based on performance. Being unable to hire (option A) and asking employees to pay more for health insurance (option D) are difficult, but they are not as hard ethically as laying off good workers.

questions.question: Why can studying management help even people who never plan to become managers?

options.a: They are likely to be managed at some point in their careers.
options.b: Everybody ends up becoming a manager.
options.c: They need to be able to outwit their managers.
options.d: Management helps people control their emotions.

questions.explanation: Most people work under managers at some point, so understanding how managers think and behave helps them work better with their bosses and understand the organization. Option B is not true, since not everyone becomes a manager. Options C and D are not the real reasons for studying management.

questions.question: Which of these shows that a company is well managed?

options.a: It builds a customer base quickly.
options.b: It finds ways to prosper even when the economy is hard.
options.c: It does not have to worry about customer loyalty.
options.d: It finds ways to prosper when the economy is booming.

questions.explanation: Many companies can make money when the economy is booming (option D), so the real test of good management is doing well when times are tough. Building customers quickly (option A) does not prove the business will last. Option C is wrong because even the best-run companies must work to keep their customers loyal.

questions.question: One common thread in the changes facing managers today is the need to rely on ______ to find ways of raising productivity.
questions.explanation: Managers increasingly recognise that the people doing the work often have the best ideas for improving it, so they draw on everyone in the organization. Outside specialists and consultants (options B and D) can help, but they do not know the work as well as the people doing it. Relying only on top managers (option C) ignores most of the knowledge in the organization.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a factor that managers have to deal with in today's tough economic climate?

options.c: employees who are unwilling to work

questions.explanation: Today's managers face fast-changing technology, an uncertain economy and strained trust between managers and employees, so options A, B and D are real challenges. Employees who are unwilling to work are not described as one of the defining pressures of the current climate, which makes C the odd one out.

questions.question: How are customers changing the job of the modern manager?

options.a: Managers are starting to see customers as opponents in a fight for survival.
options.b: Managers are letting customers take charge of planning and designing new products.
options.c: Managers are placing less weight on customer satisfaction as a key goal.
options.d: Managers are increasingly making customer satisfaction a key goal.

questions.explanation: Managers now see that organizations need customers to survive, so keeping customers satisfied has become a key goal. Option C says the opposite, and option A wrongly treats customers as enemies. Option B goes too far: customers may give input, but managers do not hand over control of product planning and design.

questions.question: When a company answers its phone promptly with a polite, helpful human operator, what does this tell the customer?

options.b: The company is wasting money on phone operators.
options.c: The company is responsive to customers' needs.

questions.explanation: Prompt, courteous and helpful service shows that the company takes its customers seriously and is ready to respond to their needs. It says nothing about whether prices are high or low (options A and D). Option B misses the point, because good customer service is an investment in keeping customers, not a waste.

questions.question: Why is innovation such an important part of a manager's job today?

options.b: Innovation gives a company a "fresh" image without real change.
options.c: New ways of doing things are always better than old ones.
options.d: Innovation gives an organization an advantage over its competitors.

questions.explanation: Innovation means finding new and better ways of doing things, which helps an organization stay ahead of its competitors. Option B describes cosmetic change, not true innovation. Option C is too absolute, since not every new idea is better than the old way.

questions.question: Which influential business thinker introduced the term "core competency"?
questions.explanation: C.K. Prahalad, writing with Gary Hamel, introduced the idea of core competencies, meaning the main strengths and capabilities that give an organization its competitive edge. Deming (option A) is known for quality management, Blanchard (option C) for leadership writing, and Taylor (option D) for scientific management.

questions.question: Which statement about managers in today's world is correct?

options.a: They are all aged between 30 and 65.
options.b: They work only in large corporations.
options.c: They work only in organizations that aim to make a profit.
options.d: The quality of employees' relationship with their direct supervisor is the most important factor in employee productivity and loyalty.

questions.explanation: Option D is correct because the way supervisors treat and relate to their people strongly shapes how productive and loyal employees are. Options A, B and C are all false: managers come in all ages, and they work in small and large organizations, non-profits as well as for-profits.

questions.question: A person who works with and through others, coordinating their work activities so that organizational goals are achieved, is ______.
questions.explanation: This is the definition of a manager: someone who coordinates and oversees other people's work so the organization reaches its goals. Options B and D describe particular kinds of managers in specific areas, so they are too narrow for a general definition. Intelligence (option A) has nothing to do with the definition.

questions.question: Titles such as agency head or plant manager are most likely to belong to which management level?
questions.explanation: Agency heads and plant managers are middle managers: they run a unit or site and sit between the top managers and the first-line supervisors. Top managers (option D) run the organization as a whole, while team leaders and first-line managers (options A and C) supervise frontline workers directly.

questions.question: Which of these is the lowest level of management?
questions.explanation: First-line managers form the lowest level of management, directly overseeing the work of nonmanagerial staff. A nonmanagerial employee (option A) is not part of management at all. A research department manager (option B) is at the middle level, and a vice president (option C) is a top manager.

questions.question: Which group of managers is also known as supervisors?
questions.explanation: First-line managers are commonly called supervisors, since they directly oversee nonmanagerial employees' day-to-day work. Middle and top managers (options B and D) are above this level. Team leader (option A) is one first-line title, but supervisor is the general name for the whole first-line level.

questions.question: Managers holding titles such as department head, project leader, plant manager or division manager are ______.
questions.explanation: These titles belong to middle managers, who sit between top management and the first-line level and manage other managers. Top managers (option B) carry titles like CEO or managing director, and first-line managers (option A) are usually called supervisors. Production manager (option C) describes a functional area, not a level of management.

questions.question: At which management level would you place a division manager?
questions.explanation: A division manager runs one part of the organization and reports to top management, which makes the role a middle management position. Top managers (option D) run the whole organization, while team leaders and first-line managers (options A and C) supervise nonmanagerial staff directly.

questions.question: ______ is the process of getting activities done efficiently and effectively with and through other people.
questions.explanation: This is the definition of management: coordinating and overseeing work so that it gets done efficiently and effectively through others. Leading and controlling (options A and D) are just two of the functions within management. Supervision (option C) is a narrower idea, linked mainly with first-line managers.

questions.question: ______ is what separates a managerial position from a nonmanagerial one.

options.d: Coordinating and integrating other people's work

questions.explanation: Managers are responsible for coordinating and integrating the work of others, which is exactly what nonmanagerial employees do not do. Raising efficiency (option C) is a goal for everyone in the organization, not something only managers do. Manipulating people (option A) and concern for the law (option B) are not what define a manager.

questions.question: A car maker that produces more cars for the same cost, but with many defects, would be ______.
questions.explanation: Producing more cars for the same cost means getting more output from the same inputs, which is an efficiency gain. But cars full of defects do not meet the goal of producing good, reliable vehicles, so effectiveness has not improved and options A and C are wrong. Option D describes only part of the efficiency idea rather than what the company achieved.

questions.question: What is meant by efficiency?

options.a: the relationship between inputs and outputs
options.c: the exponential pattern of costs and outputs
options.d: raising outputs no matter what it costs

questions.explanation: Efficiency is the relationship between inputs and outputs: getting the most output from the fewest resources. Option D is the opposite of efficiency, because ignoring cost wastes resources. Options B and C are not meaningful ways of describing the idea.

questions.question: Which list gives the functions of the management process?
questions.explanation: The management process is made up of planning, organizing, leading and controlling. Options A, B and C each include staffing or directing in place of controlling, but staffing is usually treated as part of organizing and directing as part of leading, not as separate functions.

questions.question: In successful organizations, ______.

options.a: low efficiency and high effectiveness go together
options.b: high efficiency and low effectiveness go together
options.c: high efficiency and high effectiveness go together
options.d: high efficiency and high equity go together

questions.explanation: Successful organizations both reach their goals (high effectiveness) and use their resources well (high efficiency). Options A and B each sacrifice one of the two. Option D swaps in equity, which is not part of the efficiency and effectiveness pairing.

questions.question: ______ is about the means of getting things done, while ______ is about the ends, meaning reaching organizational goals.
questions.explanation: Efficiency is about means (how well resources are used) and effectiveness is about ends (whether goals are reached). Option A swaps the two terms around. Options C and D wrongly treat goal attainment as separate from effectiveness, when the two actually mean the same thing.

questions.question: Who proposed the five management functions of planning, organizing, commanding, coordinating and controlling?
questions.explanation: Henri Fayol, the French industrialist, put forward these five functions in the early 1900s, and they later became the basis of today's four functions. Taylor (option A) is known for scientific management, and Henry Ford (option B) for mass production. Chester Barnard (option C) wrote about organizations but did not propose these functions.

questions.question: Which French industrialist identified the basic functions of management?
questions.explanation: Henri Fayol was the French industrialist who described the basic management functions. Weber (option A) was a German sociologist known for bureaucracy, Taylor (option B) was an American engineer known for scientific management, and Herzberg (option C) is known for his work on motivation.

questions.question: Writing an organization's strategic plan is an example of which management function?
questions.explanation: Planning involves defining goals and working out strategies for achieving them, and a strategic plan does exactly that. Organizing (option D) comes afterwards, arranging the work and people needed to carry out the plan. Leading (option A) deals with motivating and directing people, and coordinating (option B) is not one of the four modern functions.

questions.question: What do we call the process of monitoring, comparing and correcting?
questions.explanation: Controlling means monitoring performance, comparing it with the goals that were set and correcting any problems. Organizing (option D) is about arranging the work, and leading (option C) is about directing and motivating people. Coordinating (option B) is not the name for this process.

questions.question: Mentoring is mainly linked with which management function?
questions.explanation: Mentoring involves guiding, supporting and developing people, which is part of leading. Planning (option A) sets goals and strategies, organizing (option B) arranges tasks and structure, and controlling (option D) monitors performance, none of which centres on developing individuals the way mentoring does.

questions.question: In Mintzberg's framework, the ______ roles involve dealing with people and carrying out duties that are ceremonial and symbolic.
questions.explanation: Interpersonal roles, namely figurehead, leader and liaison, involve working with people and carrying out ceremonial and symbolic duties. Informational roles (option A) involve handling information, and decisional roles (option D) involve making choices. Technical (option C) is a type of skill, not one of Mintzberg's role groups.

questions.question: The disseminator, figurehead, negotiator, liaison and spokesperson roles matter more at the ______ levels of an organization.
questions.explanation: These roles involve representing the organization, linking it with outsiders, negotiating and sharing important information, which are tasks that grow in importance higher up the organization. At lower and supervisory levels (options A and D), the leader role matters more because managers work closely with frontline staff.

questions.question: An HR manager attending a meeting of a local professional association for human resource managers would be acting in which role?
questions.explanation: Building contacts with people outside one's own organization is the liaison role, and a meeting of fellow HR professionals is a good example. The leader role (option B) involves directing and motivating one's own staff. Disseminator (option D) means passing information on to people inside the organization, and informational (option A) is a group of roles that does not include liaison.

questions.question: Which role matters more for lower-level managers than for middle or top managers?
questions.explanation: Lower-level managers work most closely with the employees doing the work, so directing and motivating them, the leader role, matters most at this level. Spokesperson and disseminator (options C and D) become more important higher up, where managers represent the organization and share information widely. Entrepreneur (option B) is not the role that stands out at lower levels.

questions.question: Many of Mintzberg's roles fit with the basic management functions. For example, the ______ role forms part of planning.
questions.explanation: Deciding how to share out money, people and time is closely tied to planning, so resource allocation fits within the planning function. Figurehead, leader and liaison (options A, B and C) are interpersonal roles, which fit with the leading function instead.

questions.question: How much emphasis managers place on different roles appears to depend on their ______.

options.b: length of service with the organization

questions.explanation: Managers at different levels of the hierarchy emphasise different roles. For example, the leader role is more important at lower levels, while roles such as figurehead and spokesperson matter more at the top. Length of service, experience and personality (options B, C and D) may affect individuals, but level is the main factor.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of Mintzberg's interpersonal roles?
questions.explanation: Spokesperson is an informational role, because it involves passing information to people outside the organization. Figurehead, leader and liaison (options A, B and C) make up the three interpersonal roles, which involve dealing with people and ceremonial duties.

questions.question: In Mintzberg's framework, the ______ roles involve receiving, gathering and spreading information.
questions.explanation: Informational roles, namely monitor, disseminator and spokesperson, deal with collecting, receiving and passing on information. Interpersonal roles (option A) involve dealing with people and ceremonial duties, and decisional roles (option D) involve making choices. Technical (option C) is not a group of roles in this framework.

questions.question: Many of Mintzberg's roles fit with the basic management functions. For example, all three interpersonal roles belong to the ______ function.
questions.explanation: The interpersonal roles of figurehead, leader and liaison all involve dealing with people, which fits within the leading function. Planning (option B) links more with roles like resource allocator and entrepreneur, while organizing and controlling (options A and D) are about arranging and monitoring work rather than relating to people.

questions.question: All of the following managerial roles are more important at the higher levels of an organization EXCEPT ______.
questions.explanation: The leader role is the exception, because it matters most for lower-level managers who work directly with frontline employees. Disseminator, figurehead and negotiator (options B, C and D) all grow in importance higher up, where managers represent the organization, share information and negotiate on its behalf.

questions.question: The three essential managerial skills identified by Katz are ______.
questions.explanation: Katz identified three essential skills: technical, human and conceptual. Options A and B include "empirical", which is not one of his skills. Option C includes "controlling", which is a management function rather than a skill.

questions.question: Which statement about human and technical skills is true?

options.a: Human and technical skills stay equally important as managers move up.
options.b: Technical skills stay necessary while human skills decline as managers move up.
options.c: Human skills stay necessary while the need for technical skills declines as managers move up.
options.d: The need for both human and technical skills declines as managers move up.

questions.explanation: Human skills are important at every level because all managers work with people, while technical skills matter most at lower levels and become less important higher up. Option B gets this the wrong way round. Options A and D are wrong because the two skills do not change in the same way.

questions.question: Managers who have strong ______ can bring out the best in their people.
questions.explanation: Human skills are the ability to work well with others, communicate, motivate and inspire, which is what gets the best out of people. Conceptual skills (option B) help with analysing complex situations, and technical skills (option C) are specialised job knowledge. Visual skills (option D) are not one of the managerial skill types.

questions.question: A manager who gets along well with people, whether one-on-one or in a team, is showing which kind of skills?
questions.explanation: Human skills are the abilities to work well with other people, both individually and in groups, which includes communicating, motivating and leading. Option B sounds similar, but "behavioural skills" is not one of Katz's three managerial skill types (technical, human and conceptual). Option A refers to job-specific know-how, not people skills.

questions.question: Phrases like "thinking about abstract situations" and "visualising the whole" describe which type of managerial skill?
questions.explanation: Conceptual skills let a manager think through abstract and complex situations and picture the organisation as a whole and how its parts fit together. Options A and B are about dealing with people, while option C is about expertise in specific work methods and tools.

questions.question: Which of these phrases fits best with a manager's conceptual skills?

options.c: applying information to solve business problems

questions.explanation: Conceptual skills are the ability to analyse and diagnose complex situations, so using information to work out solutions to business problems is the clearest match. Motivating subordinates (option A) and talking with customers (option B) rely on interpersonal skills, while knowing the product well (option D) is technical knowledge.

questions.question: Which managerial skill is more important for first-line managers than for top managers?
questions.explanation: Technical skills, the job-specific knowledge and techniques needed to do the work, matter most at the first-line level because these managers supervise that work up close, and they become less important higher up. Human skills (option A) are tempting, but they are equally important at every level, so they are not more important at the bottom. Conceptual skills (option C) grow in importance toward the top, and empirical (option D) is not a managerial skill type.

questions.question: Which statement best defines an organisation?

options.a: the physical place where people go to work
options.b: a group of people who are all employed by one company
options.c: a deliberate arrangement of people to accomplish some specific purpose
options.d: a set of people concentrating on making profit for shareholders

questions.explanation: An organisation is a deliberate arrangement of people brought together to accomplish a specific purpose, and it has a purpose, people and a deliberate structure. Option A confuses the organisation with its building. Option D is too narrow, since schools, hospitals and charities are organisations even though they are not profit-seekers.

questions.question: All organisations share some common characteristics. Which one is usually expressed in the form of the organisation's goals?
questions.explanation: Every organisation exists for a distinct purpose, and that purpose is normally spelled out as a goal or set of goals. People (option A) and a deliberate structure (option C) are the other shared characteristics, but neither is expressed as goals. Technology (option B) is not one of the characteristics every organisation shares.

questions.question: Which shared characteristic of organisations makes clear how members relate to one another at work?
questions.explanation: Every organisation develops a deliberate structure, such as rules, job descriptions and reporting lines, that defines and clarifies members' work relationships. Option A, its people, is another shared characteristic, but people on their own do not spell out who works with whom. Option D, its purpose, explains why the organisation exists, not how members relate.

questions.question: What do we call a deliberate arrangement of people put together to achieve a specific purpose?
questions.explanation: That is the definition of an organisation: people deliberately arranged to accomplish a particular purpose. Option A, a structure, is only one feature of an organisation. Option B describes a series of activities, not a group of people.

questions.question: Compared with traditional organisations, newer organisations tend to be more
questions.explanation: New organisations are flexible and dynamic, adjusting quickly to change instead of relying on fixed arrangements. Options A, B and C describe traditional organisations, which were stable, command-oriented and rule-oriented.

questions.question: What does the "universality of management" mean?

options.a: managers in every organisation carry out the four management functions
options.b: managers in every organisation can do their jobs in exactly the same way
options.c: any organisation can employ any manager to do its management work
options.d: any manager can move to any organisation and handle any management job

questions.explanation: Universality of management means management is needed in every kind and size of organisation, at all levels and in all work areas, so every manager plans, organises, leads and controls. Option B goes too far, because how managers carry out those functions differs from one setting to another. Options C and D wrongly suggest managers are interchangeable anywhere.

questions.question: What tends to happen to organisations that are well managed?

options.a: they pick the best suppliers for their products
options.b: they compete internationally because their products are the best
options.c: they always offer the cheapest products
options.d: they build loyal customers, grow and prosper

questions.explanation: Well-managed organisations develop a loyal customer base, grow and prosper, even in hard times. Option C uses the word "always", which is too absolute, since good management does not guarantee the lowest prices. Options A and B describe things some firms do but are not the general result of good management.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the experience of managing in today's fast-changing workplace?

options.a: it gives many rewards and quick promotions
options.b: it can be a hard and thankless job
options.c: it brings few challenges, short working weeks and high pay
options.d: it comes with clear rules, permanent jobs and flexible hours

questions.explanation: Managing today can be tough and thankless: managers face heavy workloads, must deal with difficult people and situations, and depend on others to get results. Option A overstates the rewards, and options C and D describe an easy, settled job that does not match today's dynamic workplace.

questions.question: A manager's success usually depends on

options.a: how hard the manager personally works
options.b: how closely the manager watches the employees
options.c: how skilled the manager is at the technical side of the job
options.d: how well other people perform their work

questions.explanation: Managers get things done through and with other people, so their success depends on how well others perform. Option A ignores the fact that a manager's own effort cannot replace the team's output. Option C describes what matters for individual workers, not mainly for managers.

questions.question: Creating the right kind of work environment is the most important job in an organisation. What kind of environment is meant?

options.a: one that is safe and well lit so employees can see clearly
options.b: one that is clean and friendly
options.c: one where members can work to the best of their ability and the organisation can reach its goals
options.d: one that suppliers like supplying and customers like buying from

questions.explanation: The main task is building an environment where organisational members can do their best work and, through that, the organisation achieves its goals. Options A and B describe pleasant physical conditions, which help but are not the main point. Option D focuses on outsiders rather than on members doing their work.

questions.question: Which of these is commonly true of managers?

options.a: they must follow the organisation's rules and cannot make their own decisions
options.b: they switch career paths during their working lives
options.c: they get the chance to think creatively and use their imagination
options.d: they rely on their employees to guide them in dealing with their own boss

questions.explanation: One of the rewards of being a manager is the chance to think creatively and use imagination in solving problems and creating a good work environment. Option A is wrong because making decisions is a core part of every manager's job. Options B and D are not general features of management.

questions.question: Management is needed in organisations of every type and size, at every level, in every work area and in every country. What is this idea called?
questions.explanation: The universality of management is the idea that management is needed everywhere: in all types and sizes of organisations, at all levels, in all work areas and in all countries. Option A, partiality, suggests the opposite, that management applies only in some places. Options B and D are not recognised terms for this idea.

questions.question: Adam Smith argued that division of labour boosts productivity for several reasons. Which of the following was NOT one of them?

options.a: workers become more skilful and dexterous
options.b: less time is wasted switching between tasks
options.d: management keeps strict control over workers' time and motion

questions.explanation: Smith said division of labour raises productivity by increasing workers' skill and dexterity, saving time lost in changing tasks, and encouraging labour-saving inventions and machinery. Strict control of time and motion (option D) is linked to later scientific management, not to Smith. Options A, B and C are all reasons Smith gave.

questions.question: Which of these is an early example of management functions being used in practice?

options.b: the arsenal of Venice, where ships were built

questions.explanation: At the arsenal of Venice, warships were moved along canals and fitted out at each stop, an early example of planning, organising and controlling work, much like an assembly line. Option A is an invention, not a management practice, and options C and D are not examples of organised management of work.

questions.question: In Wealth of Nations, Adam Smith wrote about splitting jobs into narrow, repetitive tasks. What did he call this?
questions.explanation: Division of labour is the breaking down of jobs into narrow, repetitive tasks, and Smith argued it greatly increased productivity. Option A, the assembly line, came much later as one application of the idea. Options B and D are not management terms.

questions.question: The biggest contribution of the Industrial Revolution was replacing human power with
questions.explanation: The Industrial Revolution's major contribution was substituting machine power for human power, which made large factories possible and created a need for managers. Options A and B are forms of energy, but the big change was the use of machines. Option D is not a form of power at all.

questions.question: What did the general administrative theorists concentrate on?

options.a: making the whole organisation more effective
options.b: building mathematical models to improve management
options.c: raising the productivity and efficiency of workers
options.d: stressing the study of human behaviour in organisations

questions.explanation: General administrative theorists such as Fayol and Weber looked at what managers do and what makes good management, with the aim of making the overall organisation more effective. Option C describes scientific management, which focused on individual workers. Option B describes the quantitative approach, and option D describes organisational behaviour.

questions.question: Four management approaches developed during the first half of the twentieth century. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: The four early approaches were scientific management, general administrative theory, the quantitative approach and organisational behaviour. The systems approach (option D) became popular later, as part of more modern thinking about management. Options A, B and C are all among the four early approaches.

questions.question: Where did Frederick Taylor do most of his work?
questions.explanation: Taylor did most of his work at steel companies in Pennsylvania, where he studied how to make shop-floor work more efficient. His pig iron experiment took place in this steel setting. Option C may be tempting because of assembly lines, but those are linked with the car industry, not with Taylor's own studies.

questions.question: Frank and Lillian Gilbreth's work started in which area?
questions.explanation: Frank Gilbreth began by studying bricklaying, cutting the number of motions needed to lay a brick and greatly increasing output. Options B, C and D were not where the Gilbreths' work began.

questions.question: Frank and Lillian Gilbreth were the first to use motion pictures to study

options.a: how workers react in group settings
options.c: how workers react to pay rises
options.d: groups of workers giving each other tasks under pressure

questions.explanation: The Gilbreths filmed workers to study hand and body motions so they could remove wasted movements. They were interested in the efficiency of physical movements, not group behaviour (options A and D) or reactions to pay (option C).

questions.question: Which phrase is most closely linked with scientific management?
questions.explanation: Scientific management, associated with Taylor, used scientific methods to find the "one best way" to do a job. Option C is an economics idea, and option D is more closely linked to the later quality movement.

questions.question: What problem mainly pushed Taylor to develop a more scientific approach to management?
questions.explanation: Taylor was troubled by how inefficient workers were, since they used very different methods and often worked well below their capacity. Option B, effectiveness, is about doing the right things, while Taylor's focus was on doing the work with less waste. Options C and D were not his main concern.

questions.question: Which experiment is probably the best-known example of Taylor's scientific management?
questions.explanation: In the pig iron experiment, Taylor matched the right worker with the right tools, methods and rest breaks, and output rose sharply. Options A, C and D are not studies linked to Taylor.

questions.question: Following his scientific management principles, what kind of pay did Taylor recommend?
questions.explanation: Taylor believed workers should earn more when they produce more, so he recommended incentive pay that ties pay to output. Options A and C pay people the same regardless of how much they produce, which goes against his idea. Option B is still mainly a fixed salary.

questions.question: In scientific management, what workplace issue does a "therblig" deal with?

options.a: the best temperature for efficient work
options.c: the best speed for basic motions
options.d: the ratio of weight to movement

questions.explanation: The Gilbreths created therbligs, a scheme for classifying the basic hand motions used in a task, such as grasping or holding. Option C may look close, but therbligs name and classify the motions themselves, not their speed.

questions.question: What is general administrative theory mainly concerned with?
questions.explanation: General administrative theory looks at the entire organisation, studying what managers do and what makes the whole organisation effective. Option B is tempting because it studies managers' work, but its focus is on the overall organisation, unlike scientific management, which looks at individual workers. Option D is far too narrow.

questions.question: Fayol studied ______ management issues, while Taylor studied ______ management issues.
questions.explanation: Fayol looked at the big picture, the activities of all managers across the organisation (macro), while Taylor focused on first-line work and individual workers (micro). Option A reverses the two, and options C and D wrongly treat their focus as the same.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of Fayol's principles of management?
questions.explanation: Fayol's 14 principles include division of work, unity of command and discipline, so options A, B and C are on the list. Equality is not; the closest principle is equity, which means treating employees kindly and fairly, not treating everyone exactly the same.

questions.question: In Weber's ideal bureaucracy, choosing people for jobs on the basis of their technical qualifications is called
questions.explanation: Formal selection means people are chosen for jobs based on technical qualifications measured through exams, training or education. Option A, career orientation, means managers are career professionals rather than owners. Option C, impersonality, means rules are applied the same way to everyone without personal favour.

questions.question: Bureaucracy is described as a type of organisation marked by
questions.explanation: Weber's bureaucracy combines division of labour, a clearly defined hierarchy, detailed rules and regulations and impersonal relationships. Since A, B and C are all features of bureaucracy, D is the best answer.

questions.question: Which approach to management is also known as operations research or management science?
questions.explanation: The quantitative approach uses quantitative techniques such as statistics, optimisation models and simulations to improve decisions, and it is also called operations research or management science. Option A is the opposite in name and idea, and options C and D are not standard names for an approach to management.

questions.question: The quantitative approach grew out of mathematical and statistical solutions that were developed for

options.a: queue problems at fast-food restaurants in the 1960s
options.b: military problems during World War II

questions.explanation: The quantitative approach came from mathematical and statistical methods developed to solve military problems during World War II, which were later applied to business. Options A, C and D name other times and problems that are not where the approach began.

questions.question: Which technique do managers use to make better decisions about allocating resources?
questions.explanation: Linear programming is a mathematical technique for allocating limited resources in the best way, for example deciding how much of each product to make. Option C is used for inventory decisions, and option D is used to find relationships between variables, not mainly to allocate resources.

questions.question: Decisions about a company's best inventory levels have been strongly shaped by
questions.explanation: The economic order quantity (EOQ) model helps managers work out the best amount of stock to order and keep. Option A is a general tool for allocating resources, and option B deals with timing work, so neither is the main inventory tool.

questions.question: Which of these would NOT be linked with the quantitative approach to management?
questions.explanation: Motivating individuals is a people issue that belongs to the organisational behaviour approach, not the quantitative approach. Options A, B and D are all quantitative tools that help managers plan and decide using numbers and models.

questions.question: Which management approach is most closely associated with concern for employee motivation?
questions.explanation: Organisational behaviour studies the actions of people at work, including motivation, leadership and teamwork. Option C, scientific management, cared about worker output and used incentive pay, but its main focus was efficient methods, not motivation itself. Option A is about rules and structure.

questions.question: Which early supporter of organisational behaviour was concerned about terrible working conditions?
questions.explanation: Robert Owen was a social reformer who was disturbed by harsh working conditions and argued that money spent improving workers' lives was a good investment. Munsterberg (option B) founded industrial psychology, Follett (option C) looked at individual and group behaviour, and Barnard (option D) saw organisations as social systems.

questions.question: Which early supporter of organisational behaviour founded industrial psychology, the scientific study of people at work?
questions.explanation: Hugo Munsterberg created the field of industrial psychology, which uses scientific methods to study people at work, for example in selection and training. Owen (option A) was a social reformer, while Follett (option C) and Barnard (option D) are known for ideas about groups and cooperation.

questions.question: Who was one of the first to see that organisations could be studied in terms of individual and group behaviour?
questions.explanation: Mary Parker Follett was among the first to view organisations through individual and group behaviour, and she believed organisations should be based on a group ethic. Munsterberg (option B) focused on the psychology of individual workers, and Barnard (option D) is known for describing organisations as social and open systems.

questions.question: Which early supporter of organisational behaviour was the first to argue that organisations are open systems?
questions.explanation: Chester Barnard saw organisations as social systems that need human cooperation, and he was the first to argue that they are open systems which interact with their environment. Follett (option C) focused on group behaviour, and Owen (option A) on working conditions.

questions.question: Which four theorists belong to the early organisational behaviour approach?
questions.explanation: The early advocates of organisational behaviour were Robert Owen, Hugo Munsterberg, Mary Parker Follett and Chester Barnard. Options B, C and D each include a classical theorist: Taylor belongs to scientific management, while Fayol and Weber belong to general administrative theory.

questions.question: What was Hugo Munsterberg's major contribution?

options.b: He founded the field of industrial psychology.
options.c: He was interested in individual and group behaviour.
options.d: He saw organisations as social systems that need human cooperation.

questions.explanation: Munsterberg founded industrial psychology, the scientific study of people at work. Option A describes Robert Owen, option C describes Mary Parker Follett, and option D describes Chester Barnard.

questions.question: Munsterberg's work in industrial psychology connects easily with which other management approach?
questions.explanation: Munsterberg used scientific methods to study and select workers, which ties his industrial psychology closely to Taylor's scientific management, since both aimed to raise productivity through the scientific study of work. Option A looks at the whole organisation rather than individual workers, and option B, the quantitative approach, came later and uses mathematical models rather than the study of people. Option C is a later, broader way of viewing organisations.

questions.question: Modern management practices that use work groups to raise productivity can be traced back to which writer?
questions.explanation: Mary Parker Follett believed organisations should be built on a group ethic, and her ideas shaped today's focus on teams and work groups. Barnard (option C) stressed cooperation in organisations, but the group emphasis is most closely linked to Follett. Munsterberg (option D) focused on individual workers' psychology.

questions.question: Which statement reflects Chester Barnard's views on management?

options.a: An employee's ability and motivation are fixed in that person but differ between people.
options.b: To raise productivity, managers should focus on hiring the best employee instead of motivating current staff.
options.c: Productivity is best achieved by shielding the organisation from outside groups.
options.d: Organisations are social systems that need human cooperation.

questions.explanation: Barnard saw organisations as social systems that depend on cooperation among people. Option C contradicts his view, since he believed managers must interact with outside groups such as investors, suppliers and customers. Options A and B do not reflect his ideas.

questions.question: Which set of studies made the most important contribution to the growth of organisational behaviour?
questions.explanation: The Hawthorne studies changed how people saw workers by showing that social and group factors strongly affect behaviour and productivity. Option A refers to scientific management work, which focused on efficiency rather than group behaviour. Options B and C are not the famous early studies.

questions.question: What were the Hawthorne studies first designed to investigate?

options.a: how productive groups are compared with individuals
options.c: how lighting levels affect employee productivity
options.d: how cooperative versus competitive settings affect productivity

questions.explanation: The Hawthorne studies started as an experiment on how different lighting (illumination) levels affected workers' productivity. The surprising results led researchers to study group and social factors later, which is why option A may seem tempting, but that was not the original aim.

questions.question: Which scientist is most closely linked with the Hawthorne studies?
questions.explanation: Elton Mayo led the later stages of the Hawthorne studies, which highlighted the influence of social factors on productivity. Barnard (option D) was an early organisational behaviour thinker, but he did not run the Hawthorne studies.

questions.question: Which statement describes one finding of the Hawthorne studies?

options.a: Social norms or group standards are the main drivers of individual work behaviour.
options.b: Money matters more than the group in determining individual productivity.
options.c: Employee behaviour and feelings move in opposite directions.

questions.explanation: The Hawthorne studies found that group norms and social standards strongly shape how individuals behave at work. Option B is the opposite of the finding, since money turned out to be less important than group pressures. Option C is wrong because behaviour and sentiments were found to be closely related, not opposed.

questions.question: Workforce diversity covers differences among employees in
questions.explanation: Workforce diversity means a workforce made up of people who differ in characteristics such as gender, race, ethnicity and age. Since A, B and C are all examples of these differences, D is correct.

questions.question: TQM differs from earlier management theories because, under TQM, costs can be reduced while also

options.c: letting special teams handle reworked output

questions.explanation: TQM holds that focusing on quality and continuous improvement lowers costs and raises productivity at the same time, because less work is wasted or done over. Letting special teams handle reworked output (option C) is exactly the kind of rework TQM tries to eliminate, and raising prices or laying employees off (options A and D) are not part of the TQM idea.

questions.question: A learning organisation builds the ability to

options.a: add new training programmes even when rivals are going bankrupt
options.b: accept the usual wisdom of its industry

questions.explanation: A learning organisation is one that has developed the capacity to continuously learn, adapt and change. Option D is something learning organisations often do, but teamwork alone does not define them. Option B is the opposite, since learning organisations question conventional wisdom.

questions.question: ______ is the process of building businesses to take advantage of trends and changes that nobody else has noticed yet.
questions.explanation: Entrepreneurship is about spotting opportunities, such as trends and changes others have not seen, and starting businesses to pursue them. Option D, e-commerce, is a way of selling online, not the process of creating ventures. Option B is about splitting work into tasks.

questions.question: Knowledge management means encouraging organisational members to

options.a: raise the education level of the average employee
options.b: create new training programmes to help newcomers learn their jobs
options.c: set up an in-house corporate university, like the one McDonald's runs
options.d: systematically collect information and share it with others

questions.explanation: Knowledge management builds a learning culture in which members systematically gather knowledge and share it so the organisation performs better. Options A, B and C involve training or education, which may help, but they are not the core idea of gathering and sharing knowledge.

questions.question: Which part of e-business covers its sales and marketing side?
questions.explanation: E-commerce is the sales and marketing part of e-business, where products are bought and sold over the internet. Option A, an intranet, is an internal communication network, and option D, an extranet, links an organisation with outside partners such as suppliers.

questions.question: Which two people were pioneers of total quality management?
questions.explanation: W. Edwards Deming and Joseph Juran are the best-known pioneers of total quality management. Fayol and Weber (option A) were general administrative theorists, Taylor and Gilbreth (option B) belong to scientific management, and Owen and Munsterberg (option C) were early organisational behaviour thinkers.

questions.question: Three key themes stand out in the definition of entrepreneurship. Which of these is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: The three themes in entrepreneurship are the pursuit of opportunities, innovation and growth. Failure is a real risk for new ventures, which makes option C tempting, but it is not one of the three defining themes.

questions.question: ______ is the broad term for how an organisation does its work through electronic (internet-based) links with its key constituencies so as to reach its goals efficiently and effectively.
questions.explanation: E-business is the comprehensive term for using internet-based linkages with key groups such as customers, suppliers and employees to do the organisation's work. Option A, e-commerce, is narrower, since it covers only the sales and marketing part of e-business.

questions.question: In which category of e-business involvement does an organisation use the internet to carry out its traditional business functions better, without selling anything online?
questions.explanation: An e-business enabled organisation uses the internet to perform its traditional functions better, for example sharing information with staff or customers, but does not sell online. Option A, e-business enhanced, describes a traditional organisation that adds e-business capabilities, usually e-commerce. Option C describes a firm whose whole existence depends on the internet.

questions.question: What is an internal communication system that runs on internet technology and can be used only by an organisation's employees, for example to reach staff around the world?
questions.explanation: An intranet is an internal network built on internet technology that only the organisation's own employees can access. Option A, an extranet, also lets approved outsiders such as suppliers and customers in. Option B, a local area network, connects computers in one location but is not defined as an internet-based company system.

questions.question: An organisation whose whole existence depends on and revolves around the internet falls into which category of e-business involvement?
questions.explanation: A total e-business organisation exists because of the internet and is built entirely around it, such as an online-only marketplace. Options A and B describe traditional organisations that use the internet to add to or improve what they already do.

questions.question: The second theme of entrepreneurship involves changing, revolutionising or transforming things, or introducing new products, services or ways of doing business. What is this theme?
questions.explanation: Innovation is the entrepreneurship theme about changing, revolutionising and transforming, or introducing new products, services or methods. Option D, technology, may help innovation, but it is not the name of the theme.

questions.question: What general term describes the quality revolution that spread through both business and the public sector in the 1980s and 1990s?
questions.explanation: Total quality management (TQM) is the general term for the quality revolution of the 1980s and 1990s, built on continuous improvement and meeting customer needs. Options A, C and D are not real management terms.

questions.question: ______ means building a learning culture where members systematically gather knowledge and share it with others so the organisation performs better.
questions.explanation: Knowledge management is about creating a learning culture in which people systematically collect knowledge and share it to improve performance. Options A, B and C do not describe this gathering and sharing of knowledge.

questions.question: ______ is a management philosophy driven by continual improvement and by responding to what customers need and expect.
questions.explanation: Quality management, often called TQM, is a philosophy based on continual improvement and responding to customer needs and expectations. Option D, knowledge management, is about gathering and sharing knowledge, not about customer-driven improvement. Option B concerns meaning and purpose at work.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: One major challenge faced by Nigerian managers is:
questions.explanation: Frequent power outages are a well-known problem for Nigerian businesses, raising costs and disrupting operations. Options A and C describe advantages, not challenges, and D is not typical of the Nigerian business environment.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: Corruption affects management in Nigeria by:
questions.explanation: Corruption slows decisions, for example through demands for bribes and favours, and it wastes resources, so both B and C are correct. Option A is wrong because corruption reduces transparency rather than promoting it.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: Poor infrastructure in Nigeria can lead to:
questions.explanation: Poor roads, unreliable power and weak transport make it hard to produce goods and get them to customers on time, so delays in production and distribution follow directly. Option C is wrong because poor infrastructure raises transport and energy costs rather than lowering them. Options A and D are benefits, so poor infrastructure would not cause them.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: A solution to the lack of skilled labor in Nigeria is:
questions.explanation: Training and skill development programs build the skills that are missing in the workforce. Option A, higher salaries, may attract workers but does not create new skills. Hiring only foreign workers (C) and delaying deadlines (D) avoid the problem without solving it.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: Bureaucratic delays can be minimized by:
questions.explanation: Technology such as digital records and online processes speeds up paperwork and approvals, which cuts bureaucratic delays. Option B is unlawful and risky, and C can add more red tape. Option D does not deal with the cause of the delay.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: Which technological solution can improve Nigerian businesses?
questions.explanation: Social media lets businesses reach many customers cheaply and quickly, which makes it a practical technological improvement. Manual record-keeping and paper-based communication (B and C) are old methods, and D would hold staff back.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: An ethical approach in management promotes:
questions.explanation: Ethics is a set of principles that defines right and wrong conduct, and an ethical approach to management promotes transparency and fairness. Option A is unethical, C is unrelated, and D goes against the respect for employees that ethics requires.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: A key challenge in the Nigerian labor market is:
questions.explanation: Weak educational standards leave many job seekers without the skills employers need, which is a real challenge in the Nigerian labour market. Options A, C and D describe favourable conditions, not challenges.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: The Nigerian government can support managers by:
questions.explanation: Government can help managers most by providing good infrastructure such as power, roads and communications, which lowers business costs. Options A, C and D would all make business harder rather than easier.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: Corruption can be reduced by:
questions.explanation: Promoting ethical practices, through a code of ethics, ethical leadership and training, is how organizations reduce corruption. Options B, C and D create the very conditions in which corruption grows.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: Which view of management describes a situation in which managers are directly responsible for a company's success or failure?
questions.explanation: The omnipotent view holds that managers are directly responsible for an organization's success or failure. Option C, the symbolic view, says the opposite: much of what happens is due to outside forces the manager cannot control. A and B are not recognised views of management.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: Which event triggered the recession that began in 2008?

options.a: Renters were unable to find available housing
options.b: Consumers were unwilling to purchase electronic equipment
options.c: Businesses were unable to make loan payments
options.d: Homeowners were unable to make mortgage payments

questions.explanation: The 2008 Great Recession started in the mortgage market, when many homeowners could not keep up with their mortgage payments. That turmoil then spread to the wider credit markets and to businesses. So business loan problems, option C, came after, not first.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: Which of the following contributed most to many companies becoming highly leveraged in the lead-up to the economic downturn in 2008?
questions.explanation: Low interest rates made borrowing cheap, so many companies took on large amounts of debt, becoming highly leveraged, before 2008. Option D is the reverse, since high rates discourage borrowing. A and B are wrong because credit was easy to get at the time.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: The term "corporate social responsibility" refers to:
questions.explanation: Corporate social responsibility means a company aims to do the right things and act in ways that are good for society. Option A, legal compliance only, is the bare minimum, and C and D focus only on the company's own financial interests.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: Which of the following is an external factor affecting management?
questions.explanation: The external environment is made up of forces outside the organization that affect its performance, and government regulations are a clear example. Options A, B and D (employee skills, organizational culture and work processes) all exist inside the organization, so they are internal factors.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: The business environment includes which of the following factors?
questions.explanation: The business environment includes both internal and external factors, and the external part covers economic, social, political and technological forces. Since A, B and C each name real parts of the environment, all of the above is correct.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: The external environment of a business consists of factors that are:
questions.explanation: The external environment is made up of forces outside the organization, such as the economy and government, which managers cannot directly control. That is why they are not controllable (A), and they are often unpredictable (C) and unavoidable (D).

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: Which of the following is not a component of the microenvironment?
questions.explanation: Government policies are part of the macro (general) environment because they affect all businesses broadly. Customers (A), suppliers (B) and competitors (D) deal directly with the firm, which makes them part of its microenvironment.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: The legal environment of a business includes:
questions.explanation: The legal environment is made up of laws and rules that govern business, such as trade regulations. Employee relations (B), production techniques (C) and advertising methods (D) are internal management matters rather than legal factors.

questions.topic: The Management Environment and Integrative Managerial Issues
questions.question: Which factor is part of the macro environment?
questions.explanation: Technological change is a broad force outside the firm that affects whole industries, so it belongs to the macro environment. Suppliers (A), competitors (B) and customers (D) interact directly with the business and form its microenvironment.
