questions.explanation: In a divisional structure, each division manager is responsible for results, which is its strength, but each division often has its own staff and resources, which causes duplication. Option B is efficient precisely because it avoids duplication. Option A's weakness is dependence on one person.

questions.question: The ______________ structure is a more advanced form of the matrix in which employees work continuously on assignments aimed at completing tasks.
questions.explanation: In a project structure, employees continuously work on projects instead of returning to functional departments, which takes the matrix idea further. Option B is a traditional structure built around functions. Options A and C are not organizational structures.

questions.question: Some organizational theorists argue that an organization's ability to __________ may be its only lasting source of competitive advantage.
questions.explanation: The argument is that the ability to learn and to apply that learning may be the only sustainable competitive advantage, so both A and B are needed and D is correct. Option C, change, is related, but the claim is specifically about learning and applying it.

questions.question: Organizational learning cannot happen without ____________.
questions.explanation: Learning depends on sharing information, so without information an organization cannot learn. Options A, B and D can support learning, but information is the essential ingredient.

questions.question: Arranging and structuring work to accomplish an organization's goals is the management function called:
questions.explanation: Organizing is the function that arranges and structures work so the organization can reach its goals. Option B, planning, is about setting the goals and plans in the first place, which comes before organizing.

questions.question: In the sequence of management functions, organizing comes directly after:
questions.explanation: Organizing follows planning: once goals and plans are set, managers arrange and structure the work needed to achieve them. Option C, leading, comes after the work has been organized, not before it.

questions.question: The formal framework by which job tasks are divided, grouped and coordinated is known as the:
questions.explanation: Organizational structure is the formal framework that divides, groups and coordinates job tasks. Option A, the organizational chart, is only the picture of that structure, not the framework itself.

questions.question: The picture or diagram that shows an organization's structure is called the:
questions.explanation: An organizational chart is the visual picture of an organization's structure. Option A, organizational design, is the process of developing or changing the structure, not the drawing of it.

questions.question: Organizational design is best described as:

options.a: dividing tasks into separate, narrow jobs
options.b: developing or changing an organization's structure
options.c: grouping jobs on the basis of customer needs
options.d: drawing a picture of the reporting lines

questions.explanation: Organizational design means developing or changing an organization's structure, and it involves decisions on all six structural elements. Option D describes the organizational chart, which only pictures the structure.

questions.question: Complete the analogy: organizing is to structure as planning is to:
questions.explanation: Just as organizing produces a structure, planning produces goals, so planning is linked to goal setting. Option B, coordination, is one of the purposes of organizing, not the output of planning.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of organizing?

options.a: It divides work into specific jobs and departments
options.c: It allocates and deploys organizational resources
options.d: It establishes formal lines of authority

questions.explanation: Creating services is not one of the purposes of organizing. Organizing divides work, assigns tasks, coordinates activities, clusters jobs into units, sets up relationships and authority lines, and allocates resources, so options A and the others are all genuine purposes.

questions.question: Which of the following is a purpose of organizing?
questions.explanation: Clustering jobs into units is one of the purposes of organizing. Option C, setting long-term goals, belongs to planning, while comparing performance with standards is controlling and inspiring employees is leading.

questions.question: How many purposes of organizing are usually listed?
questions.explanation: Seven purposes are listed: dividing work, assigning tasks, coordinating tasks, clustering jobs, establishing relationships, establishing formal lines of authority, and allocating resources. Option C, six, is easy to confuse with the six elements of organizational design.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a principle of organizing?
questions.explanation: Publicity is not a principle of organizing. Unity of objective, scalar chain and parity of authority and responsibility (options C and the others) are all genuine principles that shape how a structure is built.

questions.question: The principle of organizing which holds that the structure must serve the organization's goals is:
questions.explanation: Unity of objective says the structure exists to serve the organization's goals. Option C, unity of command, sounds similar but means that each person has only one boss.

questions.question: A structure that reaches its objectives at the lowest cost and with the least waste satisfies the principle of:
questions.explanation: The efficiency principle says a structure should achieve its objectives at the lowest cost and with the least waste. Option D, unity of objective, is about the structure serving the goals, not about cost or waste.

questions.question: The principle of organizing that calls for a clear line of authority from the top of the organization to the bottom is the:
questions.explanation: The scalar chain is the principle of a clear line of authority running from top to bottom. Option B, unity of command, is related but narrower: it says each person should have only one boss.

questions.question: The principle of parity of authority and responsibility means that:

options.a: authority must be held only by top managers
options.b: authority and responsibility must be in balance
options.c: a manager can supervise only a few people
options.d: each person must report to only one boss

questions.explanation: Parity of authority and responsibility means the two must be in balance, so a person given a duty also gets enough authority to carry it out. Option D describes unity of command, a different principle.

questions.question: Work specialization is also known as:
questions.explanation: Work specialization, where each employee does part of an activity rather than the whole, is also called division of labour. Option B, departmentalization, is about grouping jobs together, not dividing tasks into jobs.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a likely result of taking work specialization too far?
questions.explanation: Too much specialization leads to boredom, fatigue, stress, poor quality, absenteeism and high turnover, so higher product quality is the odd one out. Options A and the others are all listed problems of over-specialization.

questions.question: A manufacturer in Ota gives each machine operator a wider range of tasks instead of one repetitive step. This change is best described as:
questions.explanation: Giving workers more tasks means each person does more of the whole activity, which reduces work specialization. Option D is the opposite: increasing specialization would narrow each job to fewer tasks.

questions.question: Early managers viewed work specialization as:

options.c: a threat to unity of command
options.d: a major cause of employee turnover

questions.explanation: Early managers saw work specialization as an endless way to raise productivity. Option D reflects a later realization that specialization taken too far causes problems such as high turnover.

questions.question: A consumer goods company in Ota sets up separate departments for beverages, snacks and detergents, each with its own staff. This is:
questions.explanation: Grouping jobs by product line, so each unit has everything needed for one product, is product departmentalization. Option C, functional, would group jobs by tasks such as finance, marketing and production instead.

questions.question: A Lagos bank organizes its staff into retail banking, corporate banking and government banking units. Which type of departmentalization is this?
questions.explanation: Grouping jobs by the type of customer served and their needs is customer departmentalization. Option C, product, would group by product line or service, but here the units are defined by who the bank serves.

questions.question: At a licensing office, applicants move from a forms section to a testing section and then to a payment section. The office is using:
questions.explanation: When units follow the flow of customers or products through a sequence, the grouping is process departmentalization. Option A, functional, groups by the tasks performed, but the clue here is the step-by-step flow.

questions.question: A company in Ikeja has separate finance, marketing, production and human resources departments. This grouping is:
questions.explanation: Finance, marketing, production and HR are functions, so grouping jobs this way is functional departmentalization. Option A, product, would create units around product lines such as beverages or snacks.

questions.question: Which type of departmentalization groups everything needed to make and sell one product line into a single unit?
questions.explanation: Product departmentalization brings together everything needed for one product. Option C, functional, instead groups people with similar skills, such as all accountants in one department.

questions.question: How many types of departmentalization are there?
questions.explanation: There are five types: functional, geographic, product, process and customer. Option A, four, is easy to choose by mistake because it matches the number of contingency factors.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a type of departmentalization?
questions.explanation: The five types of departmentalization are functional, geographic, product, process and customer, so hierarchical is not one of them. Options C and the others are all genuine bases for grouping jobs.

questions.question: A cross-functional team is best described as:

options.a: a team of people drawn from different functions
options.b: a team made up only of top managers
options.c: a team set up for one geographic region
options.d: a team of staff from one functional department

questions.explanation: A cross-functional team brings together people from different functions, such as designers, production workers and salespeople. Option B is wrong because a team from a single department is not cross-functional.

questions.question: Customer departmentalization has become more important today mainly because it helps firms to:

options.b: track customer needs and respond to changes in them
options.d: reduce the number of management levels

questions.explanation: Customer departmentalization helps firms keep track of what customers need and respond quickly when those needs change, which matters in a competitive environment. Option D relates to span of control, not to how jobs are grouped.

questions.question: Which element of organizational design shows who reports to whom?
questions.explanation: The chain of command is the unbroken line of authority from top to bottom, and it shows who reports to whom. Option B, span of control, tells you how many people a manager supervises, not the reporting line itself.

questions.question: A teller at a Lagos bank receives conflicting instructions from both the branch manager and the regional operations head. Which principle is being violated?
questions.explanation: Unity of command says each person should report to only one manager, so taking orders from two bosses breaks it. Option C, span of control, is about how many people one manager supervises, not how many bosses one employee has.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the chain of command from span of control?

options.a: Chain of command is the line of authority; span of control is how many people one boss supervises
options.b: Chain of command is a staff function; span of control is a line function
options.c: Chain of command means one boss per person; span of control means decisions are made at the top
options.d: Chain of command is how many people one boss supervises; span of control is the line of authority

questions.explanation: The chain of command is the line of authority, while span of control is the number of people one boss supervises. Option D simply swaps the two definitions, which is a common trap.

questions.question: Authority that lets a manager direct the work of an employee and follows the chain of command from top to bottom is:
questions.explanation: Line authority entitles a manager to direct an employee's work and runs down the chain of command. Option C, staff authority, is advisory: it supports and assists line managers rather than directing work.

questions.question: Authority that supports, assists, advises and reduces the load of line managers is called:
questions.explanation: Staff authority is advisory: it supports, assists and advises line managers and lightens their load. Option C, line authority, is the right to direct the work of employees down the chain of command.

questions.question: The legal adviser of a manufacturing company in Ota advises managers on contracts but does not direct production workers. The adviser holds:
questions.explanation: A legal adviser supports and advises line managers, which is staff authority. Option B, line authority, would apply to someone like a production manager who directs supervisors' work.

questions.question: A production manager who directs the work of the supervisors under her exercises:
questions.explanation: Directing the work of subordinates along the chain of command is line authority. Option D, staff authority, belongs to advisers such as HR specialists who support line managers rather than direct them.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts authority and power?

options.a: Authority comes from many bases; power comes only from position
options.b: Authority is the broader concept; power is part of authority
options.c: Authority is a capacity to influence; power is a right
options.d: Authority is a right; power is a capacity to influence decisions

questions.explanation: Authority is a right that comes from a position, while power is the capacity to influence decisions and can come from many places. Option C reverses the two ideas.

questions.question: Which is the broader concept, authority or power?

options.a: Neither, because they mean exactly the same thing
options.b: Power, because authority is part of power
options.c: Authority, because it comes from many bases
options.d: Authority, because power is part of authority

questions.explanation: Power is the broader concept, and authority is just one part of it. Option D reverses this, but a person can have power without any formal authority.

questions.question: The legitimacy of a manager's authority comes from:
questions.explanation: Authority is legitimate because it is attached to the position. Option B, personal charm, describes referent power, and the other two options describe expert and coercive power.

questions.question: The head of procurement at a university resigns. What happens to the authority she held?

options.a: It leaves the university with her
options.b: It passes automatically to the registrar
options.c: It is divided equally among her staff
options.d: It stays with the post for her successor

questions.explanation: Authority belongs to the position, not the person, so when a manager leaves, the authority stays with the post. Option A would only make sense if authority were personal, which it is not.

questions.question: A secretary in a Lagos firm controls who gets to see the managing director and when. She has no formal authority, yet many staff seek her favour. This shows that:

options.a: staff authority is the same as line authority
options.c: authority belongs to the person, not the post
options.d: a person can have power without authority

questions.explanation: Controlling access to the boss's diary gives the secretary influence even though her post carries little formal authority, so she has power without authority. Option B is wrong because power, not authority, is the broader concept.

questions.question: How many sources of power are commonly identified?
questions.explanation: Five are identified: legitimate, coercive, reward, expert and referent. Option B, four, is a common slip because it matches the number of contingency factors.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the five bases of power?
questions.explanation: The five bases of power are legitimate, coercive, reward, expert and referent, so functional power is not one of them. Options A and the others are all genuine bases.

questions.question: Power that comes from the ability to punish or control is:
questions.explanation: Coercive power rests on the ability to punish or control others. Option B, reward power, is its opposite: it comes from the ability to give something people value.

questions.question: A supervisor in a Port Harcourt firm gets cooperation mainly because she can recommend bonuses and give public praise. She is using:
questions.explanation: Influence based on the ability to give something valued, such as pay or praise, is reward power. Option C, coercive power, would rest on the ability to punish, not to reward.

questions.question: Staff in a university department always follow the advice of a junior IT officer on systems matters because of his special knowledge. His influence is:
questions.explanation: Influence based on special skill or knowledge is expert power. Option C, legitimate power, comes from a formal position, and a junior officer has little of that.

questions.question: Power based on personal traits that make others like or admire a person is:
questions.explanation: Referent power comes from personal traits that make others like or admire you. Option C, expert power, rests on special skill or knowledge rather than on being liked or admired.

questions.question: Which base of power is the same as authority?
questions.explanation: Legitimate power comes from one's position, which is exactly what authority is. Option A, referent power, comes from personal traits that others admire, not from the post.

questions.question: Assigning authority to another person to carry out specific duties is called:
questions.explanation: Delegation means assigning authority to another person to carry out specific duties. Option C, decentralization, is broader: it describes lower-level managers taking part in decisions across the organization.

questions.question: Why does the chain of command matter less in organizations today?

options.d: Wider use of unity of command

questions.explanation: Information technology lets employees get information and communicate without going through each level, and empowered employees make more decisions themselves, so the chain of command matters less. Option D is wrong because unity of command is part of the traditional chain of command idea, not a reason it has weakened.

questions.question: An organization has 4,096 operative staff. With a span of control of 8, how many managers does it need?
questions.explanation: With a span of 8 the organization needs 585 managers and has 5 levels including operatives. Option C, 1,365, is the number needed with a narrower span of 4, which shows how narrow spans add managers.

questions.question: An organization with 4,096 operative staff uses a span of control of 4. How many levels (including operatives) will it have?
questions.explanation: A span of 4 gives 7 levels, which produces a tall structure. Option B, five levels, is what the same organization would have with a wider span of 8.

questions.question: A narrow span of control produces which kind of structure?
questions.explanation: A narrow span means each manager supervises few people, so more levels are needed and the structure becomes tall. Option C, flat, results from a wide span.

questions.question: If a manager's span of control becomes too wide, what is the main risk?

options.a: The structure becomes taller and slower
options.b: The organization needs many more managers
options.c: Costs rise because of extra management levels
options.d: Effectiveness falls because staff get too little supervision

questions.explanation: A wider span is more efficient, but if it gets too wide, effectiveness falls because each employee receives too little supervision. Options B and the next one describe the effects of a narrow span, not a wide one.

questions.question: Which situation would allow a manager in a Lagos bank to supervise more people effectively?

options.b: Staff are spread across distant branches
options.c: Staff do complex and very different tasks
options.d: Staff are well trained and follow standardized procedures

questions.explanation: Skilled staff who follow standardized procedures need less supervision, so a wider span works. Option A, new and inexperienced staff, would call for a narrower span because they need more guidance.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the factors that decide the right span of control?

options.d: Sophistication of the management information system

questions.explanation: The span of control depends on employee training and experience, similarity and complexity of tasks, location of employees, use of standardized procedures and the sophistication of the information system, so the age of the organization is not among them. Options C and the others are genuine factors.

questions.question: Which of the following is a disadvantage of a wide span of control?

options.b: Decisions move slowly through many levels
options.d: The manager has many people to control

questions.explanation: With a wide span, one manager has many people to control, which is its main weakness. Options A and the others are actually problems of a narrow span, which needs more managers and more levels.

questions.question: Organizations have moved towards wider spans of control. Which of the following is NOT a reason for this trend?

options.c: To add more levels of management

questions.explanation: Wider spans are used to cut costs, speed up decisions, increase flexibility and empower employees, and they reduce rather than add management levels. Options B and the others are genuine reasons for the trend.

questions.question: When lower-level managers give input or actually make decisions, the organization is practising:
questions.explanation: Decentralization means lower-level managers provide input or make decisions themselves. Option D, centralization, is the opposite: decision making stays at the upper levels.

questions.question: Increasing the decision-making discretion of workers is called:
questions.explanation: Employee empowerment means giving workers more freedom to make decisions. Option B, formalization, does the opposite by guiding jobs through rules and procedures.

questions.question: In a state hospital, every decision, however small, must be signed off by the unit head. This hospital is best described as:
questions.explanation: When decisions are concentrated at the top, here with the unit head, the organization is centralized. Option A, decentralized, would mean lower-level staff give input or make decisions themselves.

questions.question: Which of the following situations favours more centralization?

options.a: The organization is facing a crisis
options.b: The company is spread out geographically
options.c: The decisions to be made are minor
options.d: Lower-level managers are capable and want a say

questions.explanation: Centralization fits when the organization faces a crisis, as well as when the environment is stable, the company is large and decisions are significant. Option D and the remaining options are conditions that favour decentralization.

questions.question: Which of the following situations favours more decentralization?

options.b: The environment is complex and uncertain

questions.explanation: A complex and uncertain environment calls for decisions to be made closer to the action, which favours decentralization. Option A, a stable environment, is one of the conditions that suits centralization.

questions.question: A bank has branches spread across many states, an open culture and capable branch managers who want a say. The design that best suits it is:
questions.explanation: Geographic spread, an open culture and capable lower-level managers who want input all favour decentralization. Option A, centralization, suits stable settings and less experienced lower-level managers.

questions.question: A university department requires every request to be made on a standard form and handled according to a detailed rulebook. This department has:
questions.explanation: Formalization is the degree to which jobs are standardized and governed by rules and procedures, so a detailed rulebook and standard forms mean high formalization. Option B would describe a department with few rules and much employee discretion.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of an organic organization?
questions.explanation: Organic organizations have wide spans of control, so narrow spans do not fit. Options D and the others, cross-hierarchical teams, free flow of information and low formalization, are all organic features.

questions.question: Which pair of features both describe a mechanistic organization?

options.b: Decentralization and wide spans of control
options.c: Free flow of information and cross-hierarchical teams
options.d: Centralization and a clear chain of command

questions.explanation: Mechanistic organizations are centralized and have a clear chain of command, along with narrow spans and high formalization. Option B and the other options list organic features.

questions.question: How many contingency factors are said to decide the right organizational structure?
questions.explanation: The four contingency factors are strategy, size, technology and environmental uncertainty. Option B, three, may be confused with the three strategic focuses of innovation, cost minimization and imitation.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the contingency factors that decide the right structure?
questions.explanation: The contingency factors are strategy, size, technology and environmental uncertainty, while formalization is one of the six elements of design that those factors shape. Options D and the others are genuine contingency factors.

questions.question: A company whose strategy is to keep bringing out meaningful and unique new products should adopt which structure?
questions.explanation: An innovation strategy needs flexibility and free flow of ideas, so it fits an organic structure. Option D, mechanistic, suits a cost-minimization strategy that needs tight control.

questions.question: A Lagos-based manufacturer competes mainly by keeping costs tightly controlled. Which structure best fits this strategy?
questions.explanation: A cost-minimization strategy needs tight control and efficiency, which a mechanistic structure provides. Option A, organic, fits an innovation strategy instead.

questions.question: A firm that copies market leaders to lower its risk and gain profit is following an imitation strategy. Which structure suits it?

options.b: A mix of mechanistic and organic

questions.explanation: An imitation strategy combines the tight cost control of a mechanistic design with the flexibility of an organic one, so it suits a mix of both. Option A fits a pure innovation strategy.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three focuses of strategic frameworks that shape structure?
questions.explanation: The three strategic focuses that shape structure are innovation, cost minimization and imitation. Diversification is not among them, while options B and the others are all part of the framework.

questions.question: Larger organizations tend to have more of all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Larger organizations have more specialization, departmentalization, centralization and rules, which makes them more mechanistic. They do not tend to have more decentralization; options A and the others are features that grow with size.

questions.question: Who studied small manufacturing firms to find out how technology relates to structure?
questions.explanation: Joan Woodward studied small manufacturing firms in southern England and grouped them by the technology they used. Option D, Henri Fayol, is linked with principles such as unity of command, not the technology studies.

questions.question: In Woodward's study, firms that produced units or small batches of custom work used:
questions.explanation: Unit production means making units or small batches, often custom work, and it is the least complex type. Option D, mass production, refers to large-batch production.

questions.question: In Woodward's classification, which type of production is the least technically complex?
questions.explanation: Unit production, which makes units or small batches, is the least complex. Option C, mass production, is moderately complex, and process production is the most complex.

questions.question: Which pairing of Woodward's technology type and best structure is correct?
questions.explanation: Woodward found that unit and process production work best with organic structures, while mass production works best with a mechanistic one. Option C is the classic trap: mass production goes with mechanistic, not organic.

questions.question: A refinery in Port Harcourt runs a continuous-process operation around the clock. In Woodward's terms, its technology is:
questions.explanation: Continuous-process production is what Woodward called process production, the most technically complex type. Option B, mass production, means large-batch production, not a continuous flow.

questions.question: A Lagos fintech firm faces rapidly changing regulation and competitors that release new products often. Which structure suits this environment?
questions.explanation: A dynamic, uncertain environment calls for a flexible, adaptive organic structure. Option B, mechanistic, suits stable environments where tight control and efficiency matter most.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the forces pushing firms to become more organic?
questions.explanation: Global competition, faster innovation by rivals, knowledge management and customers demanding higher quality and faster delivery all push firms towards organic designs. A stable, predictable market would favour a mechanistic design instead, while options B and the others are genuine pressures.

questions.question: Which of the following is a weakness of the simple structure?

options.c: Relying on one person is risky

questions.explanation: A simple structure centralizes authority in one person, which is risky, and it does not suit a growing firm. Option A, duplication of resources, is the weakness of the divisional structure.

questions.question: Which of the following is a strength of the simple structure?

options.b: It focuses division managers on results
options.c: It is fast, flexible and cheap to run
options.d: It achieves cost savings from specialization

questions.explanation: The simple structure is fast, flexible, cheap to run and has clear accountability. Option D, cost savings from specialization, is the strength of the functional structure.

questions.question: In which structure do functions chase their own goals and lose sight of the organization as a whole?
questions.explanation: In a functional structure, each department of related specialists can pursue its own goals and forget the bigger picture, and specialists may become isolated. Option D, divisional, has a different weakness: duplication of activities and resources.

questions.question: The main strength of a functional structure is:

options.d: focus on results by division managers

questions.explanation: Grouping similar specialists together gives cost savings from specialization, and people with similar tasks work together. Option D, focus on results, is the strength of the divisional structure.

questions.question: A Lagos conglomerate runs separate, self-contained units for foods, cement and sugar, each with a manager responsible for its own results. This is a:
questions.explanation: Separate, autonomous business units, each responsible for its own product and results, form a divisional structure. Option D, functional, would group jobs by occupational specialty instead of by business unit.

questions.question: As a business grows, its structure typically moves through which sequence?
questions.explanation: A simple structure often grows into a functional one and then into a divisional one as the firm takes on more employees. Option D wrongly places the functional structure before the simple one.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a traditional organizational design?
questions.explanation: The traditional designs are simple, functional and divisional, while the matrix is a contemporary design. Options A and the others are all traditional.

questions.question: Which of the following is a contemporary organizational design?
questions.explanation: The project structure, along with team, matrix, boundaryless and learning designs, is contemporary. Option D, the simple structure, is a traditional design together with functional and divisional.

questions.question: Which of the following is a weakness of the team structure?

options.a: Functions lose sight of the whole
options.c: There is no clear chain of command

questions.explanation: In a team structure there is no clear chain of command, and teams are under heavy pressure to perform. Option B, duplication of resources, is the weakness of the divisional structure.

questions.question: Which of the following is a strength of the team structure?
questions.explanation: Team structures involve and empower employees and reduce barriers between functional areas. Option A, clear accountability to one owner, is a strength of the simple structure.

questions.question: In a matrix structure, each employee reports to which two bosses?

options.a: The chief executive and the board chairman
options.b: The line manager and the staff adviser
options.c: The division manager and the team leader
options.d: The functional manager and the project manager

questions.explanation: In a matrix, each employee has two bosses: the manager of their functional department and the manager of the project they are assigned to. Option A names top governance roles, not the dual reporting of a matrix.

questions.question: Which of the following is a weakness of the matrix structure?

options.b: Relying on one person is risky

questions.explanation: Matrix structures often suffer task and personality conflicts, and assigning people to projects is complex. Option D is wrong because the matrix is actually a fluid, flexible design with faster decision making.

questions.question: Which of the following is a strength of the matrix structure?

options.a: No need to assign people to projects
options.c: A fluid, flexible design that can respond to change

questions.explanation: The matrix is a fluid, flexible design that can respond to change and allows faster decisions. Option B is wrong because the matrix breaks unity of command by giving employees two bosses.

questions.question: At an engineering consultancy in Abuja, staff move from one project to the next and have no formal department to return to between projects. This is a:
questions.explanation: In a project structure, employees work continuously on projects and carry their skills to the next one, with no formal departments to return to. Option A, matrix, is tempting, but in a matrix employees still belong to a functional department.

questions.question: What mainly distinguishes a project structure from a matrix structure?

options.a: In a project structure there are no formal departments to return to
options.b: In a project structure each employee has two bosses
options.c: In a project structure authority is held by one person
options.d: In a project structure work is grouped by function only

questions.explanation: A project structure is an advanced form of matrix in which employees have no home department to return to after a project. Option B describes the matrix itself, where each employee has a functional boss and a project boss.

questions.question: In a boundaryless organization, the horizontal boundaries are those:

options.b: between the firm and its suppliers

questions.explanation: Horizontal boundaries separate functions, while vertical boundaries separate levels. Option D describes vertical boundaries, and boundaries with suppliers and customers are external.

questions.question: Boundaries in an organization can be minimized or removed by using:
questions.explanation: Virtual and network designs remove or minimize boundaries by relying on outside specialists and suppliers. Option B lists traditional designs, which keep firm boundaries in place.

questions.question: How many forms of boundaryless organization are usually identified?
questions.explanation: Three forms are identified: virtual, network and modular. Option B, two, is tempting because only virtual and network designs are often mentioned together, but the modular form is the third.

questions.question: A Lagos logistics company keeps its own staff for core operations but outsources accounting, payroll and HR to outside firms. This is best described as a:
questions.explanation: A network organization uses its own staff for some work and outsources major or non-core functions to outside suppliers so it can focus on what it does best. Option B, virtual, relies on outside specialists hired temporarily for opportunities as they arise, rather than ongoing outsourcing of functions.

questions.question: A consulting firm in Victoria Island has five full-time staff and hires outside specialists temporarily whenever a new contract comes in. This is a:
questions.explanation: A virtual organization has a small core of full-time employees and temporarily hires outside specialists for opportunities as they arise. Option A, network, outsources major functions such as manufacturing on a continuing basis.

questions.question: A phone company buys screens, batteries and chips from outside suppliers and assembles them into finished handsets. It is a:
questions.explanation: A modular organization uses outside suppliers for product components and then assembles them into final products. Option B, network, outsources whole functions such as manufacturing, not just components for assembly.

questions.question: Teams that work across levels and with outside agencies help an organization to:
questions.explanation: Teams across levels and work with outside agencies remove internal and external boundaries, which is the idea behind the boundaryless organization. Option D is wrong because such cross-level teams weaken, not strengthen, a single line of command.

questions.question: How many current organizational design challenges are commonly identified?
questions.explanation: Four challenges are identified: keeping employees connected, managing global structural issues, building a learning organization and designing flexible work arrangements. Option A, five, matches the number of flexible work arrangements, not the challenges.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of today's organizational design challenges?
questions.explanation: Today's challenges are keeping employees connected, managing global structural issues, building a learning organization and designing flexible work arrangements. Increasing work specialization is not one of them, while options B and the others are.

questions.question: A Lagos firm's staff are spread across sites and often on the move, so managers rely on technology to keep them in touch. This addresses the challenge of:
questions.explanation: When staff are spread out and mobile, using technology to keep them in touch addresses the challenge of keeping employees connected. Option D, global structural issues, is about how structures differ across countries and cultures.

questions.question: Managing global structural issues mainly requires managers to:

options.b: widen every manager's span of control

questions.explanation: Structures differ between countries and cultures, so managers must understand how culture shapes structure. Option C describes a network organization, which is a design choice rather than the global structural challenge.

questions.question: An employee of an Ikeja insurance company works from home and stays linked to the office through the internet and video calls. This arrangement is:
questions.explanation: Working from home while linked to the workplace by technology is telecommuting. Option B, flextime, lets staff vary their hours within limits but does not by itself mean working from home.

questions.question: Staff at a Lagos hospital work four 10-hour days instead of five 8-hour days. This is:
questions.explanation: A compressed workweek means working longer hours each day but fewer days each week. Option D, flextime, keeps the weekly hours fixed but lets staff choose when to work within limits, without cutting the number of days.

questions.question: A bank requires 40 hours a week but lets staff choose their start and finish times within set limits. This arrangement is:
questions.explanation: Flextime sets a number of hours a week but allows staff to vary their hours within limits. Option A, a compressed workweek, would mean longer days and fewer working days, not flexible start and finish times.

questions.question: Two part-time lecturers in a university department split one full-time teaching post between them. This is:
questions.explanation: Job sharing is when two or more people split one full-time job. Option D, telecommuting, is about where work is done, not about dividing one job between people.

questions.question: Temporary, freelance or contract workers used as demand requires make up the:
questions.explanation: The contingent workforce consists of temporary, freelance or contract workers brought in as demand requires. Option C, the virtual organization, is a whole design with a small core plus outside specialists, not a type of work arrangement.

questions.question: In a learning organization, leadership is characterized by:

options.d: a clear and rigid chain of command

questions.explanation: Leadership in a learning organization is built on a shared vision and collaboration. Option B, strict control from the top, describes a mechanistic approach, not a learning organization.

questions.question: How is information shared in a learning organization?

options.a: Only through the formal chain of command
options.c: Openly, in a timely and accurate way

questions.explanation: A learning organization shares information openly, in a timely and accurate way. Option D, need-to-know sharing, would block the learning that depends on information.

questions.question: The culture of a learning organization is marked by:

options.d: strong relationships, community, caring and trust

questions.explanation: A learning organization's culture features strong relationships, a sense of community, caring and trust. Option B, strict rules and high formalization, describes a mechanistic organization.

questions.question: In terms of design, a learning organization is characterized by:
questions.explanation: The design of a learning organization is boundaryless, team-based and built on empowerment. Option A, a tall structure with narrow spans, belongs to a mechanistic design.

questions.question: At a Lagos bank, every employee is expected to take an active part in identifying and solving work-related problems. This is a feature of:
questions.explanation: In a learning organization, every member takes an active part in identifying and solving work-related problems. Option C, a simple structure, centralizes authority in one person, so problem solving is not spread across all members.

questions.question: How many elements of organizational design are there?
questions.explanation: There are six: work specialization, departmentalization, chain of command, span of control, centralization versus decentralization, and formalization. Option C, four, is the number of contingency factors, not design elements.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the six elements of organizational design?
questions.explanation: Environmental uncertainty is a contingency factor that influences structure, not one of the six design elements. Options D and the others are genuine elements alongside work specialization, departmentalization and centralization.

questions.question: Taken together, the six elements of organizational design decide whether a structure is:
questions.explanation: Combining the six elements, for example spans, centralization and formalization, determines whether a structure is mechanistic or organic. Option D, line or staff, refers to types of authority, not overall structure.

questions.question: Recruitment is the process of:

options.a: Locating, identifying and attracting capable applicants.

questions.explanation: Recruitment is the process of locating, identifying and attracting capable applicants for a job. Choosing which applicant to hire comes next and is called selection, so recruitment stops at building a pool of candidates. Option B describes retention, C describes performance appraisal, and D describes organizing work.

questions.question: Training helps to:
questions.explanation: Training builds employees' knowledge and skills so they can do their jobs better. Option A, motivation, can be a side benefit, but it is not the main purpose of training. Options C and D are unrelated to training.

questions.question: Which is an example of employee retention?
questions.explanation: Paying fair salaries and benefits gives employees good reason to stay, which is what retention means. Options B and C push workers away by overloading them, and D, conducting audits, is a control activity.

questions.question: Retention focuses on:
questions.explanation: Retention means keeping valued employees, and keeping them satisfied is central to that. Option A, firing employees, is the opposite of retaining them. Options C and D describe cost and workload, and longer hours usually make people want to leave.

questions.question: Recruitment involves:

options.a: Identifying and attracting qualified candidates for a job.
options.c: Hiring underqualified individuals to reduce costs.

questions.explanation: Recruitment is the process of finding and attracting qualified people to apply for a job. Options B, C and D describe poor practices that weaken hiring, not what recruitment is meant to do.

questions.question: Training employees is important because it:

options.a: Enhances skills and boosts organizational performance.

questions.explanation: Training builds employees' skills, and better-skilled staff improve how well the whole organization performs. Option B is the opposite, since training usually raises engagement. C and D are wrong because trained staff still need supervision, and training covers more than technical skills.

questions.question: Retention of employees can be improved through:
questions.explanation: People are more likely to stay in a job when they are paid fairly and their efforts are recognised. Options B, C and D would push employees to leave rather than keep them.

questions.question: The part of management concerned with getting, training, keeping and rewarding the right people is called:
questions.explanation: Human resource management (HRM) is the part of management that deals with getting, training, keeping and rewarding the right people. Option C is about producing goods and services, and option B is about setting the long-term direction of the whole firm, not about managing people as such.

questions.question: In the older list of management functions, human resource management is called:
questions.explanation: In the older list of functions, the work of HRM appears as staffing: recruiting, selecting, training, appraising and retaining employees. Option D is about arranging tasks and structure, and option A is about guiding and instructing people already in place, not getting and keeping them.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the staffing function?
questions.explanation: Budgeting is a financial planning activity, so it is not part of staffing. Staffing covers recruiting, selecting, training, appraising and retaining employees, which is why option D (performance appraisal) is part of staffing even though some students wrongly think it belongs only to controlling.

questions.question: Performance appraisal is part of which management function in the older list of functions?
questions.explanation: Appraising employees is one of the staffing activities, alongside recruiting, selecting, training and retaining them. Option D is about setting goals and deciding how to reach them, and option C is about arranging work and resources, so neither covers appraising people.

questions.question: HRM is said to be important for how many main reasons?
questions.explanation: There are three reasons: HRM can give a firm competitive advantage, it is an important part of strategy, and the way people are treated strongly affects performance. Option C leaves one of these out, while options B and A add reasons that are not part of the list.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the reasons why HRM is important?

options.a: It removes the need for managers to plan
options.b: It is an important part of an organization's strategy
options.c: The way people are treated affects performance
options.d: It can be a significant source of competitive advantage

questions.explanation: HRM does not remove the need for planning; in fact HR planning is itself one of its activities. Options B, C and D are the three real reasons HRM matters: competitive advantage, strategy and the effect of people's treatment on performance.

questions.question: The MD of a Lagos bank says, "Any rival can buy our software, but they cannot copy our well-trained, motivated staff." Which reason for the importance of HRM is she stressing?

options.b: People can be a source of competitive advantage
options.c: HRM is required by the Labour Act
options.d: HRM reduces the need for training

questions.explanation: She is saying her people give the bank an edge rivals cannot easily copy, which is the idea that people managed well can give a firm competitive advantage. Option C is wrong because laws shape HRM practices but are not the reason given here, and options D and A are not reasons HRM matters at all.

questions.question: Work practices that lead to both high individual and high organizational performance are called:
questions.explanation: High-performance work practices are those that raise both individual and organizational performance, such as self-managed teams and performance-based pay. Option C refers to programmes that improve the position of protected groups, and option D is a job preview given to applicants during selection.

questions.question: Self-managed teams, decentralised decision-making and performance-based pay are all examples of:
questions.explanation: These are all listed examples of high-performance work practices, which lift both individual and organizational performance. Option A covers ways of reducing the workforce, such as layoffs, and option B covers tools like tests and interviews used to choose applicants.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of a high-performance work practice?

options.b: Hiring for a good fit between person and job
options.d: Keeping all decisions with top management

questions.explanation: High-performance work practices include decentralised decision-making, so keeping every decision at the top is the opposite of one. Options A, B and C are all listed examples, along with self-managed teams, training and performance-based pay.

questions.question: How many activities make up the HRM process?
questions.explanation: The HRM process has eight activities, running from human resource planning to career development, arranged in three groups. Option A is tempting because there are seven decruitment options and seven appraisal methods, but the HRM process itself has eight activities.

questions.question: The eight activities of the HRM process are arranged in how many groups?
questions.explanation: The eight activities fall into three groups: identifying and selecting competent employees, giving them up-to-date skills and knowledge, and retaining competent, high-performing employees. Option C is tempting because training methods come in two groups, but the HRM process itself has three.

questions.question: Which is the first activity in the HRM process?
questions.explanation: The process starts with human resource planning, which works out how many and what kinds of people are needed. Option D is the second activity and option B is the third; you cannot recruit or select sensibly until you know what you need.

questions.question: In the HRM process, the third activity is:
questions.explanation: The order is human resource planning, then recruitment and decruitment, then selection. Option A comes second, because you must attract applicants before you can choose among them, and option D comes fourth, after people have been hired.

questions.question: Which is the eighth and final activity in the HRM process?
questions.explanation: Career development closes the HRM process as the last of the retention activities. Option A is seventh and option D is sixth; both also belong to the retention group, which is why they are easy to mix up.

questions.question: In the HRM process, orientation and training belong to the group of activities that:

options.b: Give employees up-to-date skills and knowledge
options.d: Respond to labour unions and laws

questions.explanation: Orientation and training are the two activities that give employees up-to-date skills and knowledge. Option C covers HR planning, recruitment and selection, and option A covers performance management, compensation and benefits, and career development.

questions.question: Compensation and benefits fall under which group of HRM activities?

options.c: Give employees up-to-date skills and knowledge

questions.explanation: Compensation and benefits sit in the retention group with performance management and career development, because fair pay helps keep good people. Option C contains orientation and training, and option B contains planning, recruitment and selection.

questions.question: Which set of activities makes up the group "identify and select competent employees"?

options.a: HR planning, recruitment and decruitment, selection

questions.explanation: The first group covers the three activities that bring the right people in: HR planning, recruitment and decruitment, and selection. Option B is the retention group, and options C and D mix in orientation and training, which belong to the skills and knowledge group.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the eight activities of the HRM process?
questions.explanation: Collective bargaining is how a labour union negotiates with management; unions are an external factor that affects HRM, not one of its eight activities. Options A, C and D are all among the eight activities.

questions.question: Which of the following is an external factor that affects HRM?
questions.explanation: Demographic trends, such as a more diverse and ageing workforce, come from outside the organization and shape how it recruits, trains and rewards people. Options A, B and D are things managers do inside the HRM process, not outside influences.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an external factor that affects HRM?
questions.explanation: A job specification is a document managers produce from job analysis during HR planning, so it is part of the HRM process, not an outside influence. Options A, B and D are the three external factors that affect HRM.

questions.question: An organization that represents workers and seeks to protect their interests through collective bargaining is a:
questions.explanation: A labour union represents workers and protects their interests by bargaining collectively with management over pay, hours and conditions. Option D helps people find jobs at little or no cost, and option C is a private headhunter that finds candidates for firms.

questions.question: The result of negotiations between a labour union and management, covering pay, hours and working conditions, is called a:
questions.explanation: Collective bargaining produces a collective bargaining agreement, which sets out terms such as pay, hours and working conditions. Option C is a programme to improve the position of protected groups, and option A lists the qualifications a jobholder needs.

questions.question: ASUU, which represents academic staff in Nigerian universities, negotiates with government over pay and conditions. For a university's HRM, ASUU is an example of which external factor?
questions.explanation: ASUU is the union of university academic staff, so it is a labour union, one of the external factors that shape HRM. Option B is wrong because ASUU is not a law passed by government, and option D refers to changes in the make-up of the workforce, such as age or gender.

questions.question: The Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) is best described as:

options.a: A national umbrella body for trade unions
options.c: The union of university academic staff only
options.d: A law that governs hiring and dismissal

questions.explanation: The NLC is a national umbrella body that brings Nigeria's trade unions together. Option C describes ASUU, which is one specific union, and option D describes the Labour Act, which is a law rather than a workers' organization.

questions.question: In Nigeria, a key law that limits how managers hire, pay and dismiss workers is the:
questions.explanation: The Labour Act is an important Nigerian labour law, and laws like it mean managers cannot hire, pay or fire purely as they like. Option A is a body of trade unions, not a law, and option C is an agreement negotiated between a union and management.

questions.question: Programmes that improve the position of members of protected groups, for example in hiring and promotion, are called:
questions.explanation: Affirmative action programmes aim to improve the position of protected groups in areas like hiring and promotion. Option D refers to practices that raise individual and organizational performance, and option C helps all employees plan and grow their careers.

questions.question: A manufacturer in Ota finds that its workforce is getting older and more mixed in age, gender and ethnicity, so it changes how it recruits and trains. Which external factor is at work?
questions.explanation: Changes in the age, gender and ethnic make-up of the workforce are demographic trends, one of the external factors affecting HRM. Option C would involve a workers' organization bargaining, and option A would involve government rules; neither is described here.

questions.question: Who is known as the father of industrial psychology and argued for the scientific selection of employees?
questions.explanation: Hugo Munsterberg, the father of industrial psychology, argued for scientific selection, and modern selection tests build on his work. Option D is linked with bureaucracy and formal selection by qualifications, and option B is known for the principles of management.

questions.question: Which statement best describes where the HRM process takes place?

options.a: Only inside the HR department, cut off from outside forces
options.b: Inside the external environment, which shapes every step
options.c: Only at the selection stage, where laws apply

questions.explanation: The whole HRM process sits inside the external environment, so unions, laws and demographic trends shape every step, not just one. Option A is wrong because HRM is not sealed off from the outside world, and option C wrongly limits outside influence to selection.

questions.question: The process by which managers make sure they have the right number and kinds of capable people in the right places at the right times is:
questions.explanation: Human resource planning is about having the right number and kinds of capable people in the right places at the right times. Option D defines individual jobs and the behaviours they need, and option B is about attracting applicants once the need is known.

questions.question: Human resource planning is also known as:
questions.explanation: Human resource planning is also called employment planning, because it plans how many and what kinds of people the organization will employ. Option D is one step within HR planning that defines jobs, and option C helps individual employees plan their own careers.

questions.question: Human resource planning involves how many steps?
questions.explanation: HR planning has two steps: assessing current human resources and meeting future human resource needs. Option B is the number of activities in the whole HRM process, not the steps in HR planning.

questions.question: The first step in human resource planning is to:
questions.explanation: Managers begin by assessing the people they already have before working out what they will need. Option A is the second step, and option C belongs to recruitment, the HRM activity that comes after planning.

questions.question: The second step in human resource planning is to:
questions.explanation: After assessing current staff, managers move on to meeting future human resource needs. Option C is the first step, and options B and A are separate HRM activities that come later in the process.

questions.question: A record of current employees' names, education, training, past jobs, languages and special skills is called a:
questions.explanation: A human resource inventory records what current employees bring, such as their education, languages and special skills. Option C describes a job rather than the people in it, and option B collects facts from applicants, not existing staff.

questions.question: The HR manager of a commercial bank in Lagos builds a database showing every staff member's education, past jobs, languages and special skills. She is preparing a:
questions.explanation: A database of current employees' education, past jobs, languages and skills is a human resource inventory, used to assess current human resources. Option C sets out minimum qualifications for a job, not a record of existing staff, and option D is information given to applicants.

questions.question: An assessment that defines jobs and the behaviours needed to perform them is called:
questions.explanation: Job analysis defines jobs and the behaviours needed to do them, and it comes first. Options D and B are both produced from job analysis: the description covers what the job is, and the specification covers the minimum qualifications.

questions.question: The job description and job specification are both produced from:
questions.explanation: Job analysis comes first, and both the job description and the job specification are drawn from it. Option D is a record of current employees, which helps assess current staff but does not define jobs.

questions.question: A written statement of what the job is, what the jobholder does, how and why, is a:
questions.explanation: A job description is a written statement of what the job is: what the jobholder does, how and why. Option B describes the person instead, listing the minimum qualifications, while option A is the assessment both documents come from.

questions.question: A statement of the minimum qualifications a person needs to do a job well is a:
questions.explanation: A job specification states the minimum qualifications, meaning the knowledge, skills and attitudes, a person needs to do the job well. Option D describes the job itself rather than the person, and option B gives applicants good and bad information about the job.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a job description from a job specification?

options.a: A job description lists knowledge, skills and attitudes needed
options.b: A job description describes the job; a job specification describes the person
options.c: A job description describes the person; a job specification describes the job
options.d: Both describe the minimum qualifications of the jobholder

questions.explanation: The job description describes the job (what is done, how and why), while the job specification describes the person (the minimum knowledge, skills and attitudes needed). Option C simply reverses the two, and option A gives the job specification's content to the job description.

questions.question: A job advert from a bottling company in Ota says: "Applicant must hold an OND in Mechanical Engineering and have good knowledge of safety procedures." This part of the advert comes from the:
questions.explanation: Stating the qualifications and knowledge an applicant must have describes the person, which is the job specification. Option C would explain what the jobholder does on the bottling line, not what the person must bring.

questions.question: A hospital document states that a ward clerk records patient admissions, updates files daily and sends reports to the matron so that care is not delayed. This document is a:
questions.explanation: The document says what the jobholder does, how and why, which makes it a job description. Option D would instead list the minimum qualifications a ward clerk needs, and option B records the skills of current employees.

questions.question: When managers work out future human resource needs, these needs come mainly from:

options.a: The results of last year's orientation programme
options.b: The personal preferences of current employees
options.c: The number of applicants who apply each year
options.d: The organization's mission, goals and strategy, and demand for its products or services

questions.explanation: Future needs flow from where the organization is going (its mission, goals and strategy) and from demand for what it sells. Option C is wrong because applicant numbers reflect recruitment, not how many people the organization actually needs.

questions.question: Reducing an organization's workforce is called:
questions.explanation: Decruitment is the general term for reducing an organization's workforce, and it covers several options. Option B is only one of those options, leaving jobs unfilled, and option C is the opposite activity of attracting applicants.

questions.question: Which statement best contrasts recruitment with decruitment?

options.a: Both refer to screening applicants to choose the best
options.b: Recruitment attracts capable applicants; decruitment reduces the workforce
options.c: Recruitment is temporary; decruitment is permanent
options.d: Recruitment reduces the workforce; decruitment attracts applicants

questions.explanation: Recruitment is about locating, identifying and attracting capable applicants, while decruitment is about reducing the workforce. Option D reverses them, and option A describes selection, which comes after recruitment.

questions.question: Which recruitment option has the advantages of low cost, building morale, and candidates who already know the organization?
questions.explanation: Internal search looks among current staff, so it is cheap, boosts morale, and the candidates already know the organization. Option D also uses current staff, but its stated advantage is that they know the job and stake their name on the candidate, and option C is costly.

questions.question: A main disadvantage of internal search as a recruitment option is:

options.d: Candidates tend to be less skilled

questions.explanation: Internal search can only draw from people already in the organization, so the supply is limited and it may not add diversity. Option C is the drawback of private agencies, and option A is the drawback of school and college recruiting.

questions.question: Which recruitment option has the disadvantage of bringing in many unqualified applicants?
questions.explanation: Adverts and online postings reach many people, but that wide reach also brings in many unqualified applicants. Option C does the opposite, because headhunters screen candidates carefully, and option D relies on staff who know the job.

questions.question: Private agencies and professional recruiters ("headhunters") have which main disadvantage?

options.a: High cost and little commitment to the organization
options.b: Candidates tend to be less skilled

questions.explanation: Headhunters have wide contacts and screen carefully, but they are expensive and have little commitment to the hiring organization. Option B is the drawback of public employment agencies, and option D is the drawback of advertising widely.

questions.question: Public employment agencies are free or low cost. Their main disadvantage is that:

options.a: They have a limited internal supply
options.c: Candidates tend to be less skilled

questions.explanation: Public employment agencies cost little, but the candidates they supply tend to be less skilled. Option B is the drawback of private agencies and temporary help, and option D is the drawback of school and college recruiting.

questions.question: School and college recruiting offers a large pool of candidates in one place, but its main drawback is that it provides:
questions.explanation: Campus recruiting brings a large pool of applicants together, but they are mostly entry-level, so it suits junior roles rather than senior ones. Option A is the drawback of internal search, and option C is linked with headhunters.

questions.question: A Lagos fintech firm asks its staff to recommend friends for open roles, knowing that staff understand the job and put their own reputation on the line. Which recruitment option is this?
questions.explanation: Asking current staff to recommend outsiders is an employee referral; staff know the job and stake their name on the candidate. Option A would mean filling the role from current employees themselves, not from people they recommend.

questions.question: A private hospital in Ibadan needs extra records staff for three months while it moves to a new filing system. Which recruitment option best fits this short-term need, though it is expensive?
questions.explanation: Temporary help services exist to fill short-term needs, although they are expensive. Option D mainly brings in entry-level candidates for permanent roles, and option B draws on existing staff, who are already needed in their own jobs.

questions.question: Which two recruitment options share the disadvantage that they may not add diversity to the workforce?

options.d: School recruiting and temporary help services

questions.explanation: Internal search and employee referrals both rely on current staff, so they tend to bring in similar people and may not add diversity. The other pairs have different drawbacks, such as many unqualified applicants for adverts in option C and expense for temporary help in option D.

questions.question: How many decruitment options are there?
questions.explanation: There are seven decruitment options: firing, layoffs, attrition, transfers, reduced workweeks, early retirements and job sharing. Option C is the number of HRM activities, which is a common mix-up.

questions.question: Permanent, involuntary termination of employment is called:
questions.explanation: Firing is permanent and involuntary. Option A is also involuntary but temporary, and option C forces no one out because jobs are simply left unfilled when people resign or retire.

questions.question: A temporary, involuntary termination that may last days or years is a:
questions.explanation: A layoff is involuntary but temporary, and it may last days or years. Option D is the permanent version, which is the classic trap, and option B moves people within the organization rather than ending their employment.

questions.question: A state-owned bank in Abuja decides not to replace staff who resign or retire this year, so its headcount falls without anyone being forced out. This decruitment option is:
questions.explanation: Not filling jobs left open by resignations or retirements is attrition, and with attrition no one is forced out. Options A and D both involve involuntary termination, temporary and permanent respectively.

questions.question: Which decruitment option usually does not cut costs but helps balance supply and demand for labour inside the organization?
questions.explanation: Transfers move employees sideways or downward, so they usually do not reduce costs but they rebalance labour across units. Options A, C and D all actually reduce the hours worked or the number of people employed.

questions.question: To cut its workforce, a Lagos insurance company offers attractive packages to older, senior staff who agree to leave before normal retirement age. This decruitment option is:
questions.explanation: Offering incentives to older, senior staff to retire early is the early retirement option. Option B would involve simply not replacing people who leave on their own, without any incentive package.

questions.question: During a slow season, a textile factory in Kano asks all machine operators to work 30 hours a week instead of 40 rather than letting anyone go. This decruitment option is:
questions.explanation: Having employees work fewer hours a week is the reduced workweek option. Option A would mean two or more people, usually part-timers, splitting one full-time job, which is not what is described.

questions.question: When several employees, usually two part-timers, share one full-time job, the decruitment option is called:
questions.explanation: Job sharing is when several employees, usually two part-timers, split one full-time job. Option A is a training method in which employees move sideways to learn several jobs, and option D cuts everyone's hours without splitting a job.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a decruitment option?
questions.explanation: Employee referrals are a way of recruiting new people, not of reducing the workforce. Options A, B and D are all among the seven decruitment options.

questions.question: The key difference between firing and a layoff is that:

options.a: A layoff leaves jobs unfilled after resignations
options.b: Firing is temporary, while a layoff is permanent
options.c: Firing is permanent, while a layoff is temporary
options.d: Firing is voluntary, while a layoff is involuntary

questions.explanation: Both are involuntary, but firing is permanent and a layoff is temporary. Option B reverses them, and option A describes attrition, where no one is forced out at all.

questions.question: Screening job applicants to make sure the most appropriate candidates are hired is called:
questions.explanation: Selection screens applicants so the most appropriate ones are hired. Option D comes before it and only attracts the pool of applicants, while option C happens after hiring, when new employees are introduced to the job.

questions.question: Selection is best understood as an exercise in:
questions.explanation: Selection is an exercise in prediction: managers try to forecast which applicant will do the job well. Options C and A describe what unions and management do in collective bargaining, not choosing among applicants.

questions.question: A selection decision can have how many possible outcomes?
questions.explanation: Accepting or rejecting a candidate who later succeeds or fails gives four outcomes: two correct decisions and two errors (the accept error and the reject error). Option C counts only the two errors or only the two choices, not the full set of outcomes.

questions.question: Rejecting a candidate who would have done the job well is called a(n):
questions.explanation: A reject error turns away someone who would have succeeded. Option C is the opposite mistake, hiring someone who then performs poorly, and option A would apply only if the rejected person would have failed.

questions.question: Accepting a candidate who then performs poorly is called a(n):
questions.explanation: An accept error hires someone who turns out to perform poorly. Option D is the opposite mistake of turning away someone who would have done well, and option A would apply only if the hired person later succeeded.

questions.question: A Lagos bank turns down an applicant for a credit analyst role. Two years later she is the best analyst at a rival bank. The first bank made a(n):
questions.explanation: Turning away someone who would have done the job well is a reject error, and one of its costs is losing good people to rivals. Option C would apply if the bank had hired someone who then performed poorly.

questions.question: A hospital in Enugu hires a nurse who impressed the panel, but within months her work is so poor that she must be retrained and later replaced. This is an example of a(n):
questions.explanation: Hiring someone who then performs poorly is an accept error, which brings training costs, poor work and the cost of firing and rehiring. Option D would mean the hospital had wrongly turned away a good nurse, which did not happen here.

questions.question: If an organization rejects an applicant who would later have been unsuccessful in the job, this outcome is a(n):
questions.explanation: Rejecting someone who would have failed is the right call, so it is a correct decision. Option B applies only when the rejected person would have succeeded, and option A applies only when the person was accepted and then failed.

questions.question: Which cost is most closely linked with a reject error?

options.a: Higher pension costs for senior staff
options.b: Poor work quality from the person who was hired
options.c: Possible discrimination claims and losing good people to rivals
options.d: Training costs and the cost of firing and rehiring

questions.explanation: A reject error turns good people away, so the firm may face discrimination claims and may lose talent to competitors. Options D and B are the costs of an accept error, where a poor performer has actually been hired.

questions.question: Which set of costs is linked with an accept error?

options.a: Higher fees paid to public employment agencies
options.b: Lower morale among people promoted internally
options.c: Discrimination claims and losing good people to rivals
options.d: Training costs, poor work, and the cost of firing and rehiring
