questions.explanation: An accept error brings in a poor performer, which leads to training costs, poor work and finally the cost of firing and rehiring. Option C lists the costs of a reject error, where good candidates are turned away.

questions.question: A proven relationship between a selection device and some relevant criterion, such as later job performance, is called:
questions.explanation: Validity means the device's results are proven to relate to something that matters, such as later job performance. Option D means the device measures the same thing consistently, which is a different quality: a test can be reliable without being valid.

questions.question: When a selection device measures the same thing consistently, it is said to have:
questions.explanation: Reliability means consistent measurement, so the same person gets about the same score each time. Option D is about whether the scores actually predict job success, which is a separate question from consistency.

questions.question: A manufacturer in Ota uses an aptitude test. Applicants who retake it get almost the same score each time, but the scores show no link with how well people later perform on the job. The test is:
questions.explanation: Getting about the same score each time shows the test is reliable, but since the scores do not predict job success it is not valid. Option B reverses the two ideas, and option D is wrong because a valid test must actually predict performance.

questions.question: Which statement about validity and reliability is TRUE?

options.a: A reliable test can still be invalid
options.b: Reliability means scores predict job success
options.c: A reliable test is always valid
options.d: Validity means scores are consistent over time

questions.explanation: Reliability is about consistency and validity is about prediction, so a test can give consistent scores that still do not predict job success. Option C is the common trap, and options D and B swap the two definitions.

questions.question: How many main types of selection devices are there?
questions.explanation: There are six selection devices: application forms, written tests, performance-simulation tests, interviews, background investigations and physical examinations. Option D is tempting because seven is the number of decruitment options and appraisal methods.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a selection device?
questions.explanation: Job rotation is a traditional training method in which employees move sideways to learn several jobs; it is used after hiring, not to choose applicants. Options A, B and D are all selection devices.

questions.question: Work sampling and assessment centres are both types of:
questions.explanation: Work sampling and assessment centres are performance-simulation tests, because they use actual job behaviour. Option A covers paper tests of intelligence, aptitude, personality and integrity, which do not ask candidates to perform the job.

questions.question: Which type of selection device is based on actual job behaviour?
questions.explanation: Performance-simulation tests ask candidates to actually perform job tasks, so they are based on real job behaviour. Option A measures traits such as aptitude or personality on paper, and option B only collects basic facts like education and past jobs.

questions.question: A selection device in which applicants are given a small replica of the job and asked to perform its central tasks is:
questions.explanation: Work sampling gives applicants a small replica of the job to perform its central tasks, and it suits routine, standard jobs. Option C is also a simulation, but it tests managerial potential through exercises judged by a panel.

questions.question: A Lagos law firm hiring a typist asks each applicant to type and format a sample letter in 15 minutes. This selection device is:
questions.explanation: Asking applicants to perform a core task of a routine job is work sampling. Option A is meant for testing managerial potential through group exercises and problem-solving judged by a panel, not for a standard typing job.

questions.question: Work sampling is best suited to which kind of job?
questions.explanation: Work sampling copies the central tasks of a job, so it suits routine, standard jobs where those tasks are clear. Option B is better served by assessment centres, which test managerial potential.

questions.question: Candidates for a management trainee scheme at a Lagos conglomerate spend two days doing interviews, problem-solving tasks and group exercises while a panel judges them. This is a(n):
questions.explanation: Simulation exercises such as interviews, problem-solving and group tasks judged by a panel make up an assessment centre, which tests managerial potential. Option D would give a small replica of one routine job rather than a range of managerial exercises.

questions.question: Assessment centres are mainly used to test a candidate's:
questions.explanation: Assessment centres put candidates through simulation exercises, judged by a panel, to test managerial potential. Option B would be checked by work sampling, and option C by a physical examination.

questions.question: Interviews become more valid and reliable when they are:

options.a: Informal, with questions changing for each candidate
options.b: Structured, with the same planned questions for every candidate

questions.explanation: Structured interviews use the same planned questions for everyone, which makes them more valid and reliable. Option A is the unstructured approach, where answers cannot be compared fairly because each candidate is asked something different.

questions.question: An interview that asks candidates how they handled real situations in the past is called a:
questions.explanation: A behavioural interview asks how a candidate actually handled real situations in the past. Option C puts candidates through simulation exercises to test managerial potential, and option A gives information to the candidate rather than asking about past behaviour.

questions.question: References from previous employers are often of little value because:

options.a: Referees tend to say only good things
options.d: They are too expensive to collect

questions.explanation: References are often of little value because referees tend to say only good things about the candidate. Option B describes assessment centres, and option C describes physical examinations.

questions.question: Background investigations involve:

options.b: Rating employees on a scale of 1 to 5
options.c: Checking the facts on the application and checking references
options.d: Giving applicants a small replica of the job

questions.explanation: Background investigations verify what applicants wrote on the application and check their references. Option D is work sampling, option A describes written tests, and option B is a graphic rating scale used in appraisal.

questions.question: Application forms are most useful in selection for:

options.c: Giving a realistic picture of the job

questions.explanation: Application forms collect basic facts such as name, education and past jobs, which helps screen out unqualified applicants. Option B is the job of assessment centres, and option A belongs to written tests.

questions.question: Intelligence, aptitude, personality and integrity tests belong to which selection device?
questions.explanation: Intelligence, aptitude, ability, interest, personality and integrity tests are all written tests. Option B is tempting, but performance-simulation tests use actual job behaviour, such as work sampling, rather than paper tests of traits.

questions.question: Physical examinations are used in selection mainly:

options.a: To check the facts on application forms
options.c: For jobs with physical demands, and sometimes for insurance purposes
options.d: To give applicants realistic job expectations

questions.explanation: Physical examinations are used for jobs with physical demands and sometimes for insurance purposes. Option A describes background investigations, and option D describes the purpose of a realistic job preview.

questions.question: A preview of a job that gives applicants both positive and negative information about the job and the company is a:
questions.explanation: A realistic job preview (RJP) deliberately shares both the good and the bad about the job and the company. Option A states what the job involves but is not designed to show its downsides, and option B happens after hiring.

questions.question: Giving applicants a realistic job preview is expected to:

options.a: Increase the number of accept errors

questions.explanation: An RJP gives new hires realistic expectations, which raises satisfaction and lowers turnover. Option C is the reverse of what happens, and option B is wrong because orientation is still needed to bring the newcomer into the job.

questions.question: Before hiring, a Port Harcourt oil-service firm tells applicants for offshore jobs about the good pay and also about the long weeks away from home and the harsh conditions. The firm is using a:
questions.explanation: Sharing both the attractive and the difficult sides of a job before hiring is a realistic job preview. Option C happens after someone is hired and introduces them to their unit's goals and co-workers.

questions.question: In Weber's bureaucracy, choosing people on the basis of their technical qualifications is called:
questions.explanation: Weber called the choice of people by technical qualifications formal selection. Option A is linked with Hugo Munsterberg, who argued for scientifically selecting employees, which is a different idea from Weber's.

questions.question: Introducing a new employee to the job and the organization is called:
questions.explanation: Orientation introduces a new employee to the job and the organization, helping them move from outsider to insider. Option C happens before hiring, and option A is a training method in which existing staff move between jobs.

questions.question: The two types of orientation are:

options.c: Work unit orientation and organization orientation

questions.explanation: Orientation is split into work unit orientation (the unit's goals, how the job fits, co-workers) and organization orientation (company goals, history, policies, benefits). Option A names the two groups of training methods, and option B names the two kinds of training content.

questions.question: Introducing a new employee to co-workers and explaining how the job adds to the unit's goals is part of:
questions.explanation: Work unit orientation covers the goals of the unit, how the job contributes to them, and meeting co-workers. Option D focuses on the company as a whole, such as its history, rules and HR policies.

questions.question: Explaining the company's history, philosophy, rules, pay, overtime and fringe benefits to a new employee is part of:
questions.explanation: Organization orientation covers company-wide matters such as goals, history, philosophy, procedures, rules and HR policies on pay and benefits. Option D focuses only on the employee's own unit and co-workers, and option C is given to applicants before they are hired.

questions.question: On his first day at a Lagos bank, a new graduate trainee is taken on a tour of the head office and given a talk on the bank's history and leave policy. This is:
questions.explanation: A facilities tour plus information on company history and HR policies such as leave is organization orientation. Option C would focus on his own department's goals and introduce him to his immediate co-workers.

questions.question: A main purpose of orientation is to help the newcomer:
questions.explanation: Orientation helps a new employee move from outsider to insider, which lowers anxiety and makes early mistakes and early quitting less likely. Option A reverses the idea, and option D belongs to unions and management, not to new staff.

questions.question: A good orientation programme is expected to:

options.b: Replace the need for any later training
options.c: Lower anxiety and make early quitting less likely
options.d: Raise anxiety so that newcomers work harder

questions.explanation: Good orientation lowers newcomers' anxiety and makes early mistakes and early quitting less likely. Option B is wrong because orientation does not replace training, which builds job skills over time.

questions.question: Training methods are grouped into how many broad groups?
questions.explanation: Training methods fall into two groups: traditional and technology-based. Option A is the number of groups in the HRM process, which is a common mix-up.

questions.question: E-learning (internet-based learning) is classified as a:
questions.explanation: E-learning, along with videoconferencing and recorded media, is a technology-based training method. Option A covers methods such as on-the-job training, job rotation and classroom teaching, which do not rely on technology.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a traditional training method?
questions.explanation: Videoconferencing is a technology-based training method. Options B, C and D are all traditional methods, together with on-the-job training, experiential exercises and classroom teaching.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a technology-based training method?
questions.explanation: Teaching staff face to face in a classroom is a traditional training method. Options B, C and D all rely on technology, such as the internet, phone and video links, or recorded media.

questions.question: Role play and simulations used to train staff are examples of:
questions.explanation: Role play and simulations are experiential exercises, listed among traditional training methods. Option A is tempting because simulations are also used in selection, but here they are used to train existing staff, not to choose applicants.

questions.question: Sideways transfers that let employees learn several different jobs are called:
questions.explanation: Job rotation moves employees sideways so they learn several jobs, which makes it a training method. Option B is a decruitment option where two part-timers split one job, and option C uses transfers to balance labour supply, not to build skills.

questions.question: At a university department in Lagos, a senior administrator is paired with a newly hired officer to advise and support her through her first year. This training method is:
questions.explanation: An experienced employee advising and supporting a newer one is mentoring and coaching, a traditional training method. Option A would move the new officer between several jobs, and option B is a one-off introduction to the unit rather than ongoing support.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of SPECIFIC (rather than general) training?
questions.explanation: Safety training is specific training, alongside leadership, diversity awareness, product knowledge and ethics. Options B, C and D are all examples of general training.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of GENERAL (rather than specific) training?
questions.explanation: Customer service training is general, like communication and computer skills. Options A, B and D are all specific training topics, together with safety and leadership.

questions.question: Training is the right answer to a performance problem when the employee:
questions.explanation: Training fixes a lack of ability, so it is the answer when the employee cannot do the job. Option B describes a lack of willingness, which calls for discipline or counselling rather than training.

questions.question: Which of the following is a sign that managers should consider training?
questions.explanation: More accidents is one of the signs that training may be needed, along with falling output, poorer quality and new technology. Options B, C and D all point to things going well rather than to a skills gap.

questions.question: A process of setting performance standards and appraising employee performance to reach objective HR decisions and keep records that support them is a:
questions.explanation: A performance management system sets standards and appraises performance so HR decisions are objective and backed by records. Option D is simply a record of employees' skills and backgrounds, and option B is a union-management agreement on pay and conditions.

questions.question: How many performance appraisal methods are there?
questions.explanation: There are seven appraisal methods: written essay, critical incidents, graphic rating scales, BARS, multiperson comparisons, MBO and 360-degree appraisal. Option D is the number of selection devices, and option A is the number of HRM activities.

questions.question: An appraisal method in which the evaluator writes about an employee's strengths, weaknesses, past performance and potential is the:
questions.explanation: In the written essay method the evaluator writes about strengths, weaknesses, past performance and potential. Option D is tempting because it is also written, but it records specific behaviours that separate effective from ineffective work rather than a general essay.

questions.question: The main disadvantage of the written essay appraisal method is that it:

options.c: Measures the writer's skill as much as the employee's work
options.d: Has legal concerns when ranking people

questions.explanation: A written essay may reflect how well the evaluator writes as much as how well the employee works. Option B is the drawback of graphic rating scales, and option A is a drawback of BARS.

questions.question: An appraisal method in which the evaluator records the behaviours that separate effective from ineffective job performance is the:
questions.explanation: The critical incidents method records behaviours that separate effective from ineffective work, giving rich, behaviour-based examples. Option C is a general description of the employee, and option A judges people on goals achieved, not on recorded behaviours.

questions.question: Which appraisal method gives rich, behaviour-based examples but is time-consuming and produces no numbers?
questions.explanation: Critical incidents give rich, behaviour-based examples, but they take time and do not produce numbers. Option A is the reverse, giving quick numbers but little depth, and option B is simple, with its weakness being that it reflects the writer's skill.

questions.question: A supervisor at a Lagos supermarket rates each cashier from 1 to 5 on quality, attendance and speed. This appraisal method is:
questions.explanation: Rating factors such as quality and attendance on a 1 to 5 scale is the graphic rating scale method, which is quick and gives numbers. Option A would involve recording specific behaviours rather than scoring factors on a scale.

questions.question: The main disadvantage of graphic rating scales is that they:
questions.explanation: Graphic rating scales are quick and numerical, but they provide little depth. Option B is the drawback of critical incidents, and option C is a drawback of multiperson comparisons.

questions.question: Behaviourally anchored rating scales (BARS) combine which two appraisal methods?

options.a: Critical incidents and graphic rating scales

questions.explanation: BARS combine critical incidents with graphic rating scales, so specific job behaviours are rated on a scale. The other options pair methods that BARS do not combine; for example, option B pairs a narrative method with a goal-based one.

questions.question: An appraisal method that rates specific job behaviours and combines critical incidents with graphic rating scales is:
questions.explanation: BARS rate specific job behaviours by combining critical incidents and graphic rating scales. Option A judges employees on how well set goals are achieved, and option D gathers feedback from many people around the employee.

questions.question: The main disadvantage of BARS is that it is:
questions.explanation: BARS focus on specific, measurable behaviours, but they are time-consuming and hard to build. Option C fits graphic rating scales, and option A describes multiperson comparisons, which compare people with each other.

questions.question: An appraisal method that compares one person's performance with that of others is:
questions.explanation: Multiperson comparisons rank employees against each other rather than against a standard. Option B rates each person on fixed factors, and option C judges each person on their own goals.

questions.question: Which appraisal method is hard to use with many people and raises legal concerns?
questions.explanation: Multiperson comparisons become difficult with large numbers of employees and can raise legal concerns. Option C is results-focused but time-consuming, and option D is time-consuming and gives no numbers.

questions.question: At a Lagos telecoms firm, each sales officer agrees targets with the manager at the start of the year and is appraised on how well those targets are achieved. This appraisal method is:
questions.explanation: Judging employees on how well agreed goals are achieved is MBO, a results-focused method. Option A rates specific job behaviours rather than results, and option B compares each employee with every other one.

questions.question: An appraisal method that uses feedback from supervisors, co-workers, subordinates, customers and the employee himself or herself is:
questions.explanation: 360-degree appraisal gathers feedback from all around the employee: supervisors, co-workers, subordinates, customers and self. It is thorough but time-consuming. Option B uses many people too, but it ranks employees against each other instead of collecting feedback about one person.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three kinds of multiperson comparison?
questions.explanation: Critical incidents is a separate appraisal method that records behaviours, not a way of comparing people with each other. Options A, B and D are the three kinds of multiperson comparison.

questions.question: Placing employees into groups such as "top fifth" or "second fifth" is called:
questions.explanation: Group order ranking places employees into bands such as top fifth or second fifth. Option B lists every employee from best to worst, and option D compares each employee with every other one in pairs.

questions.question: Listing employees in order from best to worst is called:
questions.explanation: Individual ranking lists employees one by one from best to worst. Option A puts them into broad groups such as the top fifth instead, and option C compares them two at a time.

questions.question: A branch manager at a Lagos bank takes her six tellers and compares each one with every other teller, marking who is stronger in each pair. This method is:
questions.explanation: Comparing each employee with every other one and rating who is stronger in each pair is paired comparison. Option C would list the tellers straight from best to worst without working through pairs.

questions.question: Multiperson comparisons differ from the other appraisal methods because they are:

options.b: Absolute, comparing person with a standard

questions.explanation: Multiperson comparisons are relative, measuring each person against other people, while the other methods are absolute, measuring each person against a standard. Option B describes those other methods, such as graphic rating scales and BARS.

questions.question: Which of the following appraisal methods is RELATIVE rather than absolute?
questions.explanation: Individual ranking is a multiperson comparison, so it is relative, measuring employees against one another. Options A, B and C are absolute methods, measuring each person against a standard or a goal.

questions.question: A production supervisor in Ota finds that a machine operator's output is poor because he has never learnt to use the new equipment. The best response is to:
questions.explanation: When poor performance comes from a lack of ability, the answer is to train or coach. Option C is meant for a lack of willingness, which is not the problem here since he simply does not know how to use the equipment.

questions.question: A hospital records officer knows exactly how to file patient records but keeps refusing to do it on time. The supervisor should respond with:
questions.explanation: When an employee can do the job but will not, the problem is willingness, which calls for discipline or counselling. Option D would only help if she lacked the ability to do the filing, which she does not.

questions.question: Actions a manager takes to enforce the organization's standards and rules are called:
questions.explanation: Discipline means the actions a manager takes to enforce the organization's standards and rules. Option B is a process that helps employees overcome performance-related problems, which is supportive rather than enforcing.

questions.question: A process designed to help employees overcome performance-related problems is:
questions.explanation: Employee counselling helps employees overcome performance-related problems. Option C is about enforcing rules and standards, and option A measures performance but does not by itself help the employee overcome problems.

questions.question: Pay that rewards employees for the job skills they can demonstrate is called:
questions.explanation: Skill-based pay rewards employees for the job skills they can demonstrate. Option A ties pay to performance rather than skills, which is the classic mix-up between the two.

questions.question: Pay in which an individual's compensation depends on performance is called:
questions.explanation: Variable pay makes an individual's compensation depend on performance. Option D rewards demonstrated skills instead, so an employee could earn more for a new skill even if results do not change.

questions.question: A Lagos insurance agent earns a commission that rises and falls with the number of policies she sells each month. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Pay that changes with the agent's sales results depends on performance, so it is variable pay. Option B would reward her for skills she can demonstrate, not for the number of policies sold.

questions.question: A Lagos hospital raises a technician's pay after he proves he can operate both the X-ray and the ultrasound machines. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Rewarding the technician for a job skill he can demonstrate is skill-based pay. Option D would tie his pay to his results or performance rather than to the skills he has shown.

questions.question: Extra, nonwage rewards such as health care, pensions and paid leave are called:
questions.explanation: Benefits are the extra, nonwage rewards in compensation, such as health care, pensions and paid leave, and some are required by law. Options C and B are the other parts of compensation, which are paid as money for the work itself or for results.

questions.question: Compensation is made up of:
questions.explanation: Compensation includes base pay, incentives and benefits. Option A leaves out incentives and benefits, and option C describes HRM activities that build skills and careers rather than rewards.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a factor that influences pay levels?
questions.explanation: Marital status is not among the factors that influence pay levels. Options A, B and C are all listed, together with tenure and performance, kind of job and business, labour or capital intensity, management's pay philosophy and profitability.

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as a factor that influences pay levels?

options.a: Whether the firm is labour- or capital-intensive

questions.explanation: Whether a firm is labour-intensive or capital-intensive is one of the listed factors influencing pay levels. Options B, C and D have nothing to do with the job, the business or the employee's performance, so they are not pay factors.

questions.question: The sequence of positions a person holds over a lifetime is called a:
questions.explanation: A career is the sequence of positions a person holds over a lifetime. Option B describes a single job, and option A is a training method that moves people between jobs for a short time.

questions.question: Career development, as an HRM activity, is best described as:

options.a: Comparing each employee with every other employee
options.b: Helping employees plan and grow their careers inside the organization
options.c: Reducing the workforce through early retirements
options.d: Introducing a new employee to the organization

questions.explanation: Career development is the HRM activity that helps employees plan and grow their careers inside the organization; employees are also expected to take charge of their own careers. Option D describes orientation, and option C is a decruitment option.

questions.question: The planned elimination of jobs in an organization is called:
questions.explanation: Downsizing is the planned elimination of jobs. Option B cuts staff only by not replacing those who leave, and option C is the reaction of employees who remain after cuts, not the cuts themselves.

questions.question: The set of attitudes, perceptions and behaviours of employees who remain after involuntary staff cuts is called:
questions.explanation: Layoff-survivor sickness describes how the employees who stay react after involuntary cuts. Option D is the planned cutting of jobs that causes it, and option A is a form of sexual harassment.

questions.question: Layoff-survivor sickness affects which group of people?

options.d: Employees who remain after the cuts

questions.explanation: Layoff-survivor sickness affects the survivors, meaning the people who stay after involuntary staff cuts. Option A is the classic trap, because the people who left are not the ones described by this term.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a sign of layoff-survivor sickness?
questions.explanation: Survivors tend to show lower, not higher, motivation. Options B, C and D are all listed signs, along with lower commitment.

questions.question: Which of the following is a recommended way to treat employees who are leaving during downsizing?

options.a: Give notice and offer severance pay and outplacement
options.b: Announce the cuts without any notice
options.c: Keep the reasons for the cuts secret

questions.explanation: Departing staff should be treated with respect: open and honest communication, notice, and help such as severance pay, extended benefits and outplacement. Options B, C and D all go against that advice.

questions.question: To help survivors after downsizing, managers should:

options.a: Avoid discussing the cuts so people forget them
options.c: Let them talk about their feelings and explain the reasons for the cuts
options.d: Hold back information to prevent rumours

questions.explanation: Managers help survivors by giving them chances to talk about their feelings and by explaining the reasons for the cuts. Options A and D keep people in the dark, which tends to worsen insecurity and the sense of unfairness.

questions.question: Any unwanted action or activity of a sexual nature that explicitly or implicitly affects a person's employment, performance or work environment is:
questions.explanation: Sexual harassment is any unwanted sexual action or activity that affects a person's employment, performance or work environment, whether explicitly or implicitly. Option B is about meaningful work in a community, and option C is a manager's enforcement of rules.

questions.question: A manager at a Lagos firm tells a junior staff member that her promotion depends on her agreeing to sexual favours. This form of sexual harassment is:
questions.explanation: Tying a job benefit such as promotion to sexual favours is quid pro quo harassment. Option D is the other form, where sexual conduct makes the workplace offensive or intimidating without a specific job benefit being traded.

questions.question: In an Ibadan office, co-workers keep sharing sexual jokes and pictures that make a colleague feel intimidated, though no job benefit is involved. This form of sexual harassment is:
questions.explanation: Sexual conduct that creates an offensive or intimidating workplace is hostile environment harassment, and it can come from co-workers, not just managers. Option C needs a job benefit to be tied to sexual favours, which is not the case here.

questions.question: Which statement about sexual harassment at work is TRUE?

options.a: It can only happen to women
options.b: It can only come from a manager
options.c: It can come from a manager or a co-worker and can happen to men or women
options.d: It counts only if a job benefit is involved

questions.explanation: Sexual harassment can come from a manager or a co-worker and can happen to men or women. Option D is wrong because hostile environment harassment involves no job benefit at all.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recommended way for managers to prevent sexual harassment?
questions.explanation: Complaints should be investigated promptly, so delaying them is the opposite of good practice. Options A, B and D are all recommended steps for preventing harassment.

questions.question: A culture in which organizational values promote a sense of purpose through meaningful work that takes place in the context of community is called:
questions.explanation: Workplace spirituality is a culture where values promote purpose through meaningful work in a community setting. Option C refers to practices that raise performance, and option D introduces new employees to the company.

questions.question: Workplace spirituality is mainly about:

options.a: Ranking employees from best to worst

questions.explanation: Workplace spirituality is about meaning and community at work, not about organized religion. Option C is the common misunderstanding of the term.

questions.question: How many features of a spiritual organization are identified?
questions.explanation: There are five features: a strong sense of purpose, focus on individual development, trust and openness, employee empowerment, and toleration of employee expression. Option B is the number of decruitment options or appraisal methods, not features of a spiritual organization.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a spiritual organization?

options.b: Strict control of what employees say

questions.explanation: Spiritual organizations tolerate employee expression, so strict control of what employees say is the opposite. Options A, C and D are all features, along with a focus on individual development.

questions.question: Which two HR costs are organizations especially trying to control?

options.a: Employee health care and employee pensions

questions.explanation: The HR costs firms are especially trying to control are employee health care and employee pensions. The other options list smaller HRM expenses that are not singled out as major cost concerns.

questions.question: A Lagos bank runs a wellness programme and rewards staff who keep healthy habits. Its main aim, as an HR cost issue, is to:
questions.explanation: Wellness programmes and rewards for healthy habits are used to cut employee health care costs. Option D is about linking pay to performance, which wellness programmes do not do.

questions.question: How do organizations mainly try to control employee pension costs?

options.b: By reducing or redesigning pension plans

questions.explanation: Firms control pension costs by reducing or redesigning their pension plans. Option C is the method used to cut health care costs, which is the other major HR cost.

questions.question: Which of the following is a recommended way of managing workforce diversity?

options.b: Widening the recruiting net and using bias-free selection

questions.explanation: Managing diversity involves widening the recruiting net, using bias-free selection, and using orientation and diversity training. Options D and C are the two recruiting channels that may not add diversity, so relying on them alone works against it.

questions.question: Innovation in management leads to:
questions.explanation: Innovation means finding new and better ways of doing things, which makes an organization more productive and competitive. Options A, C and D describe staying stuck in old routines, the opposite of innovation.

questions.question: Organizational change is best defined as:

options.a: Any alteration of people, structure or technology in an organization
options.b: A planned increase in an organization's market share
options.c: The replacement of top managers with outside consultants
options.d: The process of turning creative ideas into useful products

questions.explanation: Organizational change covers any alteration of people, structure or technology, so it is a broad idea, not one specific event. Option D describes innovation, which is only one kind of outcome, and Option C is just one possible change, not the definition.

questions.question: Any alteration of people, structure or technology in an organization is called:
questions.explanation: This is the definition of organizational change. Option A, organizational development, is a set of techniques for changing people and work relationships, so it is one tool for change rather than change itself. Option D is the last step of Lewin's model.

questions.question: Organizational change can involve which three things?
questions.explanation: Change can touch people, structure or technology, which is easy to remember as "PST". Option C mixes in terms that are not the three areas of change, and Option B is the systems view of innovation.

questions.question: A change agent is:

options.a: A force that pushes behaviour away from the status quo
options.b: A person who acts as a catalyst and takes responsibility for managing the change process
options.c: An employee who resists change because he or she prefers routine
options.d: An individual who actively supports new ideas and makes sure innovations are implemented

questions.explanation: A change agent is the catalyst who takes charge of managing the change process. Option D describes an idea champion, who pushes innovations, and Option A describes a driving force, which is a force, not a person.

questions.question: A person who acts as a catalyst and assumes responsibility for managing the change process is known as a(n):
questions.explanation: That role is the change agent. Option D, an idea champion, enthusiastically backs new ideas and innovations, which is related but not the same as managing the whole change process. Option C and Option A are forces in Lewin's model, not people.

questions.question: How many external forces for change are commonly identified?
questions.explanation: There are five external forces: the marketplace, government laws and regulations, technology, labour markets and economic changes. Option A, four, is the number of internal forces, which is why it is the easiest option to confuse.

questions.question: How many internal forces for change are commonly identified?
questions.explanation: There are four internal forces: changes in strategy, changes in the workforce, new equipment and changes in employee attitudes. Option A, five, is the number of external forces.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an external force for change?
questions.explanation: A change in strategy is decided inside the organization, so it is an internal force. The marketplace, government laws and labour markets (options A, C and D) all come from outside the organization.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an internal force for change?

options.c: Economic changes such as inflation and recession

questions.explanation: Interest rates, inflation and recession come from the wider economy, so economic changes are an external force. New equipment, workforce changes and employee attitudes (options A, B and D) all start inside the organization.

questions.question: Which of the following is an external force for change?
questions.explanation: Technology is listed among the five external forces. Option B is tempting because it sounds like technology, but buying new equipment is a decision made inside the firm, so it is an internal force.

questions.question: The federal government passes a new minimum wage law, and a commercial bank in Lagos must review its pay structure. This is an example of:

options.a: An internal force for change from changes in employee attitudes
options.b: An external force for change from government laws and regulations
options.c: An internal force for change from changes in organizational strategy
options.d: An external force for change from the marketplace

questions.explanation: A new law comes from outside the bank, so it is an external force under government laws and regulations. Option C is wrong because the bank did not choose a new strategy on its own, and Option D is wrong because the marketplace refers to competitors and customers.

questions.question: A soap manufacturer in Ota buys new machines for its factory. As a force for change, this is:

options.d: An internal force, changes in the workforce

questions.explanation: Buying new machines is the firm's own action, so it is the internal force called new equipment. Option B is the common trap: technology as a general trend is external, but new equipment bought by the firm is internal.

questions.question: A rival beverage company launches a cheaper product, and a Lagos drinks firm is forced to rethink its prices. This force for change is:

options.c: Internal, from changes in organizational strategy

questions.explanation: A competitor's action comes from outside the firm, so it is an external marketplace force. Option C is tempting because the firm may respond with a new strategy, but the force that triggered the change is the rival's move.

questions.question: An engineering firm in Port Harcourt cannot fill vacancies because there is a shortage of skilled engineers in the country. This force for change is:

options.a: Internal, from changes in employee attitudes
options.b: Internal, from changes in the workforce

questions.explanation: Labour markets are about the supply of and demand for workers, and a national shortage of engineers is a shift in that supply, so it is external. Option B refers to the make-up of the firm's own staff, such as age, education or gender, which is internal.

questions.question: A Lagos food company decides to expand into a new market in East Africa. This decision is a(n):

options.a: External force for change, the marketplace
options.b: External force for change, economic changes
options.c: Internal force for change, a change in organizational strategy
options.d: Internal force for change, new equipment

questions.explanation: Choosing to enter a new market is a strategic decision made inside the firm, so it is an internal force from strategy. Option A is tempting because markets are involved, but the marketplace force refers to outside pressures like competitors and customer needs.

questions.question: Rising interest rates and high inflation push a Nigerian microfinance bank to change how it lends. This is an example of which force for change?
questions.explanation: Interest rates, inflation and recession are examples of economic changes, an external force. Option C would apply only if a new law or regulation caused the change, and Option B concerns the supply of and demand for workers.

questions.question: Staff at a teaching hospital in Ibadan have become increasingly dissatisfied with their jobs, and management sees that something must change. This force for change is:
questions.explanation: Job dissatisfaction is the example given for changes in employee attitudes, an internal force. Option A is close, but changes in the workforce refer to its make-up, such as age, education, gender and nationality, not how staff feel.

questions.question: Over five years, a Lagos insurance firm's staff has become younger, better educated and more mixed in gender and nationality. This internal force for change is:
questions.explanation: Changes in the workforce refer to its make-up, such as age, education, gender and nationality. Option D is about how employees feel, such as job dissatisfaction, and Option C is an external force about the supply of workers in the wider economy.

questions.question: Which of the following is a strength of an internal manager acting as a change agent?

options.a: He or she brings an objective view that insiders lack
options.b: He or she is not tied to the organization's history and culture
options.c: He or she knows the organization and is more thoughtful because he or she must live with the results
options.d: He or she is free to push drastic change without living with the results

questions.explanation: An internal manager knows the organization well and must live with the outcome, which makes him or her more thoughtful. Option A is the strength of an outside consultant, and Option D describes a risk with outsiders, not a strength of insiders.

questions.question: A major weakness of an outside consultant acting as a change agent is that he or she:

options.a: Lacks an objective view of the organization
options.c: Must live with the results of the change
options.d: Knows little of the organization's history, culture, procedures and people

questions.explanation: An outsider usually knows little of the organization's history, culture, procedures and people. Option B is the weakness of an internal manager, and Option A is wrong because objectivity is actually the outsider's main strength.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about change agents is correct?

options.a: Outside consultants may push more drastic change because they do not live with the results
options.b: Internal managers bring an objective view that outsiders lack
options.c: Outside consultants tend to be more cautious than internal managers
options.d: Internal managers usually know little of the organization's culture

questions.explanation: Because an outside consultant does not have to live with the outcome, he or she may push more drastic change. Option C is the classic trap, since it is insiders who tend to be more cautious, and Option B reverses the roles, because objectivity belongs to outsiders.

questions.question: Compared with an outside consultant, an internal manager acting as a change agent is more likely to be:
questions.explanation: An internal manager must live with the results, so he or she may be overcautious. Option D and Option A describe outside consultants, who bring objectivity but may push more drastic change, and Option B is also a weakness of outsiders.

questions.question: Change agents can come from which of the following groups?

options.c: Members of the human resources department only
options.d: Managers, nonmanagers such as HR change specialists, or outside consultants

questions.explanation: Change agents can be managers, nonmanagers such as a change specialist from HR, or outside consultants. Options A, B and C each wrongly limit the role to just one group.

questions.question: For large, organization-wide changes, organizations often turn to which change agents for advice and help?
questions.explanation: For large, organization-wide changes, firms often hire outside consultants for advice and help. Option B, idea champions, push particular innovations, and Option D deals with employees' personal problems, not leading organization-wide change.

questions.question: The main strength an outside consultant brings as a change agent is:

options.b: Greater caution because he or she must live with the results
options.c: Deep knowledge of the organization's history
options.d: An objective view that insiders lack

questions.explanation: An outside consultant's key strength is objectivity, an outside view that insiders lack. Option C and Option B are strengths of an internal manager, who knows the organization and must live with the results.

questions.question: How many views (metaphors) of the change process are commonly described?
questions.explanation: There are two metaphors for the change process: the calm waters view and the white-water rapids view. Option B, three, is tempting because Lewin's model has three steps, but those are steps within one view.

questions.question: The calm waters metaphor pictures the organization as:

options.a: A team rowing against a strong current with no end
options.b: A machine that must be redesigned every year
options.c: A small raft on a river of constant, rough rapids
options.d: A large ship crossing a calm sea that meets a storm now and then

questions.explanation: In the calm waters view, the organization is like a large ship on a calm sea, with an occasional storm that breaks the normal routine. Option C is the picture used for the white-water rapids view, where change is constant.

questions.question: The white-water rapids metaphor pictures the organization as:

options.a: A small raft on a river of constant, rough rapids
options.b: A ship that is repaired once and then sails smoothly
options.c: A ship anchored safely in a harbour
options.d: A large ship crossing a calm sea that meets a storm now and then

questions.explanation: In the white-water view, the organization is like a small raft on a river where the rough water never stops, so change is constant. Option D is the calm waters picture, where change is only an occasional storm.

questions.question: In the calm waters view of change, change is seen as:

options.b: An occasional break in normal, stable life
options.c: A continual process that never settles

questions.explanation: The calm waters view treats change as an occasional disruption in an otherwise stable situation, managed once before things settle. Options A, C and D all describe the white-water rapids view, where change never stops.

questions.question: Which statement best describes managing change in the white-water rapids view?

options.a: It is done once, after which things settle
options.b: It is needed only when an occasional storm disrupts stable life
options.c: It follows the steps of unfreezing, changing and refreezing
options.d: It is a continual process, because change is natural and constant

questions.explanation: In the white-water view, change is natural and constant, so managing it is a continual process. Option A and Option B describe the calm waters view, and Option C is Lewin's model, which also belongs to calm waters.

questions.question: Lewin's three-step model of change belongs to which view of the change process?
questions.explanation: Lewin's unfreeze-change-refreeze model fits the calm waters view, where change is a break in stable equilibrium. Option D is the classic trap: the white-water view sees change as constant, so there is no stable state to refreeze into.

questions.question: The three-step change process of unfreezing, changing and refreezing was proposed by:
questions.explanation: Kurt Lewin described change as unfreezing the status quo, changing to a new state and refreezing. Option A, Fayol, is known for principles of management, and Option B, Maslow, for the hierarchy of needs, not a change model.

questions.question: The first step in Lewin's change process is:

options.c: Refreezing to make the change permanent

questions.explanation: Lewin's process starts by unfreezing the status quo, loosening the current equilibrium so change can happen. Option A, changing, is the middle step, a common trap, and Option B would actually make change harder.

questions.question: The second step in Lewin's three-step change process is:

options.c: Refreezing to make the change permanent

questions.explanation: Changing to a new state is the middle step, after unfreezing and before refreezing. Option B is the first step, Option C is the last step, and Option D is how managers refreeze, so it belongs to the third step.

questions.question: The final step in Lewin's change process, which makes the change permanent, is:
questions.explanation: Refreezing is the third step and stabilises the new situation so the change lasts. Option D is the first step and Option C the second, while Option B is an OD technique, not part of Lewin's model.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly shows Lewin's change process?
questions.explanation: Lewin's steps run unfreezing the status quo, changing to a new state, then refreezing to make the change permanent. Option D is the common error of placing changing first, when it is really the middle step.

questions.question: How many steps are there in Lewin's model of the change process?
questions.explanation: Lewin's model has three steps: unfreezing, changing and refreezing. Option B, two, is the number of change metaphors, not Lewin's steps.

questions.question: In Lewin's model, the status quo is best described as:

options.a: The final step of the change process
options.b: A force that pushes behaviour toward change

questions.explanation: The status quo is an equilibrium state, and moving away from it requires unfreezing. Option D describes the white-water view, and Option B confuses it with a driving force.

questions.question: Driving forces are forces that:

options.a: Hold back movement away from the equilibrium
options.b: Push behaviour away from the status quo
options.c: Make a change permanent after it is introduced
options.d: Cause employees to return to old habits

questions.explanation: Driving forces push behaviour away from the status quo, toward change. Option A is the definition of restraining forces, which work in the opposite direction.

questions.question: Restraining forces are forces that:

options.a: Push behaviour away from the status quo
options.b: Hold back movement away from the equilibrium
options.c: Encourage employees to accept change quickly
options.d: Stabilise a new situation after change

questions.explanation: Restraining forces hold back movement away from the equilibrium, so they resist change. Option A describes driving forces, and Option D describes the purpose of refreezing.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a way to unfreeze the status quo?

options.d: Combining an increase in driving forces with a decrease in restraining forces

questions.explanation: Restraining forces hold back change, so increasing them would keep the organization frozen. Unfreezing is done by increasing driving forces, decreasing restraining forces, or combining both, as in Option A, Option C and Option D.

questions.question: In how many ways can the status quo be unfrozen?
questions.explanation: Unfreezing can be done in three ways: increase the driving forces, decrease the restraining forces, or combine both. Option C, two, misses the option of combining the first two approaches.

questions.question: The main purpose of refreezing is to:

options.a: Increase the forces that push away from the status quo
options.b: Loosen the status quo so change can begin
options.c: Identify which employees are resisting the change
options.d: Stabilise the new situation so the change is not short-lived

questions.explanation: Refreezing stabilises the new situation; without it, the change is likely to be short-lived. Option B describes unfreezing, and Option A is one way to unfreeze, not to refreeze.

questions.question: A hospital in Abuja introduced a new patient-record procedure, but within a few weeks most staff had gone back to the old way of working. Which step of Lewin's model was most likely not done well?
questions.explanation: Refreezing stabilises a change, and without it employees may go back to the old way, which is exactly what happened. Option A is less likely because the staff did move to the new procedure for a while, and Option B is an OD technique, not a step in Lewin's model.

questions.question: How do managers refreeze a change?

options.a: By hiring an outside consultant to push more drastic change
options.b: By balancing the driving and restraining forces again, for example by rewarding the new behaviour
options.c: By increasing the driving forces until the status quo breaks
options.d: By decreasing the restraining forces before the change begins

questions.explanation: Managers refreeze by balancing the driving and restraining forces again, for example by rewarding the new behaviour. Option C and Option D are ways of unfreezing, which happens at the start of change, not the end.

questions.question: Kurt Lewin's model treats change as:

options.b: A continuous flow of rough rapids
options.c: The final output of a creative process
options.d: A break in the organization's equilibrium

questions.explanation: Lewin saw change as a break in the organization's equilibrium, which fits the calm waters view. Option A and Option B describe the white-water rapids view, where change never stops.

questions.question: Imagine a course whose length, timetable and tests change without warning, so students must stay flexible and respond quickly. This illustrates which view of change?
questions.explanation: Constant, unexpected changes that demand flexibility describe the white-water rapids view. Option C is wrong because in calm waters change is only an occasional break in stable life.

questions.question: Which view of change best fits today's uncertain and dynamic environments?
questions.explanation: Today's uncertain and dynamic environments match the white-water view, where change is constant. Option A and Option D are the same idea, since Lewin's model belongs to calm waters, which assumes long stable periods.

questions.question: Organizational change is usually grouped into how many types?

options.c: Four: structure, technology, people and finance

questions.explanation: Change is grouped into three types: structure, technology and people. Option B lists the three steps of Lewin's model, not types of change.

questions.question: Merging departments, widening spans of control and cutting management layers are examples of:
questions.explanation: These actions change authority relationships, coordination and job design, so they are structural change. Option D is wrong because OD works on people's attitudes and relationships, not on the organization chart.

questions.question: Automation, computerization and the introduction of new machines are examples of:
questions.explanation: Changes to equipment, tools, work processes and methods are technological change. Option B is about authority relationships and job design, and Option A is about attitudes and behaviour.

questions.question: Training, team building and OD programmes are examples of which type of change?
questions.explanation: Training, team building and OD programmes change attitudes, expectations, perceptions and behaviour, which is people change. Option D would involve the organization chart, and Option C is a view of the change process, not a type of change.

questions.question: Automation is best described as:

options.a: Structural change that removes layers of management
options.b: People change that trains staff to use new skills
options.c: Technological change that replaces certain tasks done by people with machines
options.d: A survey that measures employees' attitudes to new technology

questions.explanation: Automation is technological change in which machines take over certain tasks that people used to do. Option A is structural change, and Option B is people change, even if it involves technology training.

questions.question: People change focuses on changing employees':

options.a: Spans of control and job design

questions.explanation: People change works on attitudes, expectations, perceptions and behaviour. Option D is the focus of technological change, while Option C and Option A are the focus of structural change.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an element of structure that structural change works on?
questions.explanation: Attitudes and perceptions are the target of people change, not structural change. Span of control, formalization and departmentalization (options B, C and D) are all elements of structure.

questions.question: A Lagos bank moves from a simple structure to a team-based structure, cuts two management layers and gives branch managers more decision-making authority. This is mainly:
questions.explanation: Changing the structural design, cutting layers and shifting centralization are all structural change. Option C is tempting because teams are involved, but the change here is to the design of the structure, not to attitudes, and Option D is an OD technique.

questions.question: A cement manufacturer in Ogun State installs a computerized production line that replaces several manual tasks. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Installing computerized equipment that takes over manual tasks is technological change, specifically automation. Option C would involve authority relationships or job design, and Option A would target attitudes and behaviour.

questions.question: People change in organizations is usually carried out through:
questions.explanation: People change is usually done through organizational development, which targets attitudes and working relationships. Option A is technological change and Option C is structural change.

questions.question: Organizational development (OD) refers to:

options.a: Technological change that replaces tasks done by people with machines
options.b: Changes in authority relationships, coordinating mechanisms and job design
options.c: The process of turning creative ideas into useful products
options.d: Techniques or programmes to change people and the nature and quality of interpersonal work relationships

questions.explanation: OD is a set of techniques or programmes aimed at changing people and the quality of their working relationships. Option A is automation, Option B is structural change, and Option C is innovation.

questions.question: Techniques or programmes designed to change people and the nature and quality of interpersonal work relationships are known as:
questions.explanation: This is the definition of organizational development (OD), the main tool for people change. Option B works on the organization chart, and Option A is a technique for reducing resistance, not a programme for improving relationships.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the popular OD techniques?
questions.explanation: Negotiation is a technique for reducing resistance to change, not an OD technique. Survey feedback, process consultation and intergroup development (options A, B and D) are three of the four OD techniques, along with team building.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the popular OD techniques?
questions.explanation: Team building is one of the four OD techniques. Option A is technological change, Option D is a way of reducing resistance, and Option C is a way of reducing stress.

questions.question: Survey feedback as an OD technique involves:

options.a: An outside consultant helping managers understand how interpersonal processes affect work
options.b: Activities that help a work group set goals and clarify each member's role
options.c: Changing the stereotypes that work groups hold about each other
options.d: Using a questionnaire to assess employees' attitudes and perceptions about the change, then using the results to spot and solve problems

questions.explanation: Survey feedback uses a questionnaire to measure how employees see the change and then uses the results to solve problems. Option A is process consultation, Option B is team building, and Option C is intergroup development.

questions.question: Process consultation is an OD technique in which:

options.a: An outside consultant helps managers understand how interpersonal processes affect the way work is done
options.b: Work groups change the attitudes and perceptions they hold about each other
options.c: A powerful group is offered something of value to accept a change
options.d: A questionnaire is used to measure employees' attitudes about a change

questions.explanation: In process consultation, an outside consultant helps managers see how interpersonal processes affect the way work gets done. Option D is survey feedback, Option B is intergroup development, and Option C is negotiation, a resistance-reduction technique.

questions.question: Team building as an OD technique consists of:

options.a: Activities that change the attitudes and stereotypes different work groups hold about each other
options.b: Merging small departments into larger teams
options.c: A questionnaire that assesses employees' attitudes toward a planned change
options.d: Activities that help work groups set goals, build good working relationships and clarify each member's role and responsibilities

questions.explanation: Team building helps a work group set goals, build good relationships and clarify each member's role. Option A describes intergroup development, which works between groups, and Option B is a structural change, not an OD technique.

questions.question: An OD technique that changes the attitudes, stereotypes and perceptions that work groups hold about each other is called:
questions.explanation: Intergroup development works on how groups see each other, changing attitudes, stereotypes and perceptions between them. Option C is tempting, but team building works within a single group rather than between groups.

questions.question: At a Lagos bank, the marketing and finance departments distrust each other and see each other badly. Which OD technique best fits this problem?
questions.explanation: The problem lies between two groups, so intergroup development, which changes how groups see each other, is the right fit. Option A is the most tempting, but team building works within one group, not between departments.

questions.question: A new project team at an Ota manufacturing firm is unsure who does what and has not agreed on its goals. Which OD technique should management use?
questions.explanation: Team building helps a group set goals and clarify each member's role and responsibilities, which is exactly this team's problem. Option A is for tension between different groups, and Option C is a resistance technique, not OD.

questions.question: Before restructuring, a Nigerian telecom firm wants to find out how its staff feel about the planned change and uses a questionnaire to do so. This OD technique is:
questions.explanation: Using a questionnaire to assess staff attitudes and then acting on the results is survey feedback. Option D uses an outside consultant to observe interpersonal processes, and Option B is a resistance technique based on explaining the change.

questions.question: A department head at a university cannot understand why staff meetings keep failing. An outsider sits in, observes and explains how the interpersonal processes are hurting the work. This is:
questions.explanation: An outside consultant helping a manager see how interpersonal processes affect work is process consultation. Option B relies on a questionnaire rather than observation, and Option C is a resistance technique where those affected join the decision.

questions.question: What is the key difference between team building and intergroup development?

options.a: Team building is used for powerful groups, while intergroup development is used for anxious employees
options.b: Team building uses questionnaires, while intergroup development uses outside consultants
options.c: Team building is structural change, while intergroup development is technological change
options.d: Team building works within one group, while intergroup development works between groups

questions.explanation: Team building looks within a single group, while intergroup development looks between groups, such as two departments that see each other badly. Option B confuses them with survey feedback and process consultation, and Option C is wrong because both are OD techniques for people change.

questions.question: Organizational development is the main tool for which type of change?
questions.explanation: OD is the main tool for people change because it focuses on attitudes and relationships. Option B works on the organization chart and Option D on machines and methods, which OD does not target.

questions.question: OD techniques focus mainly on:
questions.explanation: OD focuses on attitudes and relationships, not machines or charts. Option B is the concern of technological change and Option A of structural change.

questions.question: How many main reasons why people resist change are commonly identified?
questions.explanation: There are four reasons: uncertainty, habit, concern over personal loss, and the belief that the change is not in the organization's best interest. Option B, six, is the number of techniques for reducing resistance, not the reasons for it.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the reasons people resist change?
questions.explanation: Tolerating ambiguity is a cultural variable that encourages innovation, so it would make people more open to change, not less. Uncertainty, habit and concern over personal loss (options A, B and C) are three of the four reasons for resistance.

questions.question: Resistance to change caused by uncertainty arises because:

options.a: People fear losing status, money or friendships
options.b: People sincerely believe the change will harm the organization
options.c: Change replaces the known with the unknown

questions.explanation: Uncertainty means change swaps what people know for what they do not know, which makes them uneasy. Option D is habit, Option A is concern over personal loss, and Option B is the belief that the change is not in the organization's best interest.

questions.question: Clerks at a Lagos insurance office have filled out paper forms the same way for fifteen years and simply prefer to keep doing it that way. Their resistance to a new system is mainly due to:

options.d: Belief that the change is not in the organization's best interest

questions.explanation: A preference for familiar routine is resistance due to habit. Option A would apply if the clerks were worried about what the unknown new system would bring, and Option D would apply if they thought the system would hurt the firm.

questions.question: After a merger is announced, a senior manager at a Nigerian bank resists because he fears losing his title, authority and some benefits. This resistance comes from:

options.b: Belief that the change is not in the organization's best interest

questions.explanation: Fear of losing status, money, authority, friendships or benefits is concern over personal loss. Option A is tempting because a merger is uncertain, but this manager's worry is specifically about what he personally stands to lose.

questions.question: A quality supervisor at a food processing plant in Ota sincerely thinks a new production method will lower product quality, so she resists it. Her reason for resisting is:

options.d: Belief that the change is not in the organization's best interest

questions.explanation: When a worker genuinely thinks a change will harm the organization, the resistance comes from the belief that the change is not in the organization's best interest. Option B would involve fear for her own status or pay, which is not her concern here.

questions.question: Staff at a state hospital are nervous about a planned restructuring because nobody knows what their new roles and routines will look like. Their resistance is mainly due to:

options.c: Belief that the change is not in the organization's best interest

questions.explanation: Not knowing what the change will bring means the known is being replaced by the unknown, which is resistance from uncertainty. Option D would mean they simply prefer their routine, and Option A would mean they fear losing something specific like status or pay.

questions.question: Which employees tend to resist change the most?

options.a: Those who have a lot invested in the current system, such as long-serving staff
options.b: Outside consultants brought in to manage the change
options.c: Newly hired staff with no attachment to the current system
options.d: Employees who have nothing to lose from the change

questions.explanation: People with a lot invested in the current system resist more because they have more to lose, which is often true of older or long-serving staff. Option C and Option D describe people with little at stake, who would resist less.

questions.question: Which statement about resistance to change is correct?

options.a: Resistance can give stability and predictability and lead to useful debate, but it slows adaptation
options.b: Resistance is always harmful and should be removed by force
options.c: Resistance only comes from employees who are poorly trained
options.d: Resistance speeds up adaptation and progress

questions.explanation: Resistance is not always bad: it can bring stability, predictability and useful debate about whether a change is wise, though it slows adaptation and progress. Option B ignores these benefits, and Option D reverses the downside of resistance.

questions.question: How many techniques for reducing resistance to change are commonly identified?
questions.explanation: There are six techniques: education and communication, participation, facilitation and support, negotiation, manipulation and co-optation, and coercion. Option A, four, is the number of reasons for resistance and also the number of OD techniques.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the techniques for reducing resistance to change?
questions.explanation: Survey feedback is an OD technique for assessing attitudes, not one of the six techniques for reducing resistance. Participation, negotiation and facilitation and support (options A, C and D) are all on that list.

questions.question: Education and communication is the best technique for reducing resistance when:

options.a: Resistance comes from a powerful group
options.b: Resisters have the expertise to contribute

questions.explanation: Education and communication clears up misunderstandings, so it suits resistance caused by misinformation. Option B calls for participation, Option C for facilitation and support, and Option A for negotiation.

questions.question: Participation is the most appropriate technique for reducing resistance when:

options.a: Resisters have the expertise to make a contribution
options.b: A powerful group's support is needed

questions.explanation: Participation brings those affected into the decision, which makes sense when they have expertise to contribute. Option C is the case for education and communication, and Option B is the case for manipulation and co-optation or coercion.

questions.question: Facilitation and support is best used when resisters are:
questions.explanation: Facilitation and support, such as counselling and skills training, helps people who are fearful and anxious make needed adjustments. Option A calls for education and communication, Option D for participation, and Option B for negotiation, manipulation or coercion.

questions.question: Negotiation is the technique to use when resistance to change:

options.b: Comes from fearful and anxious employees
options.d: Comes from people with useful expertise

questions.explanation: Negotiation is used when resistance comes from a powerful group, because something of value can "buy" their commitment. Option A calls for education and communication, Option B for facilitation and support, and Option D for participation.

questions.question: Which three techniques for reducing resistance all involve a powerful group?

options.a: Education and communication, negotiation, and manipulation and co-optation
options.b: Negotiation, manipulation and co-optation, and coercion
options.d: Education and communication, participation, and facilitation and support

questions.explanation: Negotiation, manipulation and co-optation, and coercion are all linked to a powerful group. Each of the other options includes participation or education and communication, which are used for resisters with expertise and for misinformation, not for powerful groups.

questions.question: A drawback of education and communication as a way to reduce resistance is that it:

options.b: Can be expensive and has no guarantee of success
options.c: May not work when trust and credibility are lacking
options.d: Opens the door for others to demand deals

questions.explanation: Education and communication depends on people believing the message, so it may fail when trust and credibility are missing. Option B is the drawback of facilitation and support, Option A of coercion, and Option D of negotiation.

questions.question: The main drawbacks of participation as a technique for reducing resistance are that it:

options.a: Can be costly and invites others to demand deals
options.b: Can backfire and damage the change agent's credibility
options.c: Takes time and may produce a poor solution

questions.explanation: Involving people in the decision takes time, and the group may arrive at a poor solution. Option B is the drawback of manipulation and co-optation, and Option A is the drawback of negotiation.

questions.question: A drawback of facilitation and support as a technique for reducing resistance is that it:

options.a: Can be expensive and has no guarantee of success
options.b: Takes time and may produce a poor solution
options.c: May not work when trust is lacking

questions.explanation: Counselling, training and paid leave cost money, and there is no guarantee they will work. Option B is the drawback of participation, Option C of education and communication, and Option D of coercion.

questions.question: Negotiation as a technique for reducing resistance has which drawback?

options.a: It can be costly and opens the door for others to demand deals
options.b: It takes time and may produce a poor solution
options.c: It may not work when trust and credibility are lacking

questions.explanation: Buying commitment through negotiation can be costly, and once one group gets a deal, others may demand one too. Option D is the drawback of coercion, Option C of education and communication, and Option B of participation.

questions.question: Which drawback is specifically associated with coercion?

options.a: It can be expensive with no guarantee of success
options.b: It takes time and may produce a poor solution
options.c: It may not work when trust is lacking
options.d: It may be illegal and may undermine the change agent's credibility

questions.explanation: Coercion uses threats or force, so it may be illegal and can damage the change agent's credibility. Option B is the drawback of participation, Option A of facilitation and support, and Option C of education and communication.

questions.question: A drawback of manipulation and co-optation is that it:

options.a: May not work when trust and credibility are lacking
options.b: Can backfire, and the change agent may lose credibility
options.c: Takes time and may produce a poor solution
options.d: Can be expensive with no guarantee of success
