questions.explanation: Manipulation and co-optation rely on covert influence, so if people find out, it can backfire and the change agent may lose credibility. Option C is the drawback of participation, Option D of facilitation and support, and Option A of education and communication.

questions.question: Which advantage is shared by manipulation and co-optation and by coercion?

options.a: They help people make needed adjustments
options.c: They are a cheap and easy way to gain support

questions.explanation: Both manipulation and co-optation and coercion are a cheap and easy way to win a powerful group's support. Option B is the advantage of education and communication, Option D of participation, and Option A of facilitation and support.

questions.question: The main advantage of participation as a way to reduce resistance is that it:

options.b: Is a cheap and easy way to gain support
options.c: Can buy the commitment of a powerful group

questions.explanation: Bringing people into the decision raises their involvement and acceptance of the change. Option D is the advantage of education and communication, Option C of negotiation, and Option B of manipulation and co-optation or coercion.

questions.question: Co-optation as a technique for reducing resistance means:

options.a: Using direct threats such as transfer or loss of promotion
options.b: Explaining the reasons for the change through meetings and memos
options.c: Exchanging something of value, such as a special pay package
options.d: "Buying off" resistance leaders by giving them a key role in the change decision

questions.explanation: Co-optation mixes manipulation and participation by giving resistance leaders a key role in the decision to win them over. Option A is coercion, Option C is negotiation, and Option B is education and communication.

questions.question: Co-optation is best described as a combination of:
questions.explanation: Co-optation is a mix of manipulation and participation: leaders are given a role in the decision, but mainly to buy off their resistance. Option D is tempting because co-optation involves a role in the decision, but it does not exchange something of value as negotiation does.

questions.question: Manipulation as a technique for reducing resistance refers to:

options.a: Bringing those affected by the change into the decision
options.c: Direct threats or force, such as threats of transfer
options.d: Covert attempts to influence, such as twisting facts or holding back bad information

questions.explanation: Manipulation is covert influence, such as twisting facts or withholding bad news. Option C is coercion, which is open and direct, Option A is participation, and Option B is facilitation and support.

questions.question: A manufacturing firm in Ota tells resisting staff that they will be transferred to a remote plant or get poor performance reviews unless they accept the new shift system. The firm is using:
questions.explanation: Direct threats such as transfer, loss of promotion or bad performance reviews are coercion. Option C is tempting, but manipulation is covert, such as twisting facts, while these threats are open and direct.

questions.question: To win the support of a powerful staff union for a new branch network, a Lagos bank offers union members a special pay package. This technique is:
questions.explanation: Exchanging something of value, such as a special pay package, to reduce resistance is negotiation. Option A would mean giving the union's leaders a key role in the decision, not a pay deal.

questions.question: Nurses at a Lagos hospital are anxious about a new electronic records system, so management provides counselling, new-skills training and a short paid leave. This technique is:
questions.explanation: Counselling, therapy, skills training and short paid leave are forms of facilitation and support, used when resisters are fearful and anxious. Option B would mainly involve explaining the reasons for the change to correct misinformation.

questions.question: False rumours spread at a cement plant that a new process will lead to mass sackings. Management holds meetings and sends memos to explain the real reasons for the change. This is:
questions.explanation: Explaining the reasons for a change through talks, memos and meetings to correct misinformation is education and communication. Option D is wrong because manipulation twists facts or hides bad news, while this management is sharing accurate information.

questions.question: A university faculty plans a new curriculum and invites experienced lecturers, who know the subject well, to help design it. This approach to reducing resistance is:
questions.explanation: Bringing those affected into the decision, especially when they have expertise to contribute, is participation. Option C is tempting, but co-optation gives resistance leaders a role mainly to buy off their opposition, not to use their expertise.

questions.question: A telecom firm in Lagos gives the most vocal opponent of a restructuring a seat on the planning committee, mainly so that he will stop opposing it. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Giving a resistance leader a key role in the decision to buy off his opposition is co-optation. Option D is tempting because he joins the decision, but here the aim is to silence opposition rather than use expertise.

questions.question: Change often creates which reaction in employees?
questions.explanation: Change often creates stress for employees, which is why managers must manage both. Option B is the ability to combine ideas, and Option A and Option C are things managers do, not employee reactions.

questions.question: Stress is best defined as:

options.a: Barriers that keep people from doing what they desire
options.b: A chronic sense of time urgency and an excessive competitive drive
options.d: The adverse reaction people have to excessive pressure placed on them from extraordinary demands, constraints or opportunities

questions.explanation: Stress is the adverse reaction to excessive pressure from extraordinary demands, constraints or opportunities. Option A defines constraints and Option C defines demands, which are sources of pressure rather than stress itself, and Option B describes a Type A personality.

questions.question: The adverse reaction people have to excessive pressure placed on them from extraordinary demands, constraints or opportunities is called:
questions.explanation: This is the definition of stress. Option C is opposition to a change, and Option B is one specific cause of stress, where expectations are hard to meet at the same time.

questions.question: In the study of stress, constraints are:

options.a: Barriers that keep us from doing what we desire
options.d: Expectations that are hard to meet at the same time

questions.explanation: Constraints are barriers that stop us from doing what we desire. Option C is the definition of demands, Option D is role conflict, and Option B is interpersonal demands.

questions.question: In the study of stress, demands are defined as:

options.a: Barriers that keep us from doing what we desire
options.c: Unclear expectations about what to do
options.d: More being expected than time allows

questions.explanation: Demands are defined as the loss of something desired. Option A is the definition of constraints, Option D is role overload, and Option C is role ambiguity.

questions.question: Stress symptoms are grouped into which three categories?
questions.explanation: Stress symptoms are physical, psychological or behavioural. Option B mixes up the causes of stress, Option C lists the variables that foster innovation, and Option A lists some job-related stressors.

questions.question: Headaches, higher blood pressure and faster heart and breathing rates are which type of stress symptom?
questions.explanation: Changes in metabolism, heart rate, breathing and blood pressure, plus headaches, are physical symptoms. Option C covers feelings like anxiety and boredom, and Option A covers actions like absenteeism and smoking.

questions.question: Job dissatisfaction, tension, irritability, boredom and procrastination are which type of stress symptom?
questions.explanation: These are psychological symptoms, which affect a person's mental and emotional state. Option B, behavioural, covers observable actions such as absenteeism, turnover and changes in eating or smoking.

questions.question: Increased absenteeism, higher turnover and more smoking or drinking are which type of stress symptom?
questions.explanation: Absenteeism, turnover and changes in smoking or drinking are actions, so they are behavioural symptoms. Option A covers feelings like tension and anxiety, and Option B is a group of causes of stress, not a symptom type.

questions.question: During month-end at a Lagos bank, a teller starts fidgeting, speaking rapidly and having trouble sleeping. These are mainly:
questions.explanation: Rapid speech, fidgeting and sleep problems are listed as behavioural symptoms. Option B is tempting, but physical symptoms are bodily changes such as blood pressure and heart rate, and Option D describes causes rather than symptoms.

questions.question: The causes of stress (stressors) fall into how many broad groups?

options.b: Three: structural, cultural and human resource
options.c: Two: organizational factors and personal factors

questions.explanation: Stressors fall into two groups: organizational (job-related) factors and personal factors. Option A lists the types of stress symptoms, not the causes, and Option B lists the variables that foster innovation.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an organizational (job-related) cause of stress?
questions.explanation: Personality type is a personal factor, together with family issues and personal economic problems. Role demands, task demands and organizational leadership (options B, C and D) are all job-related stressors.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a personal factor that causes stress?
questions.explanation: Interpersonal demands, pressure from co-workers, are an organizational (job-related) factor. Family issues, personal economic problems and personality type (options B, C and D) are the three personal factors.

questions.question: As a cause of stress, task demands relate to:

options.a: A management style that creates fear and anxiety
options.c: The job itself, including its design, working conditions and layout
options.d: Pressure from the role a person plays

questions.explanation: Task demands come from the job itself: its design, working conditions and physical layout. Option D is role demands, Option B is interpersonal demands, and Option A is organizational leadership.

questions.question: Role conflict refers to:

options.a: Expectations that are hard to meet at the same time
options.c: More being expected than time allows

questions.explanation: Role conflict happens when a person faces expectations that are hard to satisfy at the same time. Option C is role overload, Option D is role ambiguity, and Option B is interpersonal demands.

questions.question: Role overload occurs when:

options.a: There are too many rules and little participation
options.b: More is expected of a person than time allows
options.c: Expectations are hard to meet at the same time

questions.explanation: Role overload means more is expected than the available time permits. Option D is role ambiguity, Option C is role conflict, and Option A is the organization structure stressor.

questions.question: Role ambiguity exists when:

options.a: A manager uses fear to push performance
options.b: Expectations are hard to meet at the same time
options.c: Expectations are unclear and the person is not sure what to do
options.d: More is expected than time allows

questions.explanation: Role ambiguity means the person does not clearly understand what is expected of him or her. Option D is role overload and Option B is role conflict, the other two kinds of role demands.

questions.question: A newly hired officer at a Lagos microfinance bank has no job description and is never told what her supervisor expects of her. The stressor she faces is:
questions.explanation: Unclear expectations about what to do are role ambiguity. Option B would mean she has too much to do in the time available, and Option D would mean she faces expectations that clash with each other.

questions.question: A junior doctor at a Lagos hospital is expected to handle far more patients and paperwork each shift than the shift's hours allow. This stressor is:
questions.explanation: When more is expected than time allows, the stressor is role overload. Option B would mean the doctor does not know what is expected, and Option D would mean expectations that are hard to meet together.

questions.question: A sales manager in Ibadan is told by one director to cut costs sharply and by another to expand the sales team at the same time. This stressor is best described as:
questions.explanation: Expectations that are hard to meet at the same time are role conflict. Option A would be about having too much to do in too little time, and Option B would be about unclear expectations, while here they are clear but clash.

questions.question: As a job-related cause of stress, interpersonal demands are:

options.a: Pressure from the role a person plays
options.b: Pressure from co-workers, such as poor support or bad relationships
options.c: Too many rules and too little chance to take part in decisions
options.d: The job's design, working conditions and layout

questions.explanation: Interpersonal demands come from co-workers, such as poor support or bad relationships. Option A is role demands, Option C is the organization structure stressor, and Option D is task demands.

questions.question: Organization structure becomes a cause of stress when there are:

options.a: Too many rules and too little chance to take part in decisions
options.b: Abundant resources and minimal time pressure
options.c: Too few rules and too much freedom

questions.explanation: Excessive rules and little opportunity to participate in decisions make structure a stressor. Option D describes setting clear goals with feedback, which actually reduces stress, and Option B describes conditions that foster innovation.

questions.question: Organizational leadership becomes a cause of stress when:

options.a: The job's working conditions and layout are poor
options.b: Co-workers give each other poor support
options.c: Management uses a style that creates tension, fear and anxiety, with unrealistic pressure to perform
options.d: An employee faces family and money problems

questions.explanation: Organizational leadership is a stressor when management's style creates tension, fear and anxiety and sets unrealistic pressure to perform. Option B is interpersonal demands, Option A is task demands, and Option D describes personal factors.

questions.question: A Type A personality is characterised by:

options.a: High self-confidence, persistence and energy in backing new ideas
options.b: A chronic sense of time urgency, an excessive competitive drive and difficulty enjoying leisure
options.c: A relaxed manner without time urgency or impatience
options.d: A preference for routine and dislike of change

questions.explanation: Type A people feel constant time urgency, are excessively competitive and find it hard to enjoy leisure. Option C describes Type B, and Option A describes the traits of an idea champion.

questions.question: Compared with a Type A person, a Type B person is:

options.a: More likely to feel hostility and anger
options.d: Relaxed, without time urgency or impatience

questions.explanation: Type B people are relaxed and do not feel time urgency or impatience. Options A, B and C all describe Type A characteristics.

questions.question: Research suggests that the harmful part of the Type A personality is:
questions.explanation: Research points to hostility and anger as the damaging part of Type A behaviour, not the hurry. Option C is the tempting trap, since time urgency is a Type A trait but not the harmful element.

questions.question: Which statement about stress is correct?

options.a: Stress is not always bad; it can bring opportunity, and it becomes a problem when it is excessive
options.b: Stress is always harmful and should be removed completely
options.c: Stress shows only as physical symptoms
options.d: Stress comes only from personal factors, never from the job

questions.explanation: Stress can bring opportunity, like the push an athlete feels before a big event, and becomes a problem only when it is excessive. Option D ignores job-related causes, and Option C ignores psychological and behavioural symptoms.

questions.question: Setting clear goals with feedback, for example through MBO, helps reduce stress mainly by reducing:
questions.explanation: Clear goals and feedback tell employees what is expected, which reduces role ambiguity. Option C and Option A are personal factors that goal-setting does not address.

questions.question: A realistic job preview, as a way to reduce stress, is given during:
questions.explanation: A realistic job preview is given during selection so applicants know what the job really involves before they accept it. Option A is a step in Lewin's change model, and Option B and Option D are OD techniques.

questions.question: Employee assistance programmes (EAPs) help reduce stress by:

options.b: Offering help such as counselling for employees' personal problems
options.c: Replacing tasks done by people with machines
options.d: Increasing the driving forces for change

questions.explanation: EAPs give employees help such as counselling for personal problems, along with time-management training. Option C is automation and Option A is structural change, neither of which targets stress directly.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a way for managers to reduce employee stress?

options.a: Redesigning jobs to give more autonomy and feedback
options.b: Raising performance targets suddenly with unrealistic pressure to perform

questions.explanation: Unrealistic pressure to perform is part of the organizational leadership stressor, so it adds stress rather than reducing it. Wellness programmes, better communication and job redesign (options A, C and D) are all ways to reduce stress.

questions.question: Wellness programmes that help reduce stress typically focus on:

options.a: Fitness, healthy eating and stopping smoking
options.b: Counselling for personal legal problems only

questions.explanation: Wellness programmes promote fitness, healthy eating and stopping smoking. Option B sounds like an EAP, Option C is structural change, and Option D is survey feedback.

questions.question: Careful employee selection reduces stress mainly because it:

options.c: Matches people to jobs so that their abilities fit the job
options.d: Removes the need to communicate during change

questions.explanation: Careful selection matches people to jobs so their abilities fit what the job requires, which lowers stress. Option D is wrong because communication still matters during change, and Option B would actually increase stress.

questions.question: Creativity is best defined as:

options.a: The ability to combine ideas in a unique way or to make unusual associations between ideas
options.b: Any alteration of people, structure or technology
options.c: Actively and enthusiastically supporting new ideas until they are implemented
options.d: Taking a creative idea and turning it into a useful product, service or method of operation

questions.explanation: Creativity is the ability to combine ideas uniquely or make unusual links between them. Option D is the definition of innovation, which puts the idea to use, and Option C describes what idea champions do.

questions.question: Innovation is best defined as:

options.b: Taking a creative idea and turning it into a useful product, service or method of operation
options.c: The ability to combine ideas in a unique way
options.d: Changing the attitudes groups hold about each other

questions.explanation: Innovation turns a creative idea into a useful product, service or method of operation. Option C and Option A both describe creativity, which produces the idea but does not put it to use.

questions.question: "The ability to combine ideas in a unique way or to make unusual associations between ideas" defines:
questions.explanation: This is the definition of creativity. Option B is the classic trap, because innovation is not the ability to combine ideas; it is turning a creative idea into something useful.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes creativity from innovation?

options.a: Creativity applies only to products, while innovation applies only to services
options.b: Creativity and innovation mean exactly the same thing
options.c: Creativity produces the idea, while innovation puts it to use
options.d: Innovation produces the idea, while creativity puts it to use

questions.explanation: Creativity produces the new idea, and innovation turns it into a useful product, service or method. Option D reverses the two, which is the most common mistake.

questions.question: A design team at a Lagos fintech produces dozens of original ideas every month, but none of them ever becomes a working product. The firm is:

options.c: Both highly creative and highly innovative

questions.explanation: Having many new ideas shows creativity, but innovation requires turning those ideas into results. Option D reverses this, since innovation is exactly the step this firm is missing.

questions.question: In the systems view of innovation, the inputs are:

options.c: A creative environment, process and situation
options.d: Abundant resources and minimal time pressure

questions.explanation: The inputs are creative people and groups. Option C is the transformation stage and Option A is the outputs stage of the same model.

questions.question: In the systems view of innovation, the transformation stage consists of:

options.c: A creative environment, process and situation

questions.explanation: The transformation stage is a creative environment, process and situation that turns inputs into outputs. Option A is the inputs and Option B is the outputs.

questions.question: In the systems view of innovation, the outputs are:

options.a: A creative environment, process and situation

questions.explanation: The outputs are innovative products and work methods. Option B is the inputs and Option A is the transformation stage.

questions.question: Which three sets of variables have been found to foster innovation?
questions.explanation: Innovation is fostered by structural, cultural and human resource variables. Option A lists stress symptoms, Option B is the systems view of innovation, and Option C lists job-related stressors.

questions.question: An organic structure, abundant resources and frequent communication between units are which type of variable that fosters innovation?
questions.explanation: Organic structure, abundant resources and frequent inter-unit communication are structural variables. Option D would include things like accepting ambiguity and tolerating risk, and Option C would include training and job security.

questions.question: Accepting ambiguity, tolerating the impractical and tolerating risk are which type of variable that fosters innovation?
questions.explanation: These are cultural variables, describing the values and attitudes an innovative organization holds. Option A covers design features like an organic structure and resources, and Option D covers training, job security and idea champions.

questions.question: Offering high job security and actively promoting training and development are which type of variable that fosters innovation?
questions.explanation: Training and development, high job security and encouraging idea champions are human resource variables. Option A is tempting, but cultural variables are about values such as tolerating risk and conflict.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a structural variable that fosters innovation?
questions.explanation: Accepting ambiguity is a cultural variable. Organic structure, minimal time pressure and work and nonwork support (options A, C and D) are all structural variables.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a cultural variable that fosters innovation?

options.b: Focusing on ends rather than means

questions.explanation: Abundant resources is a structural variable. Tolerating conflict, focusing on ends rather than means, and giving positive feedback (options B, C and D) are all cultural variables.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a human resource variable that fosters innovation?

options.a: Encouraging people to become idea champions

questions.explanation: Keeping external controls low is a cultural variable. High job security, encouraging idea champions and promoting training and development (options A, C and D) are the three human resource variables.

questions.question: An organic structure fosters innovation because it:

options.a: Has many rules that keep everyone focused
options.b: Concentrates all decisions at the top
options.c: Is flexible and adapts quickly, with low formalization, centralization and specialization
options.d: Relies on high specialization of tasks

questions.explanation: An organic structure has low formalization, centralization and specialization, so it is flexible and adapts quickly. Options A, B and D describe a mechanistic, rule-heavy structure, which stifles new ideas.

questions.question: Why is minimal time pressure listed as a structural variable that fosters innovation?

options.b: Extreme time pressure lowers creativity, even though people think it helps
options.c: Time pressure has no effect on creativity

questions.explanation: Extreme time pressure actually lowers creativity, even though many people believe it helps. Option A states the popular but mistaken belief.

questions.question: Abundant resources foster innovation because they allow a firm to:

options.d: Buy innovations, afford failures and try many ideas

questions.explanation: Plenty of resources let a firm buy innovations, afford failures and try out many ideas. Option A, Option B and Option C would all discourage innovation.

questions.question: At a paint manufacturer in Ota, staff who try new ideas that fail are not punished, and mistakes are treated as chances to learn. Which variable that fosters innovation does this show?

options.a: High job security, a human resource variable

questions.explanation: Letting staff try new things without fear of punishment, and treating mistakes as learning, is tolerating risk, a cultural variable. Option A is close, since job security also reduces fear of being fired, but the scenario is about the culture's attitude to failure.

questions.question: High job security is listed as a human resource variable that fosters innovation because it:

options.a: Reduces the fear of being fired for making mistakes

questions.explanation: High job security reduces the fear of being fired for mistakes, so people are more willing to try new ideas. Option C would lower creativity, and Option D would stifle new ideas.

questions.question: Having an open-system focus as a cultural variable that fosters innovation means the organization:

options.d: Focuses on means rather than ends

questions.explanation: An open-system focus means watching the environment and responding to it. Option B, Option D and Option A reverse the cultural variables, which call for low external controls, a focus on ends and tolerance of conflict.

questions.question: Idea champions are individuals who:

options.a: Act as catalysts and manage the whole change process
options.b: Actively and enthusiastically support new ideas, build support, overcome resistance and make sure innovations are implemented
options.c: Resist change because they have a lot invested in the current system
options.d: Use questionnaires to assess staff attitudes

questions.explanation: Idea champions enthusiastically back new ideas, build support, overcome resistance and see innovations through. Option A describes a change agent, who manages the change process as a whole, and Option C describes the people most likely to resist change.

questions.question: Which set of traits is shared by idea champions?

options.a: Low self-confidence and dependence on others
options.b: A preference for routine and caution
options.d: Very high self-confidence, persistence, energy and a tendency to take risks

questions.explanation: Idea champions have very high self-confidence, persistence, energy and a tendency to take risks. Option B describes resistance through habit, and Option C describes the harmful side of the Type A personality.

questions.question: Encouraging people to become idea champions is which type of variable that fosters innovation?
questions.explanation: Encouraging people to become idea champions is one of the three human resource variables, alongside training and high job security. Option D is tempting, but cultural variables are about values such as tolerating risk and ambiguity.

questions.question: A software engineer at an Abuja tech firm passionately promotes a new mobile payment idea, wins support from other departments, overcomes objections and pushes until the product is launched. She is acting as a(n):

options.d: Change agent from outside the firm

questions.explanation: Enthusiastically backing a new idea, building support, overcoming resistance and seeing it implemented is what an idea champion does. Option D is wrong because she is inside the firm and is pushing one innovation, and Option A is an outsider who explains interpersonal processes.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The study of the actions of people at work is known as:
questions.explanation: Organizational behaviour (OB) is the study of the actions of people at work, covering both individuals and groups. Option A deals with staffing activities such as recruiting and training, and Option D is about finding the one best way to do a task, so neither is the study of people's actions at work.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In organizational behaviour, the term 'behaviour' refers to:

options.a: The norms shared by members of a group
options.c: The attitudes people hold about their jobs
options.d: The personality traits a person inherits

questions.explanation: Behaviour simply means the actions of people, and OB studies those actions at work. Option C describes attitudes, which are evaluative statements rather than actions, and Option A describes norms, which are shared group standards.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Organizational behaviour focuses on which two areas?
questions.explanation: OB looks at two areas: how individuals behave at work and how groups behave. Option A names two topics studied under individual behaviour, not the two broad areas, and Option C names visible features of the organization rather than behaviour.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The three goals of organizational behaviour are to:
questions.explanation: OB aims to explain why people behave as they do, predict how they will behave, and influence that behaviour. Option B borrows the names of management functions, and Option A describes steps in the control process, not the goals of OB.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the goals of organizational behaviour?
questions.explanation: OB has three goals: to explain, predict and influence behaviour, so eliminating behaviour is not one of them. Options D, C and A are exactly the three goals.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: How many employee behaviours do managers specifically want to explain, predict and influence?
questions.explanation: There are six: employee productivity, absenteeism, turnover, organizational citizenship behaviour, job satisfaction and workplace misbehaviour. Option D is easy to confuse with the seven factors that influence individual behaviour, which is a different list.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the six employee behaviours that managers want to explain, predict and influence?
questions.explanation: Job involvement is one of the four job-related attitudes, not one of the six employee behaviours. Absenteeism, turnover and organizational citizenship behaviour (Options C, B and D) are all on the list of six, together with productivity, job satisfaction and workplace misbehaviour.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Employee productivity is best described as:

options.a: Discretionary behaviour that is not part of the formal job
options.b: An employee's general attitude towards his or her job
options.c: Failure to show up for work
options.d: A performance measure of both efficiency and effectiveness

questions.explanation: Productivity measures performance in terms of both efficiency and effectiveness. Option C is absenteeism, Option A is organizational citizenship behaviour and Option B is job satisfaction.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Failure to show up for work is called:
questions.explanation: Absenteeism means not showing up for work. Option A, turnover, is leaving the organization for good, and the two are often swapped in exams; Option D is putting in less effort in a group, not being absent.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Voluntary and involuntary permanent withdrawal from an organization is known as:
questions.explanation: Turnover is permanent withdrawal from the organization, whether the person resigns or is let go. Option B, absenteeism, is only failing to show up, and Option C is the last stage of a temporary group, not an employee leaving the firm.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In one year, 40 staff of a Lagos bank resigned and left for other banks, and 10 more were dismissed. Which employee behaviour does this describe?
questions.explanation: Turnover covers both voluntary (resigning) and involuntary (being dismissed) permanent withdrawal from the organization. Option B would apply only if the staff stayed employed but failed to show up for work.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Discretionary behaviour that is not part of an employee's formal job requirements but helps the organization work well is called:
questions.explanation: Organizational citizenship behaviour (OCB) is discretionary: nobody can order it, yet it helps the organization run well. Options D and A are job-related attitudes, not behaviours, and Option B is a measure of efficiency and effectiveness.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: At a manufacturing plant in Ota, Bola often stays late without being asked to help a colleague finish a team task, and she speaks well of the company to outsiders. Her behaviour is an example of:
questions.explanation: Helping a colleague, staying late to finish a team task and speaking well of the organization are classic examples of OCB, which is voluntary and not part of the formal job. Option B measures efficiency and effectiveness of performance in general, not voluntary extra-role helping.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Any intentional employee behaviour that could harm the organization or people in it is called:
questions.explanation: Workplace misbehaviour is any intentional behaviour that could harm the organization or the people in it. Option A is conflict that stops a group from reaching its goals, and Option D is reduced effort in a group, which is not defined by intent to harm.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Workplace misbehaviour takes four forms. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: The four forms of workplace misbehaviour are deviance, aggression, antisocial behaviour and violence. Absenteeism is a separate employee behaviour (failure to show up for work), not a form of misbehaviour.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: As one of the six employee behaviours managers study, job satisfaction refers to:

options.a: An employee's general attitude towards his or her job
options.b: How far an employee sees job performance as important to self-worth
options.c: Discretionary behaviour that helps the organization work well
options.d: How far an employee identifies with the organization and wants to stay

questions.explanation: Job satisfaction is an employee's general attitude towards his or her job. Option D describes organizational commitment and Option B describes job involvement, two other job-related attitudes.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In the 'organization as an iceberg' view, which of the following lies below the water (hidden)?
questions.explanation: The hidden part of the iceberg holds attitudes, perceptions, group norms, informal interactions and interpersonal and intergroup conflicts. Options B, A and D are formal, visible features that sit above the water.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In the 'organization as an iceberg' view, which of the following is visible above the water?
questions.explanation: Formal authority is part of the visible organization, together with strategies, objectives, policies and procedures, structure, technology and chain of command. Options A, D and C are hidden below the surface and harder to see.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Why is organizational behaviour compared to an iceberg?

options.a: Organizations are cold and impersonal places to work
options.b: Formal structure matters more than people's attitudes
options.c: Most of what drives behaviour at work lies below the surface and is harder to see
options.d: Only top managers can see the whole organization

questions.explanation: The iceberg image shows that the visible parts of an organization, such as structure and rules, are only a small part; attitudes, perceptions and norms sit hidden below and drive much of behaviour. Option B reverses the point, because the hidden human side is what matters most and is hardest to understand.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven factors that influence individual behaviour?
questions.explanation: The seven factors are personal ones: biography/demography, age, gender, societal responsibilities, marital status, personality, and values and attitudes. Organizational structure is a visible feature of the organization, not a factor of the individual.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the five factors that change individual behaviours?
questions.explanation: The five factors that change individual behaviours are demographic/biological factors, personality, values and attitudes, motivation and learning. Options A and D are visible organizational features, and Option B is a property of groups.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Who founded industrial psychology, the scientific study of people at work?
questions.explanation: Hugo Munsterberg founded industrial psychology, and his work links easily with scientific management. Option D, Robert Owen, is remembered for his concern about terrible working conditions, not for founding a field of study.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Industrial psychology is best described as:

options.a: The study of group decision making
options.b: The study of organizations as open systems
options.c: The scientific study of people at work
options.d: The study of how lighting affects productivity

questions.explanation: Industrial psychology, founded by Hugo Munsterberg, is the scientific study of people at work. Option D describes how the Hawthorne Studies began, and Option B relates to Chester Barnard's view of organizations.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which early supporter of organizational behaviour is best known for his concern about terrible working conditions?
questions.explanation: Robert Owen was concerned about the terrible working conditions of his time. Option D, Munsterberg, founded industrial psychology, and Option C, Barnard, saw organizations as social and open systems.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Who was one of the first to see that organizations could be studied through individual and group behaviour, and to whom the modern use of work groups is traced?
questions.explanation: Mary Parker Follett was one of the first to recognise that organizations could be viewed through individual and group behaviour, and the modern use of work groups traces back to her. Option D is tempting because Barnard also stressed human cooperation, but he is known for seeing organizations as social and open systems.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Who argued that organizations are social systems that need human cooperation and was the first to argue that they are open systems?
questions.explanation: Chester Barnard saw organizations as social systems requiring human cooperation and was the first to argue that they are open systems. Option A, Follett, is linked with studying organizations through individual and group behaviour.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The Hawthorne Studies originally began as tests of how which factor affects worker productivity?
questions.explanation: The Hawthorne Studies started as experiments on how lighting levels affect productivity. Their famous finding about social norms came later, so Option C, group size, and the other options were not the starting point.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The Hawthorne Studies concluded that the main drivers of individual work behaviour are:

options.d: Physical working conditions such as lighting

questions.explanation: The Hawthorne Studies found that social norms or group standards are the main drivers of individual work behaviour, which is why they made the biggest contribution to OB. Option D is tempting because the studies began by testing lighting, but lighting turned out not to be the main driver.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The Hawthorne Studies are most closely associated with:
questions.explanation: The Hawthorne Studies are linked with Elton Mayo and made the biggest contribution to OB of all the early efforts. Option C, Munsterberg, is linked with industrial psychology rather than the Hawthorne experiments.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which approach to management is most closely tied to concern for employee motivation?
questions.explanation: Organizational behaviour, with its focus on people's actions at work, is the approach most closely tied to concern for employee motivation. Option A, scientific management, focused mainly on finding the best way to do a task rather than on motivation.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following early efforts made the biggest contribution to organizational behaviour?
questions.explanation: The Hawthorne Studies made the biggest contribution to OB because they showed that social norms and group standards drive individual work behaviour. Option C founded industrial psychology, an important but smaller contribution.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Evaluative statements, either favourable or unfavourable, about objects, people or events are called:
questions.explanation: Attitudes are evaluative statements, favourable or unfavourable, that show how a person feels about something. Option B, perception, is the process of giving meaning to the environment by organizing and interpreting sensory impressions, and Option A, norms, are standards shared by a group.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Attitudes mainly show:

options.a: How a person organizes sensory impressions
options.b: How a group defines its leadership
options.c: How behaviour is shaped by its consequences
options.d: How a person feels about something

questions.explanation: Attitudes are evaluative statements that show how a person feels about objects, people or events. Option A describes perception and Option C describes operant conditioning.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: How many components does an attitude have?
questions.explanation: An attitude has three components: cognitive, affective and behavioural. Option A, four, is the number of job-related attitudes, which is a different list.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The component of an attitude made up of beliefs, opinions, knowledge and information is the:
questions.explanation: The cognitive component holds a person's beliefs, opinions, knowledge and information. Option C, the affective component, is about emotions and feelings, and Option B is the intention to behave in a certain way.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The emotional or feeling part of an attitude is called the:
questions.explanation: The affective component is made up of emotions and feelings. Option A, the cognitive component, is made up of beliefs and knowledge, which is the most common mix-up.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The component of an attitude that refers to an intention to behave in a certain way is the:
questions.explanation: The behavioural component is the intention to act in a certain way towards someone or something. Option B, the affective component, is the feeling part that often comes before that intention.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The statement "Discrimination is wrong" reflects which component of an attitude?
questions.explanation: "Discrimination is wrong" is a belief or opinion, which belongs to the cognitive component. Option B would be a feeling such as disliking someone, and Option A would be an intention such as avoiding someone.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The statement "I dislike Ade because he discriminates" reflects which component of an attitude?
questions.explanation: Disliking someone is an emotion or feeling, so it is the affective component. Option B would be a belief such as "discrimination is wrong", and Option A would be an intention such as "I will avoid Ade".

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The statement "I will avoid Ade" reflects which component of an attitude?
questions.explanation: "I will avoid Ade" states an intention to act in a certain way, which is the behavioural component. Option D is tempting because the intention grows out of a feeling of dislike, but the affective component is the feeling itself, not the planned action.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A nurse at a teaching hospital in Lagos says, "I feel frustrated and upset about the new night-shift roster." Which component of her attitude is she expressing?
questions.explanation: Feeling frustrated and upset is an emotion, so she is expressing the affective component. Option D would be a belief or piece of information about the roster, and Option A would be a stated intention, such as planning to ask for a transfer.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a component of an attitude?
questions.explanation: An attitude has three components: cognitive, affective and behavioural. Perception is a separate process of organizing and interpreting sensory impressions, not a component of an attitude.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: How many job-related attitudes are commonly identified?
questions.explanation: There are four job-related attitudes: job satisfaction, job involvement, organizational commitment and employee engagement. Option D, three, is the number of attitude components, and Option B, six, is the number of employee behaviours.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The degree to which a person identifies with his or her job, takes an active part in it and sees job performance as important to self-worth is called:
questions.explanation: Job involvement is about how far a person identifies with the job itself and ties self-worth to performing it well. Option C is about identifying with the organization and wanting to stay, which exams often swap with job involvement.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The degree to which an employee identifies with a particular organization and its goals and wishes to remain a member is called:
questions.explanation: Organizational commitment is about identifying with the organization and its goals and wanting to stay a member. Option A, job involvement, is about identifying with the job rather than the organization, and Option C, cohesiveness, describes attraction to a group.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: When employees are connected to, satisfied with and enthusiastic about their jobs, this is known as:
questions.explanation: Employee engagement means being connected to, satisfied with and enthusiastic about the job. Option B focuses on identifying with the job and tying self-worth to it, while Option D is a behaviour, not an attitude.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four job-related attitudes?
questions.explanation: Organizational citizenship behaviour is one of the six employee behaviours, not a job-related attitude. The four job-related attitudes are job satisfaction, job involvement, organizational commitment and employee engagement.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: What is the main difference between job involvement and organizational commitment?

options.a: Job involvement is a behaviour; organizational commitment is an attitude
options.b: Job involvement is about the organization; organizational commitment is about the job
options.c: Job involvement applies to managers; organizational commitment applies to workers
options.d: Job involvement is about identifying with the job; organizational commitment is about identifying with the organization

questions.explanation: Job involvement concerns the job itself, while organizational commitment concerns the organization and the wish to remain a member. Option B is the classic exam swap of the two, and Option A is wrong because both are job-related attitudes.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Tunde, an accountant at a manufacturing firm in Ota, believes strongly in the company's goals and says he would like to stay with the firm for the rest of his career, whatever role he holds. Which job-related attitude does he show most strongly?
questions.explanation: Identifying with the company and its goals and wanting to stay a member, regardless of role, is organizational commitment. Option A, job involvement, would focus on his particular job and how his self-worth depends on performing it, not on loyalty to the firm.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A lecturer in a university department feels that how well she teaches her courses is central to her sense of self-worth, and she takes an active part in every aspect of her job. Which job-related attitude is this?
questions.explanation: Identifying with the job, taking an active part in it and seeing performance as important to self-worth is job involvement. Option C would be about identifying with the university as an organization and wanting to stay there.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Any incompatibility or inconsistency between attitudes, or between behaviour and attitudes, is called:
questions.explanation: Cognitive dissonance is the inconsistency a person experiences between two attitudes, or between what he believes and how he behaves. Option C, role conflict, is facing different role expectations at the same time, which is about roles rather than attitudes.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The theory of cognitive dissonance was proposed by:
questions.explanation: Leon Festinger proposed cognitive dissonance theory. Option C, Skinner, is associated with operant conditioning, and Option A, Holland, with personality-job fit.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The effort a person puts into reducing cognitive dissonance depends on several factors. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.c: How important the elements causing the dissonance are
options.d: How much influence the person believes he or she has over the elements

questions.explanation: The three factors are the importance of the elements causing the dissonance, the influence the person believes he or she has over them, and the rewards involved. Age is not one of these factors, even though it does influence individual behaviour in general.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A production manager in Ota believes firms should not pollute, but he is told to dump waste into a nearby river. He feels less uncomfortable about this because the job pays very well. Which factor is reducing his dissonance?
questions.explanation: The high pay is a reward, and rewards are one of the three factors that affect how much dissonance a person feels. Option A would apply if he saw the issue itself as unimportant, which is not what the scenario says.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: When people notice an inconsistency between their attitudes and their behaviour, they typically:

options.b: Change the attitude or the behaviour, or find a reason for the gap
options.c: Ignore it, since inconsistency causes no discomfort
options.d: Ask others in the group to change their attitudes

questions.explanation: People seek consistency, so when they notice inconsistency they change the attitude or the behaviour, or develop a reason for the gap. Option C contradicts the idea of dissonance, which is uncomfortable precisely because people want consistency.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Managers commonly measure employees' attitudes using:
questions.explanation: Attitude surveys are the tool managers use to find out how employees feel about their work. Option A, the MBTI, is a personality assessment, not an attitude measure.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Employees who are satisfied with their jobs tend to have:

options.a: No difference in absenteeism or turnover

questions.explanation: Satisfied employees tend to show up more and stay longer, so both their absenteeism and their turnover are lower. Option B gets the relationship backwards, and Option C is wrong because satisfaction lowers turnover as well as absenteeism.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which statement about satisfied and engaged employees is correct?

options.a: They tend to give better customer service
options.b: They tend to have higher turnover
options.c: They are more likely to engage in workplace misbehaviour
options.d: They tend to put in less effort when working in groups

questions.explanation: Satisfied, engaged employees tend to give better customer service. Option B is wrong because satisfaction is linked with lower, not higher, turnover.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The unique combination of emotional, thought and behavioural patterns that affect how a person reacts to situations and interacts with others is called:
questions.explanation: Personality is a person's unique combination of emotional, thought and behavioural patterns. Option A, an attitude, is an evaluative statement about something, and Option C is the ability to notice and manage emotional cues.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A person's personality comes from:
questions.explanation: Personality is shaped by both heredity (genes) and environment. Options D and B each give only half of the picture.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following correctly lists the three factors that influence personality?
questions.explanation: Perception, emotions and religion are the three factors that influence personality. Option A lists the factors that influence perception, and Option C lists the factors used in attribution theory.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the Big Five personality traits?
questions.explanation: The Big Five are openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism (OCEAN). Locus of control is an important personality trait, but it is listed among the other traits, not in the Big Five.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In the Big Five model, a person who is imaginative, curious and artistically sensitive scores high on:
questions.explanation: Openness to experience covers being imaginative, curious and artistically sensitive. Option A, extraversion, is about being sociable, talkative and assertive.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In the Big Five model, being responsible, dependable, persistent and achievement-oriented describes:
questions.explanation: Conscientiousness describes people who are responsible, dependable, persistent and achievement-oriented. Option A, agreeableness, is about being good-natured, cooperative and trusting.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which Big Five trait describes a person who is sociable, talkative and assertive?
questions.explanation: Extraversion is the Big Five trait for being sociable, talkative and assertive. Option C, agreeableness, is about being good-natured and cooperative, which is different from being outgoing and assertive.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In the Big Five model, a person who is good-natured, cooperative and trusting is high on:
questions.explanation: Agreeableness covers being good-natured, cooperative and trusting. Option D, extraversion, is about being sociable, talkative and assertive.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which Big Five trait describes a person who is tense, anxious and insecure?
questions.explanation: Neuroticism describes being tense, anxious and insecure; its opposite end is emotional stability. Option A, introversion, is the opposite of extraversion on the MBTI social interaction dimension, not a Big Five trait about anxiety.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In some versions of the Big Five, neuroticism is replaced by its opposite end. That opposite is:
questions.explanation: Emotional stability (being calm and secure) is the opposite end of neuroticism; they are the same trait seen from opposite ends. Option C, extraversion, is a separate Big Five trait about sociability.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which Big Five trait is most consistently linked to job performance?
questions.explanation: Conscientiousness, being responsible, dependable and achievement-oriented, is the trait most consistently linked to job performance. Option D, extraversion, may help in social jobs, but it is not the trait most consistently tied to performance.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The memory aid OCEAN is used to remember:

options.d: The five dimensions of emotional intelligence

questions.explanation: OCEAN stands for openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism, the Big Five traits. Option D is tempting because emotional intelligence also has five dimensions, but they are self-awareness, self-management, self-motivation, empathy and social skills.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: How many personality types does the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) produce?
questions.explanation: The MBTI combines four dimensions, each with two ends, to give 16 personality types. Option D, 4, is the number of dimensions, not the number of types.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: How many dimensions does the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) use?
questions.explanation: The MBTI uses four dimensions: social interaction, preference for gathering data, preference for decision making and style of making decisions. Option B, 16, is the number of personality types those dimensions produce, and Option C, 5, is the number of Big Five traits.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: On the MBTI, the social interaction dimension runs between:
questions.explanation: Social interaction is the Extravert (E) versus Introvert (I) dimension. Option C is preference for gathering data, Option A is preference for decision making and Option D is style of making decisions.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: On the MBTI, the Sensing (S) versus Intuitive (N) dimension reflects a person's:
questions.explanation: Sensing versus Intuitive is about how a person prefers to gather data. Option A is the Feeling versus Thinking dimension, and Option B is the Perceptive versus Judgemental dimension.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: On the MBTI, a person's preference for decision making is described as:
questions.explanation: Preference for decision making is the Feeling (F) versus Thinking (T) dimension. Option A is preference for gathering data, and Option D describes locus of control, which is not part of the MBTI.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: On the MBTI, the Perceptive (P) versus Judgemental (J) dimension describes a person's:
questions.explanation: Perceptive versus Judgemental is the style of making decisions. Option C is tempting because it also mentions decisions, but preference for decision making is the Feeling versus Thinking dimension.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A person who believes "I control my own fate" has:
questions.explanation: An internal locus of control is the belief that you control your own fate. Option A, an external locus, is the belief that luck, chance or other people control your fate.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Chidi, a sales officer at a bank in Lagos, missed his target and says it was because of bad luck and his boss's unfair allocation of customers. Chidi most likely has:
questions.explanation: People with an external locus of control believe luck, chance or others control their fate, and they blame bosses or luck for poor results. Option A would lead Chidi to see the missed target as the result of his own actions.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Compared with people who have an external locus of control, people with an internal locus of control tend to be:

options.b: More likely to behave the same way in every situation
options.c: More satisfied with their jobs and more involved in them
options.d: Less satisfied and more likely to blame others

questions.explanation: Internals are more satisfied with their jobs and more involved. Option D describes externals, Option A describes people with low self-esteem, and Option B describes low self-monitors.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A person who is pragmatic, keeps emotional distance and believes that ends can justify means is high in:
questions.explanation: Machiavellianism ('Mach') describes someone who is pragmatic, emotionally distant and believes the ends justify the means. Option C, self-monitoring, is the ability to adjust behaviour to the situation, which is a different trait.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: High Machiavellians are most likely to do well in jobs that:

options.a: Involve working alone with no contact with others
options.b: Require bargaining or reward winning, such as sales or negotiating
options.c: Require following fixed routines with no room for judgement
options.d: Depend mainly on cooperation and trust

questions.explanation: High Machs do well in jobs that need bargaining or that reward winning, such as sales or negotiating. Option D fits agreeable people better, since High Machs keep emotional distance and are pragmatic rather than trusting.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The degree to which people like or dislike themselves is called:
questions.explanation: Self-esteem is how much people like or dislike themselves. Option D, self-monitoring, is the ability to adjust behaviour to the situation, and Option B, self-awareness, is a dimension of emotional intelligence.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which statement about self-esteem is correct?

options.a: People with low self-esteem prefer unconventional jobs
options.b: People with low self-esteem are more open to outside influence
options.c: People with high self-esteem avoid risk in their job choices
options.d: Self-esteem is the ability to adjust behaviour to the situation

questions.explanation: Low self-esteem people are more open to outside influence. High self-esteem people take more risks in job choice and like unconventional jobs, so Options C and A reverse the pattern, and Option D defines self-monitoring.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Funmi, a marketing executive in Lagos, is formal and reserved with senior clients, lively at staff parties, and patient with junior staff, changing her behaviour to suit each situation. She is best described as:

options.b: A person with an external locus of control

questions.explanation: High self-monitors adjust their behaviour to each situation and can show a different face in public. Option C, a low self-monitor, behaves the same way everywhere.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A factory manager in Ota regularly makes quick decisions based on very little information. In terms of personality, he is:
questions.explanation: Managers who take quick decisions on little information are high risk-takers; risk-taking is the willingness to take chances. Option B, self-monitoring, is about adjusting behaviour to situations, not about how much information a person needs before deciding.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A person who spots opportunities, shows initiative, takes action and keeps going until meaningful change happens has:
questions.explanation: A proactive personality spots opportunities, shows initiative, acts and persists until change happens. Option C is wrong because externals believe outside forces control their fate, which is the opposite of driving change yourself.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The ability to notice and manage emotional cues and information is called:
questions.explanation: Emotional intelligence (EI) is the ability to notice and manage emotional cues and information. Option D, empathy, is only one of EI's five dimensions, and Option C, self-monitoring, is about adjusting behaviour to situations.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a dimension of emotional intelligence?
questions.explanation: The five dimensions of EI are self-awareness, self-management, self-motivation, empathy and social skills. Conscientiousness is one of the Big Five personality traits, not an EI dimension.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: How many dimensions of emotional intelligence are there?
questions.explanation: Emotional intelligence has five dimensions: self-awareness, self-management, self-motivation, empathy and social skills. Option C, four, is the number of MBTI dimensions.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Emotional intelligence matters at all levels of an organization, but it is especially important in jobs that:

options.b: Need a lot of social interaction

questions.explanation: EI matters for success at all levels, especially in jobs that need a lot of social interaction, because those jobs depend on reading and managing emotions. Options A and D describe jobs with little contact with others, where EI matters less.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The theory that job satisfaction is highest and turnover lowest when a person's personality matches the job is associated with:
questions.explanation: Holland's personality-job fit theory holds that satisfaction is highest and turnover lowest when personality and job match. Option B, Festinger, proposed cognitive dissonance, and Option D, Skinner, is linked with operant conditioning.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of Holland's six personality types?
questions.explanation: Holland's six types are realistic, investigative, social, conventional, enterprising and artistic. 'Conscientious' sounds similar to 'conventional', but conscientiousness is a Big Five trait, not a Holland type.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which statement about personality across cultures is correct?

options.a: The Big Five appear across many cultures, while locus of control differs between cultures
options.b: Locus of control is the same in all cultures, while the Big Five differ
options.c: Personality traits have no link with culture at all
options.d: Neither the Big Five nor locus of control appears outside one culture

questions.explanation: The Big Five traits appear across many cultures, but locus of control differs because some cultures believe more strongly that people can control their environment. Option B reverses the two.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The process by which we give meaning to our environment by organizing and interpreting sensory impressions is called:
questions.explanation: Perception is the process of giving meaning to our environment by organizing and interpreting sensory impressions. Option A, attribution, is about judging the causes of people's behaviour, and Option C, learning, is a relatively permanent change in behaviour from experience.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The three factors that influence perception are the:

options.c: Perceiver, the target and the situation

questions.explanation: Perception is shaped by the perceiver, the target being perceived and the situation. Option D gives the three factors of attribution theory, and Option A gives the factors that influence personality.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three factors that influence perception?
questions.explanation: Perception depends on the perceiver, the target and the situation. Consensus is one of the three factors in attribution theory, not a factor of perception.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Two supervisors at a Lagos hospital watch the same nurse handle a patient and form very different views of her performance. This is best explained by differences in:

options.c: The perceivers' attitudes, interests, experience and expectations

questions.explanation: Two people can see the same thing and perceive it differently because of the perceiver's attitudes, interests, experience and expectations. Option B is about the nurse's own beliefs about control, which would not explain why the two observers disagree.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The theory that explains how we judge people differently depending on whether we see the cause of their behaviour as internal or external is called:
questions.explanation: Attribution theory explains how we judge people depending on whether we attribute their behaviour to internal causes (under their control) or external causes (forced by the situation). Option B is about learning by observation and experience, and Option A is about inconsistency between attitudes and behaviour.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Attribution theory uses which three factors to decide whether behaviour is internally or externally caused?
questions.explanation: The three attribution factors are distinctiveness, consensus and consistency. Option C lists the factors that influence perception, Option B lists shortcuts for judging others, and Option D lists factors in reducing cognitive dissonance.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In attribution theory, asking whether a person acts differently in different situations (whether the behaviour is unusual for him or her) concerns:
questions.explanation: Distinctiveness asks whether the behaviour is unusual for that person across different situations. Option C, consensus, compares the person with others in the same situation, and Option D, consistency, looks at the person's behaviour over time.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In attribution theory, asking whether others in the same situation behave the same way concerns:
questions.explanation: Consensus asks whether other people in the same situation act the same way; if they do (high consensus), the behaviour is judged external. Option C, consistency, asks whether the same person behaves this way over time.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In attribution theory, asking whether a person behaves the same way over time concerns:
questions.explanation: Consistency asks whether the person behaves this way regularly over time; high consistency points to an internal cause. Option C, consensus, compares the person with others in the same situation rather than with his or her own past behaviour.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In attribution theory, high consistency in a person's behaviour leads observers to judge the behaviour as:
questions.explanation: When a person behaves the same way over time (high consistency), observers attribute the behaviour to internal causes under the person's control. High distinctiveness and high consensus point to external causes, which is why Options C and D are wrong here.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In attribution theory, if everyone in the same situation behaves the same way (high consensus), the behaviour is likely to be judged as:
questions.explanation: High consensus means others in the same situation act the same way, which suggests the situation, not the person, caused the behaviour, so it is judged external. Option B would follow from high consistency, not high consensus.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Emeka, a clerk at a bank in Lagos, comes in late. All his colleagues arrive on time, Emeka is late most days, and he is also late for church and social events. How is his manager likely to explain his lateness?

options.b: As a result of high consensus
options.d: As a result of high distinctiveness

questions.explanation: Low consensus (others are on time), high consistency (often late) and low distinctiveness (late in other settings too) all point to an internal cause. Options B and D are wrong because consensus and distinctiveness are both low in this case.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: When judging the behaviour of others, the tendency to underestimate the influence of external factors and overestimate internal factors is called:
questions.explanation: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency, when judging others, to give too little weight to outside factors and too much to internal ones. Option A, self-serving bias, is about how we explain our own successes and failures, not other people's behaviour.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The tendency to credit our own successes to internal factors such as ability and effort, while blaming our failures on external factors such as luck, is called:
questions.explanation: Self-serving bias is crediting our own success to ability or effort and blaming our failures on outside factors. Option A, the fundamental attribution error, concerns how we judge other people, not ourselves.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: When her branch beat its targets, a bank manager in Lagos said it was due to her hard work and skill. When the branch missed its targets the next year, she blamed the poor economy. This illustrates:
questions.explanation: Taking credit for success (internal factors) and blaming failure on outside conditions (external factors) is self-serving bias. Option A would involve judging someone else's behaviour, not her own results.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
