questions.question: A supervisor in Ota decides that a new worker missed a delivery deadline because he is lazy, without considering that a truck breakdown delayed the goods. The supervisor is making:
questions.explanation: Blaming another person's poor result on internal causes (laziness) while ignoring outside factors (the truck breakdown) is the fundamental attribution error. Option B, self-serving bias, applies to explaining one's own successes and failures.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the shortcuts people use in judging others?
questions.explanation: The four shortcuts are selectivity, assumed similarity, stereotyping and the halo effect. Consistency is one of the three factors in attribution theory, not a shortcut.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Assuming that other people are like us is a judging shortcut also known as the 'like me' effect. Its formal name is:
questions.explanation: Assumed similarity, or the 'like me' effect, is assuming that others are like us. Option A, stereotyping, judges a person by our view of the group he or she belongs to, not by our own characteristics.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: During interviews at a firm in Lagos, a manager rates a candidate highly on every quality simply because the candidate is very good-looking. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: The halo effect is forming a general impression of someone from a single characteristic, such as looks or intelligence. Option C, stereotyping, would involve judging the candidate by a group he or she belongs to.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A hiring officer assumes that a candidate will be poor at numbers simply because of the group the candidate belongs to, without assessing the candidate's actual skills. This judging shortcut is:
questions.explanation: Stereotyping is judging someone on the basis of our view of the group he or she belongs to. Option C, the halo effect, forms a general impression from one personal characteristic rather than from group membership.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Taking in only bits and pieces of what we observe, based on our interests, background and attitudes, is the judging shortcut called:
questions.explanation: Selectivity means we absorb only parts of what we observe, filtered by our interests, background and attitudes. Option C, assumed similarity, is assuming others are like us.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Any relatively permanent change in behaviour that occurs as a result of experience is called:
questions.explanation: Learning is any relatively permanent change in behaviour that results from experience. Option C, shaping, is a method managers use to build up learning in steps, not the definition of learning itself.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The theory that behaviour is a function of its consequences, known as operant conditioning, is associated with:
questions.explanation: B. F. Skinner developed operant conditioning, which holds that behaviour is a function of its consequences. Option C, Festinger, proposed cognitive dissonance theory.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The learning theory which holds that behaviour is a function of its consequences is:
questions.explanation: Operant conditioning says people behave in ways that bring desired consequences and avoid undesired ones, so behaviour is a function of its consequences. Option B, social learning theory, stresses learning by observing others and through direct experience.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The theory that people learn by observing others and through direct experience is called:
questions.explanation: Social learning theory says people learn both by watching others and through their own direct experience. Option A, operant conditioning, focuses on consequences that follow a behaviour rather than on observing others.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Social learning depends on four processes. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: The four processes of social learning are attentional, retention, motor reproduction and reinforcement. Extinction is a method of shaping behaviour by removing a reward, not a social learning process.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A supervisor at a manufacturing company in Ota praises a worker each time he finishes his batch ahead of schedule, and the worker does so more often. This is:
questions.explanation: Positive reinforcement follows a behaviour with something pleasant, such as praise, which strengthens the behaviour. Option D, negative reinforcement, also strengthens behaviour, but by removing something unpleasant rather than adding something pleasant.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A manager in Lagos keeps nagging an officer about late reports, and stops nagging as soon as the officer submits on time. The officer now submits on time to avoid the nagging. This is:
questions.explanation: Negative reinforcement strengthens a behaviour by removing something unpleasant, here the nagging. Option A, punishment, would apply a penalty to weaken a behaviour, which is not what is happening.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes negative reinforcement from punishment?

options.a: They are two names for the same method
options.b: Both weaken behaviour, but punishment is harsher
options.c: Negative reinforcement strengthens behaviour by removing something unpleasant; punishment weakens behaviour
options.d: Negative reinforcement weakens behaviour; punishment strengthens it

questions.explanation: Negative reinforcement is not punishment: it strengthens behaviour by taking away something unpleasant, while punishment applies a penalty to weaken behaviour. Option B is the common trap of treating negative reinforcement as a form of punishment.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A hospital in Lagos suspends a cleaner without pay for repeatedly ignoring safety rules. Which method of shaping behaviour is being used?
questions.explanation: Punishment applies a penalty, such as suspension without pay, to weaken an undesired behaviour. Option C is the classic trap: negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant to strengthen a behaviour.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Removing the reward that has been keeping a behaviour going, so that the behaviour weakens, is called:
questions.explanation: Extinction weakens behaviour by withdrawing the reward that kept it going. Option C, punishment, also weakens behaviour, but by applying a penalty rather than removing a reward.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which two methods of shaping behaviour weaken behaviour?
questions.explanation: Punishment and extinction both weaken behaviour, while positive and negative reinforcement both strengthen it. Option C is the common mistake of treating negative reinforcement as if it weakens behaviour.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Guiding learning in graduated steps by systematically reinforcing each step that moves a person closer to the desired behaviour is called:
questions.explanation: Shaping behaviour means reinforcing each small step that brings a person closer to the desired behaviour. Option C, operant conditioning, is the broader theory that behaviour is a function of its consequences, not the step-by-step method itself.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: What is the main lesson for managers from learning theories?

options.a: Focus only on what they say, since staff ignore what managers do
options.b: Rely mainly on punishment, because it changes behaviour fastest
options.c: Reward the behaviour they want and model it themselves, because staff learn from what managers do
options.d: Avoid rewards, because they weaken desired behaviour

questions.explanation: Managers should reward the behaviours they want and model those behaviours, because staff learn from what managers do and not only from what they say. Option A is wrong because social learning shows employees learn by observing others, including their managers.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following are identified as current issues in organizational behaviour?

options.b: Generational differences at work and managing negative behaviour
options.c: Span of control and chain of command

questions.explanation: Two current OB issues are generational differences in the workplace and managing negative behaviour such as workplace misbehaviour. Option D relates to the early Hawthorne lighting experiments, not current issues.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Two or more interacting and interdependent individuals who come together to achieve specific goals form a:
questions.explanation: A group is two or more interacting and interdependent individuals who come together to achieve specific goals. Option B, a work team, goes further: its members work intensely on a common goal with positive synergy, mutual accountability and complementary skills.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which feature describes informal groups rather than formal groups?

options.a: Members have assigned roles and responsibilities
options.b: They are officially recognised by the organization
options.c: They form spontaneously, without official designation
options.d: They have a defined hierarchy, rules and procedures

questions.explanation: Informal groups are spontaneous, unstructured, based on relationships and not officially recognised. Options D, A and B are all features of formal groups.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of formal groups?

options.a: They are based on personal connections and social needs
options.b: They have a defined hierarchy, rules and procedures
options.c: They are formed for a specific organizational purpose
options.d: They are officially recognised by the organization

questions.explanation: Being based on relationships, personal connections and social needs is a feature of informal groups. Formal groups are purposeful, structured, have assigned roles and are officially recognised, as Options C, B and D state.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Staff at a university department in Lagos who regularly meet for lunch and chat because they enjoy each other's company form a:
questions.explanation: A friendship group like this forms naturally, has no official designation and is based on personal relationships, so it is an informal group. Options B and D are the two types of formal group, which the organization sets up for its own purposes.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a formal group?

options.a: Colleagues who meet for football after work
options.b: A friendship group of staff who eat lunch together
options.c: The finance department of a bank
options.d: A social club formed by employees

questions.explanation: Departments such as marketing and finance are formal groups, formed for a specific organizational purpose and officially recognised. Options B, D and A are informal groups that form spontaneously around social needs.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A formal group determined by the organization chart, made up of a supervisor and his or her direct subordinates, is a:
questions.explanation: A command group is set by the organization's hierarchy: a supervisor and the people who report directly to him or her, following the chain of command. Option D, a task group, brings people together to complete a specific task within a set timeframe and often disbands afterwards.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A hospital in Lagos brings together staff from several units to plan and complete a new patient records system within three months, after which the group will be disbanded. This is a:
questions.explanation: A task group is formed to complete a specific, defined task or project within a set timeframe and is often temporary. Option B, a command group, is a permanent supervisor-and-subordinates unit defined by the organization chart.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: At a manufacturing company in Ota, the production supervisor and the eight machine operators who report directly to him form a:
questions.explanation: A supervisor and his or her direct subordinates, as shown on the organization chart, make up a command group. Option D, a task group, is formed for a specific project within a set time, not by reporting lines.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The two types of formal group are:
questions.explanation: Formal groups come in two types: command groups, set by the hierarchy, and task groups, formed for a specific task. Option C names informal groups, and Option A names types of work team.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: How many stages of group development are there?
questions.explanation: Groups develop through five stages: forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning. Option B, four, is the number of stages a permanent group goes through, because adjourning applies only to temporary groups.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following shows the correct order of the stages of group development?
questions.explanation: Groups first form, then go through conflict (storming), then develop cohesion (norming), then focus on the task (performing), and temporary groups finally adjourn. Option B is the most common mistake, putting norming before storming.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: What is the third stage of group development?
questions.explanation: The order is forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning, so norming is the third stage. Option C, storming, is the second stage, when members fight over control.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The stage of group development marked by conflict over who will control the group and what it will do is:
questions.explanation: Storming is the stage of intragroup conflict over who controls the group and what it does, and it ends with a clear leadership hierarchy. Option A, forming, is marked by uncertainty as people join, not by open conflict over control.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The first stage of group development, in which people join and the group defines its purpose, structure and leadership amid much uncertainty, is:
questions.explanation: Forming is when people join the group and work out its purpose, structure and leadership, with a lot of uncertainty. Option A, storming, comes next and involves conflict over control.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The stage of group development in which close relationships and cohesiveness develop and shared expectations are set is:
questions.explanation: In norming, members develop close relationships and cohesiveness and agree on shared expectations. Option D, performing, follows once that structure is accepted and energy moves to the task.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The stage of group development in which the group structure is accepted and energy goes into the task is:
questions.explanation: In performing, the structure is fully functional and accepted, so members put their energy into the task. Option A, norming, is the earlier stage in which that structure and cohesion are still being built.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The final stage of development for temporary groups, in which they wrap up activities and prepare to break up, is:
questions.explanation: Adjourning is the stage in which a temporary group, such as a task force, wraps up and prepares to break up. Option D, performing, is the last stage for permanent groups, not the wrap-up stage of temporary ones.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: For a permanent work group, which stage of group development is the last stage?
questions.explanation: For permanent groups, performing is the last stage. Option D, adjourning, applies only to temporary groups such as task forces that break up when their work is done.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The storming stage of group development ends when:

options.a: A clear leadership hierarchy has emerged
options.b: Members have agreed on the task and are fully productive
options.c: The group breaks up after finishing its task
options.d: New members first join the group

questions.explanation: Storming ends with a relatively clear hierarchy of leadership within the group. Option B describes performing, and Option C describes adjourning.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Behaviour patterns expected of someone occupying a given position in a social unit are called:
questions.explanation: A role is the set of behaviour patterns expected of someone in a given position. Option C, norms, are standards shared by all group members, not expectations tied to one position.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A unit head at a bank in Lagos is expected by his regional manager to cut overtime, while his staff expect him to fight for more overtime pay. He is experiencing:
questions.explanation: Role conflict happens when an individual faces different role expectations at the same time, like a manager expected to please both the boss and his staff. Option C is about inconsistency within one person's attitudes and behaviour, not clashing expectations from others.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Standards or expectations that are accepted and shared by a group's members are called:
questions.explanation: Norms are standards or expectations accepted and shared by group members. Option A, roles, are expectations attached to a particular position rather than shared by the whole group.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Common group norms typically cover:
questions.explanation: Common norms cover work effort and performance, as well as dress and loyalty. Option A describes the formal structure, which is set by the organization rather than shared informally by group members.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In the Asch study, people compared line lengths after others in the room deliberately gave a wrong answer, and many went along with the wrong answer. The study shows:

options.a: That people credit success to their own ability
options.b: The pressure to conform to group norms
options.c: That large groups are better at problem solving
options.d: The effect of lighting on productivity

questions.explanation: Asch found that many people conformed to an obviously wrong group answer, showing the strong pressure to conform to group norms. Option D relates to the start of the Hawthorne Studies, and Option A describes self-serving bias.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A prestige grading, position or rank within a group is called:
questions.explanation: Status is a prestige grading, position or rank within a group, and it can be formal or informal. Option B, a role, is the behaviour expected in a position, not the prestige attached to it.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of informal status in a group?

options.a: A member's education, age or skill
options.b: The size of a member's office
options.d: A member's position on the organization chart

questions.explanation: Informal status comes from things like education, age or skill. Options C and B are sources of formal status, such as titles and offices.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: For status to work well in a group, members need to believe that:

options.b: Everyone has exactly the same status
options.d: Status is based only on age

questions.explanation: Group members need to believe the status hierarchy is fair; if they do not, it creates problems in the group. Option B is wrong because groups naturally have different status levels, formal and informal.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which statement about group size is correct?

options.a: Small groups finish tasks faster, while large groups are better for problem solving and diverse input
options.b: Group size has no effect on how a group performs
options.c: Large groups finish tasks faster, while small groups give more diverse input
options.d: Small groups are always better than large groups

questions.explanation: Small groups complete tasks faster, while large groups (about 12 or more) are better for problem solving and getting diverse input. Option C reverses the two findings.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The tendency for individuals to put in less effort when working collectively than when working alone is called:
questions.explanation: Social loafing is reduced individual effort when working in a group compared with working alone. Option D, groupthink, is pressure on an individual to align his or her opinion with the group, not reduced effort.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A manager in a Lagos firm notices social loafing in a large project group. The best way to reduce it is to:

options.a: Make each person's contribution identifiable and measurable
options.b: Reward only the group's total output

questions.explanation: Social loafing happens when individual effort cannot be identified, so making each person's contribution measurable reduces it. Option B would make the problem worse, because rewarding only total output hides who did what.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The degree to which members are attracted to a group and share its goals is called:
questions.explanation: Cohesiveness is how far members are attracted to the group and share its goals. Option C, organizational commitment, is about identifying with the whole organization, not with a particular group.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A group with high cohesiveness whose goals are aligned with the organization's goals will most likely show:
questions.explanation: High cohesiveness combined with goals aligned to the organization produces a strong increase in productivity. Option C, a moderate increase, is the result of low cohesiveness with aligned goals.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A highly cohesive group whose goals are NOT aligned with the organization's goals will most likely show:
questions.explanation: When a highly cohesive group pursues goals that conflict with the organization's, productivity falls, because the group's strength works against the organization. Option B is the result of low cohesiveness with goals not aligned.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A group with low cohesiveness but goals aligned with the organization's goals will most likely show:
questions.explanation: Low cohesiveness with aligned goals gives a moderate increase in productivity. Option A, a strong increase, needs both high cohesiveness and aligned goals.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A group with low cohesiveness and goals NOT aligned with the organization's goals will most likely show:
questions.explanation: Low cohesiveness with goals not aligned has no significant effect on productivity. Option C, a decrease, happens when cohesiveness is high but goals are not aligned.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: When a group puts heavy pressure on an individual to align his or her opinion with the opinions of the others, this is called:
questions.explanation: Groupthink is the heavy pressure a group places on an individual to bring his or her opinion into line with the others. Option B, social loafing, is about reduced effort, and Option A, cohesiveness, is simply attraction to the group.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of group decision making?

options.a: It increases acceptance of the solution
options.c: It provides more complete information and knowledge

questions.explanation: Being time-consuming is a disadvantage of group decision making. Options C, D and A are advantages, together with greater legitimacy.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is a disadvantage of group decision making?
questions.explanation: Minority domination, where a few members control the outcome, is a disadvantage, along with time cost, pressure to conform and ambiguous responsibility. Options A, B and D are all advantages of deciding as a group.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is an advantage of group decision making?
questions.explanation: Group decisions tend to be seen as more legitimate, which is one of their advantages along with more information, more alternatives and greater acceptance. Options A, D and C are all disadvantages.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In group decision making, 'ambiguous responsibility' means that:

options.a: Members feel pressure to agree with the majority
options.b: It is unclear which member is accountable for the final decision
options.c: The group takes too long to decide

questions.explanation: Ambiguous responsibility is the disadvantage that, because the whole group decides, no single member is clearly responsible for the outcome. Option D is minority domination and Option A is pressure to conform, which are separate disadvantages.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A group whose members work intensely on a specific, common goal using positive synergy, individual and mutual accountability, and complementary skills is a:
questions.explanation: A work team is defined by intense work on a common goal, positive synergy, individual and mutual accountability and complementary skills. Option B, a task group, is brought together for a defined task but does not by definition have these team features.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following correctly contrasts groups and teams?

options.a: Groups have shared goals; teams have individual goals
options.b: Groups have high interdependence; teams have limited interdependence
options.c: Groups put heavy emphasis on collaboration; teams put less
options.d: Groups have individual accountability; teams have shared accountability

questions.explanation: In groups accountability is individual, while in teams it is shared. Options A, B and C reverse the real differences: teams, not groups, have shared goals, high interdependence and heavy emphasis on collaboration.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In terms of focus, groups and teams differ because:

options.a: Groups focus on individual performance; teams focus on collective performance
options.b: Both focus only on collective performance
options.c: Groups focus on collective performance; teams focus on individual performance
options.d: Both focus only on individual performance

questions.explanation: Groups focus on individual performance, while teams focus on collective performance. Option C reverses the difference.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: How many key differences between groups and teams are commonly identified?
questions.explanation: There are five differences: accountability, goals, interdependence, focus and collaboration. Option A, eight, is the number of characteristics of effective teams.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the points on which groups and teams differ?
questions.explanation: Groups and teams differ on accountability, goals, interdependence, focus and collaboration. Organization size is not one of these points.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Teams are said to create positive synergy. This means that:

options.a: Conflict is completely removed from the team
options.b: Each member works alone towards a personal goal
options.c: The whole is greater than the sum of the parts
options.d: The team needs no leader at all

questions.explanation: Positive synergy means the team's combined effort produces more than the members could achieve separately; the whole is greater than the sum of the parts. Groups do not create this, so Option B, which describes individual work, is the opposite idea.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: How does leadership typically differ between groups and teams?

options.a: In a group leadership is shared; in a team one leader is in charge
options.b: Both always have a single leader with full control
options.c: In a team leadership is often shared; in a group one leader is clearly in charge and delegates
options.d: Neither groups nor teams have leaders

questions.explanation: Team leadership is often shared among members, while a group has one leader who is clearly in charge and delegates work. Option A reverses the two.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: How many types of work team are commonly identified?
questions.explanation: There are four types: problem-solving, self-managed, cross-functional and virtual teams. Option C, five, is the number of differences between groups and teams.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A team made up of members from the same department who meet to improve work activities or solve specific problems is a:
questions.explanation: A problem-solving team draws members from the same department to improve work or solve problems. Option D, a cross-functional team, draws members from different specialities or departments.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A formal group of employees with no manager, responsible for a complete work process or segment, is a:
questions.explanation: A self-managed team operates without a manager and is responsible for a complete work process or segment. Option B, a command group, is the opposite: it is built around a supervisor and his or her direct subordinates.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A bank in Lagos sets up a team of staff from operations, IT, marketing and legal to design a new mobile banking product. This is a:
questions.explanation: A cross-functional team brings together members from different specialities or departments. Option D, a problem-solving team, draws its members from the same department.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: A software firm has developers in Lagos, Abuja and Port Harcourt who never meet in person and work together through video calls and shared online tools. They form a:
questions.explanation: A virtual team uses technology to link members who are physically apart. Option B is about members coming from different departments, not about being linked by technology across locations.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: What is the key difference between a problem-solving team and a self-managed team?

options.a: Problem-solving teams are linked only by technology, while self-managed teams meet face to face
options.b: Problem-solving teams draw members from different departments, while self-managed teams use one department
options.c: Problem-solving teams make suggestions but usually cannot carry them out, while self-managed teams plan, schedule, assign work and decide for themselves
options.d: Problem-solving teams have no manager, while self-managed teams report to a supervisor

questions.explanation: Problem-solving teams can recommend improvements but usually cannot implement them, whereas self-managed teams take full responsibility for planning, scheduling, assigning work and deciding. Option D reverses the role of the manager, and Option A describes a virtual team.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: How many characteristics of effective teams are commonly identified?
questions.explanation: Effective teams have eight characteristics: clear goals, relevant skills, mutual trust, unified commitment, good communication, negotiating skills, appropriate leadership, and internal and external support. Option B, five, is the number of differences between groups and teams.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the characteristics of effective teams?
questions.explanation: Effective teams have clear goals, relevant skills, mutual trust, unified commitment, good communication, negotiating skills, appropriate leadership, and internal and external support. Strict individual competition works against the shared goals and collaboration that define teams.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the characteristics of effective teams?
questions.explanation: Internal and external support is one of the eight characteristics of effective teams. Options A and D are disadvantages of group decision making, and Option C reduces group effort.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Perceived incompatible differences that result in interference or opposition are called:
questions.explanation: Conflict is perceived incompatible differences that lead to interference or opposition. Option D, cognitive dissonance, is inconsistency within a person's own attitudes or between attitudes and behaviour.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: How many views of conflict are commonly identified?
questions.explanation: There are three views of conflict: traditional, human relations and interactionist. Option D, five, is the number of conflict-handling styles.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The view that conflict is bad and must be avoided is the:
questions.explanation: The traditional view holds that conflict is bad and must be avoided. Option D, the human relations view, sees conflict as natural and inevitable and not necessarily negative.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The view that conflict is a natural and inevitable outcome in any group and need not be negative is the:
questions.explanation: The human relations view says conflict is natural and inevitable and need not be negative. Option C, the interactionist view, goes further by arguing that some conflict is actually necessary for a group to perform well.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The view that some conflict is necessary for a group to perform effectively is the:
questions.explanation: The interactionist view holds that some conflict is necessary for a group to perform well. Option B, the human relations view, accepts conflict as natural but does not argue that it is necessary for performance.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: What is the difference between functional and dysfunctional conflict?

options.a: Functional conflict supports group goals and improves performance; dysfunctional conflict prevents the group from reaching its goals
options.b: Functional conflict is about relationships; dysfunctional conflict is about tasks
options.c: Functional conflict is always avoided; dysfunctional conflict is encouraged
options.d: Functional conflict occurs only in teams; dysfunctional conflict occurs only in groups

questions.explanation: Functional conflict supports the group's goals and improves its performance, while dysfunctional conflict stops the group from reaching its goals. Option B is wrong because relationship conflict is almost always dysfunctional, not functional.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Conflict over the content and goals of the work is called:
questions.explanation: Task conflict concerns the content and goals of the work. Option D, process conflict, is about how the work gets done, and Option C, relationship conflict, is about interpersonal relationships.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Conflict about how work gets done is called:
questions.explanation: Process conflict is conflict over how the work gets done, such as who does what. Option D, task conflict, is about the content and goals of the work rather than the method.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Two officers in a university department constantly clash because of personal dislike for each other, not because of the work itself. This type of conflict is:
questions.explanation: Relationship conflict focuses on interpersonal relationships, and it is almost always dysfunctional. Option D, task conflict, would be about the content and goals of their work.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which type of conflict is almost always dysfunctional?
questions.explanation: Relationship conflict is almost always dysfunctional. Options C and B describe levels of conflict that can actually be functional for a group.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the five conflict-handling styles?
questions.explanation: The five conflict-handling styles are avoiding, accommodating, forcing, compromising and collaborating. Delegating is a way of assigning work, not a way of handling conflict.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Withdrawing from or suppressing a conflict is the conflict-handling style called:
questions.explanation: Avoiding means withdrawing from or suppressing the conflict. Option B, accommodating, deals with the conflict by putting the other party's needs first, rather than stepping away from it.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: In a dispute over leave dates, a nurse at a Lagos hospital lets her colleague have the dates she wanted, putting the colleague's needs above her own. Which conflict-handling style is she using?
questions.explanation: Accommodating is putting the other party's needs above your own. Option B, compromising, would require both nurses to give up something, not one side giving way completely.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Satisfying your own needs at the expense of the other party is the conflict-handling style called:
questions.explanation: Forcing means satisfying your own needs at the other party's expense. Option D, accommodating, is the opposite: putting the other party's needs above your own.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Two department heads at a manufacturing firm in Ota both want the full training budget. They agree that each will take half and drop some planned courses. This is:
questions.explanation: Compromising is a style in which each side gives up something. Option A, collaborating, would look for a win-win solution that fully satisfies both parties rather than each giving something up.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The conflict-handling style that seeks a win-win solution satisfying all parties is:
questions.explanation: Collaborating aims for a win-win solution that satisfies everyone involved. Option D, compromising, settles the conflict by having each side give up something, so no party is fully satisfied.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: What tends to happen to a group that has too little conflict?

options.a: It moves straight to the adjourning stage
options.b: It becomes dull and slow to change

questions.explanation: Too little conflict makes a group dull and slow to change, while too much makes it chaotic. Option D describes the effect of too much conflict.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: The three ways managers can shape team behaviour are:
questions.explanation: Managers shape team behaviour by selecting people with teamwork skills, training them in areas like problem solving and conflict management, and rewarding cooperation and team results. Option B lists stages of group development, and Option C lists methods of shaping individual behaviour.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: When a manager uses rewards to shape team behaviour, the rewards should mainly recognise:

options.a: Only the individual with the highest output
options.c: Cooperation and team results, not only individual effort

questions.explanation: To build teamwork, rewards should recognise cooperation and team results, not only individual effort. Option A would encourage members to compete rather than work together.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Global teams bring more ideas, but they commonly face problems of:

options.c: Too few members to share work

questions.explanation: Global teams bring more ideas but face problems of language, culture and trust. Option B is the opposite of their real strength, which is a wider range of ideas.

questions.topic: Individual Behaviour, Groups and Work Teams
questions.question: Teams take more time and resources than individuals working alone. They are most appropriate when:

options.a: The work is simple and can be done by one person
options.b: Speed matters more than anything else
options.c: The work is complex, needs different perspectives and members depend on one another
options.d: Members work on unrelated individual tasks

questions.explanation: Teams are worth their extra time and resources when the work is complex, needs different perspectives and requires interdependence. Options A and D describe work an individual can handle alone, where a team adds cost without benefit.

questions.question: Motivation refers to:
questions.explanation: Motivation is the process that energizes and directs employees to put in effort toward goals, so encouraging them to work effectively fits best. Option A, punishment, is not motivation in the management sense. Options C and D describe workload and supervision.

questions.question: According to Maslow, the highest level of need is:
questions.explanation: In Maslow's hierarchy, self-actualization, the need to reach one's full potential, sits at the top. Physiological needs (A) are at the bottom, followed by safety (B), then social needs, then esteem (C), which is just below self-actualization.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of intrinsic motivation?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic motivation comes from inside a person, such as the satisfaction of achieving something. Promotions, salary increases and bonuses (A, C and D) are all external rewards given by the organization, so they are extrinsic motivators.

questions.question: Extrinsic motivation is driven by:

options.b: External rewards like bonuses or recognition.

questions.explanation: Extrinsic motivation comes from outside rewards such as pay, bonuses, promotions or recognition. Options A and C describe inner drives, which are intrinsic motivation. Team collaboration (D) is a way of working, not a type of motivation.

questions.question: Maslow's "safety needs" in motivation include:
questions.explanation: Safety needs cover security and protection, such as a stable job and health insurance. Recognition and respect (A) are esteem needs, and personal growth (C) is self-actualization. Financial independence (D) is not one of Maslow's safety needs as such.

questions.question: Maslow's theory is important in management because it:
questions.explanation: Maslow's hierarchy shows that people are driven by different levels of needs, which helps managers understand what motivates each employee. Option C is wrong because the theory covers social, esteem and growth needs as well as money. Options A and D contradict the theory.

questions.question: Motivating employees effectively requires:

options.a: Understanding their individual needs and goals.

questions.explanation: People are motivated by different things, so managers need to understand each employee's needs and goals. Option C, a one-size-fits-all approach, ignores those differences. Options B and D remove the feedback that helps managers motivate staff.

questions.question: Which of the following is not an assumption of Maslow's theory?

options.a: People's behaviour is not based on their needs
options.b: A person moves to the next higher level of the hierarchy only when the lower need is satisfied
options.c: Satisfaction of such needs influences their behaviour
options.d: A satisfied need can no longer motivate a person; only the next higher-level need can motivate him

questions.explanation: Maslow's theory assumes that behaviour is driven by needs, so saying behaviour is NOT based on needs contradicts it. Options B, C and D are real assumptions of the theory: people move up the hierarchy as lower needs are met, needs shape behaviour, and a satisfied need stops motivating.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a content theory of motivation
questions.explanation: Vroom's expectancy theory is a process theory: it explains how people decide how much effort to put in, based on what they expect to get. Options A, B and C, from McClelland, Herzberg and Maslow, are content theories, because they focus on what needs motivate people.

questions.question: Which of the following is not an example of a financial incentive?
questions.explanation: Job enrichment is a non-financial incentive: it makes work more interesting by adding variety, responsibility and control. Profit sharing, perquisites (perks) and co-partnership all give employees money or money's worth, so they are financial incentives.

questions.question: Identify the correct sequence of steps involved in the motivation process.

options.a: Unsatisfied need, tension, drives, search behaviour, satisfied behaviour, reduction of tension
options.b: Tension, drives, search behaviour, unsatisfied need, satisfying behaviour, reduction of tension
options.c: Search behaviour, reduction of tension, unsatisfied need, tension, drives, satisfied behaviour
options.d: Drives, search behaviour, unsatisfied need, tension, satisfying behaviour, reduction of tension

questions.explanation: Motivation starts with an unsatisfied need. The need creates tension, the tension creates drives, and the drives lead to search behaviour. When the need is satisfied, the tension is reduced. Options B, C and D jumble this order, for example by putting tension or drives before the need that causes them.

questions.question: These needs are most basic in the hierarchy of motivation theory and correspond to primary needs
questions.explanation: Physiological needs, such as food, water, shelter and sleep, form the base of Maslow's hierarchy. They are the primary needs for survival. Option D, security needs, comes next, and B and C are higher-level needs.

questions.question: The process by which a person's efforts are energized, directed and sustained toward attaining a goal is known as:
questions.explanation: Motivation is exactly this process: effort that is energized, directed and kept going until a goal is reached. Option A is the wider function of influencing people, of which motivating is only one part, so it is not the term defined here.

questions.question: Motivation is best described as the process by which a person's efforts are:

options.a: Energized, directed and sustained toward attaining a goal
options.b: Combined into tasks that form complete jobs
options.c: Rewarded or punished according to their consequences
options.d: Compared with the inputs and outcomes of relevant others

questions.explanation: Motivation means effort that is energized, given direction and sustained toward a goal. Option C describes reinforcement theory, which looks at consequences after behaviour rather than defining motivation itself.

questions.question: How many key elements make up the definition of motivation?
questions.explanation: Motivation has three elements: energy, direction and persistence. Option D is wrong because leaving out any one of these, such as persistence, gives an incomplete picture of motivated effort.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three elements of motivation?
questions.explanation: The three elements of motivation are energy, direction and persistence, so satisfaction is the odd one out. Options B, C and D are all genuine elements: intensity of drive, effort channelled toward goals, and continued effort over time.

questions.question: Which element of motivation is described as a measure of intensity or drive?
questions.explanation: Energy is the intensity or drive behind a person's effort. Option B is about where that effort is channelled (toward organizational goals), not how intense it is.

questions.question: The element of motivation that refers to effort being channelled toward organizational goals is:
questions.explanation: Direction means the effort is pointed toward goals the organization wants. Option D only measures how intense the effort is; intense effort aimed at the wrong things is not what organizations need.

questions.question: Bisi, a sales officer at a bank in Lagos, keeps calling prospective customers week after week despite many rejections, until she meets her deposit target. Which element of motivation does she mainly show?
questions.explanation: Persistence is about continuing to put in effort over time to achieve goals, which is what Bisi does despite rejections. Option D, energy, is the intensity of effort at a point in time, while her story is mainly about keeping going.

questions.question: A manager notices that some very energetic employees are putting great effort into activities that do not help the organization. Which element of motivation is missing?
questions.explanation: High energy alone is not enough; effort must also have the right direction, toward goals the organization wants. Option B is wrong because these employees clearly have plenty of energy already.

questions.question: How many steps are there in the motivation process?
questions.explanation: The motivation process has six steps: unsatisfied need, tension, drives, search behaviour, satisfied need and reduction of tension. Option B misses one stage, usually the final reduction of tension.

questions.question: The motivation process begins with:
questions.explanation: Everything starts with an unsatisfied need, which then creates tension. Option B is the second step; tension is the result of the unsatisfied need, not its starting point.

questions.question: In the motivation process, what does an unsatisfied need directly create?
questions.explanation: An unsatisfied need creates tension, the second step of the process. Option C comes next: drives are produced by the tension, not directly by the need.

questions.question: What is the third step in the motivation process?
questions.explanation: The order is unsatisfied need, tension, drives, so drives is the third step. Option A is the second step and option C is the fourth.

questions.question: In the motivation process, which step immediately follows drives?
questions.explanation: Drives push the person to search for ways to satisfy the need, so search behaviour comes next. Option D only comes after the search has succeeded.

questions.question: The final step in the motivation process is:
questions.explanation: When the need is met, tension falls, so reduction of tension is the sixth and last step. Option D is the fifth step; meeting the need is what causes the tension to reduce afterwards.

questions.question: Motivation that comes from inside the person, such as enjoying the work itself, is called:
questions.explanation: Intrinsic motivation comes from within, such as a personal sense of achievement or enjoying the work itself. Option B is driven by external rewards like pay, bonuses or promotion.

questions.question: Ngozi, a nurse at a hospital in Ibadan, takes extra shifts mainly to earn overtime bonuses and improve her chances of promotion. Her motivation is mainly:
questions.explanation: Extrinsic motivation is driven by external rewards such as pay, bonuses and promotion, which is what Ngozi is chasing. Option C would apply if she worked the shifts mainly because she enjoys the work itself.

questions.question: A lecturer in a university department spends extra evenings refining her course simply because she enjoys the work itself. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Enjoying the work itself is a classic driver of intrinsic motivation, which comes from inside the person. Option A would need an external reward, such as a bonus or promotion, to be the driver.

questions.question: Which of these would drive extrinsic motivation in an employee?

options.a: Feeling a personal sense of achievement
options.c: Being promoted to a higher post
options.d: Taking pride in doing a task well

questions.explanation: Promotion is an external reward, so it drives extrinsic motivation. Options A and B come from inside the person and are therefore intrinsic.

questions.question: Which of the following is a process theory of motivation?
questions.explanation: Process theories explain how motivation works, and Adams's equity theory is one of them, along with Vroom's expectancy and Locke and Latham's goal-setting theory. Options B, C and D are content theories, which explain what motivates people.

questions.question: Content theories of motivation differ from process theories in that content theories focus on:

options.b: How people compare their rewards with others

questions.explanation: Content theories such as Maslow, Herzberg and McClelland explain what motivates people. Option C describes process theories, such as Vroom's expectancy theory, which explain how motivation works.

questions.question: Locke and Latham's goal-setting theory is classified as a:
questions.explanation: Goal-setting theory explains how motivation works, so it sits with Vroom and Adams among the process theories. Option B is wrong because content theories, like Maslow's, explain what motivates rather than how.

questions.question: Motivating employees is part of which management function?
questions.explanation: Motivating employees falls under leading, also called directing. Option A is about checking performance against standards, and option B is about setting goals, so neither is where motivation sits.

questions.question: The hierarchy of needs theory of motivation was proposed by:
questions.explanation: Abraham Maslow proposed that people have five needs arranged in a hierarchy from physiological to self-actualization. Option B, Herzberg, is known for the two-factor theory of motivators and hygiene factors, not a hierarchy.

questions.question: How many levels of needs are there in Maslow's hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Maslow's hierarchy has five levels: physiological, safety, social, esteem and self-actualization. Option D is the number of needs in McClelland's theory, which is a common mix-up.

questions.question: In Maslow's hierarchy, which need is at the second level, directly above physiological needs?
questions.explanation: Safety needs, such as protection from harm, job security and pensions, come second. Option C, social needs for belonging and friendship, comes third, after safety is satisfied.

questions.question: Which need occupies the third level of Maslow's hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Social needs for affection, belonging, acceptance and friendship sit at level three. Option C, esteem, is the fourth level and only becomes dominant once social needs are largely met.

questions.question: In Maslow's hierarchy, esteem needs are found at which level?
questions.explanation: Esteem is the fourth level, just below self-actualization. Option C is wrong because the fifth and highest level is self-actualization, not esteem.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly shows Maslow's needs from lowest to highest?
questions.explanation: Maslow's order runs physiological, safety, social, esteem and then self-actualization at the top. Option A swaps safety and social, but safety needs must be met before belonging becomes the main concern.

questions.question: Maslow's lower-order needs are:
questions.explanation: The lower-order needs are the first two levels, physiological and safety. Option C wrongly includes social needs, which belong with esteem and self-actualization among the higher-order needs.

questions.question: According to Maslow, lower-order needs are satisfied mainly:

options.b: Internally, through personal growth and self-respect
options.d: Externally, through things like pay, contracts and tenure

questions.explanation: Lower-order needs (physiological and safety) are satisfied mainly from outside the person, for example by pay, contracts and tenure. Option B describes higher-order needs, which are satisfied internally.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a higher-order need in Maslow's hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Safety is a lower-order need, together with physiological needs. Options A, C and D are the three higher-order needs, which are satisfied internally.

questions.question: A manufacturer in Ota introduces a pension scheme and protects workers from harm on the factory floor. Which level of Maslow's needs is it mainly addressing?
questions.explanation: Protection from harm and pensions are examples of safety needs at work. Option D, physiological needs, covers food, water, shelter and the basic pay needed to buy them.

questions.question: Staff at a new branch of a Lagos bank say they mainly want to feel accepted and to make friends with their colleagues. Which of Maslow's needs is dominant for them?
questions.explanation: Social needs cover affection, belonging, acceptance and friendship. Option C, esteem, is about self-respect, status and recognition rather than simply fitting in with others.

questions.question: A senior accountant in Abuja is mainly driven by wanting a respected title, status and recognition from colleagues. Which of Maslow's needs is most active?
questions.explanation: Status, recognition and attention are the external side of esteem needs. Option A, social needs, is about belonging and friendship, not being looked up to.

questions.question: Which of the following is an EXTERNAL esteem factor in Maslow's hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Maslow splits esteem into internal factors (self-respect, autonomy, achievement) and external factors (status, recognition, attention). Status is external because it comes from how others see you, while options C, A and B are internal.

questions.question: A professor in a university department says her main aim now is to grow and achieve her full potential as a scholar. Which need is she trying to satisfy?
questions.explanation: Self-actualization is about growth, achieving one's potential and self-fulfilment. Option C, esteem, is about self-respect, status and recognition, which is close but is not the same as reaching one's full potential.

questions.question: According to Maslow, what happens once a need has been substantially satisfied?

options.a: It must be satisfied again before any other need can arise
options.b: It no longer motivates, and the person moves up to the next level
options.c: It becomes a stronger motivator than before
options.d: It turns into a hygiene factor that prevents dissatisfaction

questions.explanation: Maslow held that a substantially satisfied need stops motivating, so the person moves up to the next need. Option D borrows Herzberg's language of hygiene factors, which belongs to a different theory.

questions.question: Which of the following is an assumption of Maslow's hierarchy of needs?

options.a: Needs come in a fixed order
options.b: People compare their input-outcome ratios with others
options.c: Behaviour depends only on its consequences
options.d: A satisfied need continues to motivate

questions.explanation: Maslow assumed that behaviour is based on needs, that needs come in a fixed order and that a satisfied need stops motivating. Option C describes reinforcement theory, and option D contradicts Maslow directly.

questions.question: Theory X and Theory Y were proposed by:
questions.explanation: Douglas McGregor described two sets of assumptions managers hold about workers, a negative Theory X and a positive Theory Y. Option C, Maslow, proposed the hierarchy of needs instead.

questions.question: Under Theory X, managers assume that workers:

options.c: See work as a natural activity

questions.explanation: Theory X is the negative view: workers have little ambition, dislike work, avoid responsibility and must be closely controlled. Options A, B and C are Theory Y assumptions.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a Theory Y assumption about workers?

options.a: They accept and actually seek responsibility
options.b: They must be closely controlled to work well
options.c: They see work as a natural activity

questions.explanation: Needing close control is a Theory X assumption, part of McGregor's negative view of workers. Options A, C and D all reflect the positive Theory Y view.

questions.question: A production manager in an Ota factory believes his workers have little ambition, so he watches them closely all day. His view of workers reflects:
questions.explanation: Believing workers lack ambition and must be closely controlled is the Theory X view. Option A, Theory Y, assumes workers can direct themselves and seek responsibility.

questions.question: Because he believed Theory Y assumptions were more valid, McGregor proposed:

options.a: Heavier use of punishment to stop unwanted behaviour
options.c: Removing responsibility from jobs to reduce stress
options.d: Participation in decisions and responsible, challenging jobs

questions.explanation: McGregor favoured Theory Y and proposed participation in decisions, responsible and challenging jobs, and good group relations. Option B fits Theory X thinking, which he considered less valid.

questions.question: Which statement about McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y is correct?

options.a: McGregor believed Theory X assumptions were more valid
options.b: Research has proved that Theory Y assumptions are valid
options.c: There is no evidence that acting on Theory Y always makes workers more motivated
options.d: Theory X represents a positive view of workers

questions.explanation: There is no evidence that either set of assumptions is valid, or that acting on Theory Y always raises motivation. Option B overstates the evidence, and option A is wrong because McGregor favoured Theory Y.

questions.question: The motivation-hygiene theory, also called the two-factor theory, was developed by:
questions.explanation: Frederick Herzberg split work factors into motivators and hygiene factors, hence the two-factor or motivation-hygiene theory. Option A, McClelland, is linked with the needs for achievement, power and affiliation.

questions.question: In Herzberg's theory, hygiene factors:

options.a: Are intrinsic factors linked to the work itself
options.b: Are the needs at the top of the hierarchy
options.c: Remove dissatisfaction but do not motivate

questions.explanation: Hygiene factors, such as pay, policy and working conditions, only remove dissatisfaction; they do not motivate. Option D describes motivators, which create satisfaction.

questions.question: Which of the following is a motivator in Herzberg's two-factor theory?
questions.explanation: Responsibility is one of Herzberg's motivators, along with achievement, recognition, the work itself, advancement and growth. Options A, B and D are hygiene factors that only prevent dissatisfaction.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a hygiene factor in Herzberg's theory?
questions.explanation: Advancement is a motivator, because it relates to growth in the job itself. Options A, C and D are hygiene factors, which only stop workers from being dissatisfied.

questions.question: In Herzberg's two-factor theory, salary is classified as:
questions.explanation: Salary is a hygiene factor: poor pay causes dissatisfaction, but good pay alone does not motivate. Option C is the common trap, since things like recognition, not salary, are the motivators.

questions.question: According to Herzberg, the opposite of satisfaction is:
questions.explanation: Herzberg argued that satisfaction and dissatisfaction lie on separate scales, so the opposite of satisfaction is no satisfaction. Option B is the traditional view that Herzberg rejected.

questions.question: On Herzberg's separate scales, the opposite of dissatisfaction is:
questions.explanation: Herzberg's second scale runs from dissatisfaction to no dissatisfaction, which is where hygiene factors act. Option D is wrong because removing dissatisfaction does not automatically create satisfaction.

questions.question: A Lagos bank improves its working conditions, supervision and company policies. Staff stop complaining, but they are not any more motivated. Which idea best explains this?
questions.explanation: Working conditions, supervision and policy are hygiene factors: fixing them removes dissatisfaction and makes workers calm, not motivated. Option A, Theory Y, is about managers' positive assumptions about workers, not about which factors motivate.

questions.question: Herzberg's motivators are mainly related to:

options.b: The working conditions around the job

questions.explanation: Herzberg said that to motivate, managers must use the motivators, which are about the job itself, such as responsibility and achievement. Options A, B and C are hygiene factors that surround the job.

questions.question: In Herzberg's theory, hygiene factors and motivators are respectively described as:
questions.explanation: Hygiene factors are extrinsic, while motivators are intrinsic. Option C reverses the pair, which is a common error.

questions.question: Herzberg's work led to growing interest in which approach to job design?
questions.explanation: Herzberg's focus on motivators in the job itself drove interest in job enrichment, which adds responsibility to jobs. Option B, job enlargement, only adds more tasks of the same kind.

questions.question: The three-needs theory of motivation is associated with:
questions.explanation: David McClelland identified the needs for achievement, power and affiliation. Option D, Maslow, proposed five needs arranged in a hierarchy.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the needs in McClelland's three-needs theory?
questions.explanation: McClelland's three needs are achievement, power and affiliation. Esteem is a level in Maslow's hierarchy, not one of McClelland's needs.

questions.question: In McClelland's theory, the drive to succeed and excel in relation to a set of standards is the need for:
questions.explanation: The need for achievement (nAch) is the drive to excel against a set of standards. Option B, power, is about making others behave in ways they would not otherwise have behaved.

questions.question: The need to make others behave in a way they would not have behaved otherwise is McClelland's need for:
questions.explanation: This is the need for power (nPow), which is about influencing others' behaviour. Option C, achievement, is about excelling against standards rather than controlling people.

questions.question: An administrative officer at a hospital in Enugu cares most about having friendly and close relationships with her co-workers. In McClelland's terms she is high in the need for:
questions.explanation: The need for affiliation (nAff) is the desire for friendly and close interpersonal relationships. Option B, safety, belongs to Maslow's hierarchy rather than McClelland's three needs.

questions.question: According to McClelland, high achievers prefer jobs that offer:

options.a: Shared responsibility, delayed feedback and low risk
options.b: Close supervision, fast feedback and no risk
options.c: Personal responsibility, little feedback and very high risk
options.d: Personal responsibility, fast feedback and moderate risk

questions.explanation: High achievers like personal responsibility, fast feedback and moderate risk, and they avoid tasks that are very easy or very hard. Option C is wrong because high achievers prefer moderate risk, not very high risk.

questions.question: McClelland found that the best managers tend to be:

options.a: High in the need for achievement and low in the need for power
options.b: High in the needs for both affiliation and achievement
options.c: High in the need for power and low in the need for affiliation
options.d: High in the need for affiliation and low in the need for power

questions.explanation: The best managers tend to be high in power and low in affiliation. Option A is tempting, but a high need to achieve does not by itself make someone a good manager.

questions.question: Goal-setting theory of motivation was proposed by Edwin Locke and later developed with:
questions.explanation: Goal-setting theory is credited to Edwin Locke, later developed with Gary Latham. Option A, Vroom, proposed expectancy theory, which is a different process theory.

questions.question: Goal-setting theory states that:

options.a: People compare their input-outcome ratios with others
options.b: Setting specific and challenging goals motivates people
options.c: Behaviour is a function of its consequences
options.d: A satisfied need no longer motivates

questions.explanation: Goal-setting theory holds that specific and challenging goals motivate people. Option C is the central idea of reinforcement theory, which looks at consequences after behaviour.

questions.question: According to goal-setting theory, which kind of goals lead to higher performance?

options.a: Very difficult goals that cannot realistically be reached
options.b: Vague, easy goals with no feedback
options.c: Clear, difficult but attainable goals accompanied by feedback
options.d: General goals such as 'do your best'

questions.explanation: Goals that are clear, difficult but attainable and accompanied by feedback lead to higher performance. Option D is wrong because goals that are too difficult cause discouragement.

questions.question: Compared with a general instruction to 'do your best', specific goals:

options.b: Only work when the employee sets them alone
options.c: Have exactly the same effect on performance

questions.explanation: Specific goals raise performance more than a vague 'do your best'. Option B is wrong because a goal does not need to be self-set to work; assigned goals can also be effective.

questions.question: According to goal-setting theory, difficult goals, once accepted:

options.a: Only matter when combined with punishment
options.c: Result in lower performance than easy goals
options.d: Result in higher performance than easy goals

questions.explanation: Once employees accept them, difficult goals produce higher performance than easy ones. Option B confuses accepted hard goals with goals that are too difficult, which are the ones that discourage people.

questions.question: In SMART goals, the letter S stands for:
questions.explanation: S stands for Specific: the goal is clear and well defined, answering who, what, where, when and why. Option A sounds similar, but a goal can be simple and still vague.

questions.question: Which SMART element requires that progress can be tracked with numbers, percentages or other concrete indicators?
questions.explanation: Measurable means progress can be tracked with concrete indicators such as numbers or percentages. Option C, specific, is about the goal being clear and well defined, not about how progress is tracked.

questions.question: A SMART goal that is realistic, challenging but within reach, satisfies which element?
questions.explanation: Achievable (also called attainable) means the goal is realistic, challenging but within reach. Option B, relevant, is about how well the goal fits wider objectives and values.

questions.question: The SMART element which requires that a goal fits the person's or organization's overall objectives and values is:
questions.explanation: Relevant means the goal fits the overall objectives and values of the person or organization. Option C, achievable, is about whether the goal is realistic, not whether it fits the bigger picture.

questions.question: A department head at a university sets the goal 'publish two research papers', but gives no date by which they must be done. Which SMART element is missing?
questions.explanation: Time-bound goals have a specific deadline, and this goal has none. Option D is already met, because 'two papers' is a number that can be tracked.

questions.question: A branch manager at a Lagos bank changes the goal 'increase deposits' to 'increase savings deposits by 15% by the end of the third quarter'. The new goal is better mainly because it is:

options.a: Set without any input from the manager
options.c: Easier to achieve than the old goal

questions.explanation: The rewritten goal names exactly what to increase, by how much and by when, so it is specific, measurable and time-bound. Option C is wrong because the change makes the goal clearer, not easier.

questions.question: Achievable is included in SMART goals mainly because goals that are too difficult:
questions.explanation: Goals that are too difficult discourage people, which is why SMART requires goals to be achievable. Option D mixes up two elements: a very hard goal can still be measured.

questions.question: In goal-setting, which type of feedback is considered more powerful?

options.a: Feedback given after the goal has been abandoned
options.b: Feedback given by a supervisor once a year
options.c: Self-generated feedback, where the employee tracks their own progress

questions.explanation: Self-generated feedback, where employees track their own progress, is more powerful than feedback from others. Option B is feedback from others, and coming only once a year it does little to show the gap while work is going on.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of allowing employees to participate in setting their goals?

options.a: It always produces higher performance than assigned goals
options.b: They are more likely to accept a hard goal
options.c: It removes the need for feedback
options.d: It makes goals easier to reach

questions.explanation: Participation makes people more likely to accept a difficult goal. Option A is wrong because participation does not always beat assigned goals in terms of performance.

questions.question: In goal-setting theory, a person's belief that they are capable of performing a task is called:
questions.explanation: Self-efficacy is a person's belief that they can do the task, and it affects how well goal-setting works. Option A, goal commitment, is how determined someone is to reach the goal, not their belief in their own ability.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a condition that affects the results of goal-setting?
questions.explanation: Goal commitment, self-efficacy, the type of task and national culture all affect how well goals work. Hygiene factors come from Herzberg's two-factor theory and are not a condition of goal-setting.

questions.question: Management by objectives (MBO), in which goals are agreed between manager and employee, applies the ideas of:
questions.explanation: MBO uses goals agreed between manager and employee, which is the goal-setting idea in practice. Option A, reinforcement theory, focuses on consequences after behaviour rather than on goals set beforehand.

questions.question: The theory which holds that behaviour is a function of its consequences is:
questions.explanation: Reinforcement theory says behaviour is a function of its consequences. Option B, goal-setting, looks at the goal before the action rather than the consequence after it.

questions.question: Consequences that, coming immediately after a behaviour, increase the chance that the behaviour will be repeated are called:
questions.explanation: Reinforcers are consequences that follow a behaviour straight away and make it more likely to happen again. Option B, motivators, is Herzberg's term for job factors that create satisfaction.

questions.question: Reinforcement theory is most closely linked with:
questions.explanation: Reinforcement theory is linked to B. F. Skinner. Option D, Edwin Locke, is the name behind goal-setting theory.

questions.question: Reinforcement theory differs from most other motivation theories because it:

options.a: Focuses mainly on the goals people set before acting
options.b: Depends on comparisons with relevant others
options.c: Is built on a fixed hierarchy of five needs
options.d: Ignores inner needs, goals and expectations and looks only at consequences

questions.explanation: Reinforcement theory ignores inner needs, goals and expectations and looks only at what happens after a person acts. Option A describes goal-setting theory instead.
