questions.question: According to reinforcement theory, how should managers deal with unwanted behaviour where possible?

options.a: Reward it so it stops naturally
options.b: Ignore it rather than punish it
options.c: Set a harder goal for the employee

questions.explanation: Managers should ignore rather than punish unwanted behaviour where possible. Option D is tempting, but punishment's effect is often temporary and it can have unpleasant side effects.

questions.question: Which statement about punishment is correct in reinforcement theory?

options.a: It is the best long-term way to change behaviour
options.b: It has no effect on behaviour at all
options.c: It increases the chance that a behaviour will be repeated
options.d: It stops behaviour faster, but the effect is often temporary and can have unpleasant side effects

questions.explanation: Punishment stops behaviour faster, but the effect is often temporary and can have unpleasant side effects. Option A is wrong for that reason, which is why ignoring unwanted behaviour is preferred.

questions.question: A supervisor at a factory in Ota praises a machine operator immediately after he finishes a batch ahead of schedule. The operator starts finishing early more often. This is best explained by:
questions.explanation: Praise given right after the behaviour acted as a reinforcer, making the behaviour more likely to be repeated. Option B would apply if a target had been set before the work began; here it is the consequence after the action that matters.

questions.question: Goal-setting theory and reinforcement theory differ in that goal-setting focuses on __________, while reinforcement focuses on __________.

options.a: The goal before the action; the consequence after the action
options.c: The consequence after the action; the goal before the action

questions.explanation: Goal-setting is about the goal before the action, while reinforcement is about the consequence after the action. Option C simply reverses the two.

questions.question: The way tasks are combined to form complete jobs is called:
questions.explanation: Job design is the way tasks are combined to form complete jobs. Option B, job scope, is narrower: it is just the number of tasks a job has and how often they are repeated.

questions.question: The number of different tasks a job requires and how often those tasks are repeated is known as:
questions.explanation: Job scope is the number of different tasks in a job and how often they are repeated. Option C, job depth, is the degree of control employees have over their work.

questions.question: The degree of control employees have over their work is called:
questions.explanation: Job depth is the degree of control employees have over their work. Option C, job scope, counts the tasks in the job rather than the control the person has over them.

questions.question: Horizontal expansion of a job by increasing job scope is known as:
questions.explanation: Job enlargement expands a job horizontally by adding more tasks of the same kind, increasing its scope. Option B, job enrichment, is vertical expansion that adds planning and evaluating responsibilities.

questions.question: Vertical expansion of a job by adding planning and evaluating responsibilities is known as:
questions.explanation: Job enrichment expands a job vertically by adding planning and evaluating responsibilities. Option C, job enlargement, only adds more tasks of the same kind without more control.

questions.question: Job enlargement and job enrichment are respectively described as:

options.b: Vertical and horizontal expansion of a job
options.c: Horizontal and vertical expansion of a job
options.d: Increases in job depth and job scope

questions.explanation: Enlargement is horizontal (more tasks) and enrichment is vertical (more responsibility). Option B reverses them, and option D reverses the link to scope and depth.

questions.question: Job enrichment increases a job's:
questions.explanation: Job enrichment increases job depth, meaning the employee gains more control through planning and evaluating responsibilities. Option D describes job enlargement, which raises scope.

questions.question: A clerk at a bank in Lagos who used to only sort mail is now also asked to deliver it and copy documents. His level of control over the work is unchanged. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Adding more tasks of the same kind without more control is job enlargement. Option D, job enrichment, would require giving him planning or evaluating responsibilities.

questions.question: A records officer at a hospital in Ibadan is now allowed to plan the delivery routes for files and check the quality of the work done. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Adding planning and quality-checking duties gives the officer more control and responsibility, which is job enrichment. Option A, job enlargement, would only add more tasks at the same level.

questions.question: The job characteristics model (JCM) was developed by:
questions.explanation: Hackman and Oldham developed the job characteristics model with its five core job dimensions. Option A, Locke and Latham, are associated with goal-setting theory.

questions.question: How many core job dimensions are there in the job characteristics model?
questions.explanation: The JCM has five core dimensions: skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy and feedback. Option D, three, is the number of critical psychological states, not the dimensions.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the five core job dimensions in the job characteristics model?
questions.explanation: Growth-need strength is a personal trait that affects how well the model works, not a core job dimension. Options B, C and D are all among the five core dimensions.

questions.question: In the JCM, the degree to which a job requires a range of activities, skills and talents is called:
questions.explanation: Skill variety is how far a job needs a range of activities, skills and talents. Option A, task identity, is about completing a whole, identifiable piece of work.

questions.question: The JCM dimension describing how far a job requires completion of a whole, identifiable piece of work is:
questions.explanation: Task identity is the degree to which a job involves completing a whole, identifiable piece of work. Option A, task significance, is about how much the job affects other people.

questions.question: A nurse at a teaching hospital in Lagos knows that her work directly affects whether patients recover. Which core job dimension is high in her job?
questions.explanation: Task significance is how much a job affects the lives or work of other people, which is clearly high for a nurse. Option B, task identity, is about completing a whole piece of work, not the impact on others.

questions.question: In the job characteristics model, freedom and discretion in scheduling the work and choosing methods is called:
questions.explanation: Autonomy is the freedom and discretion a worker has over scheduling and methods. Option A, job scope, is simply the number of tasks in the job and how often they are repeated.

questions.question: In the JCM, direct and clear information about how well one is performing is called:
questions.explanation: Feedback is the core dimension that gives direct, clear information on how well one is performing. Option C, reinforcement, is a separate theory about consequences that follow behaviour.

questions.question: How many critical psychological states does the job characteristics model identify?
questions.explanation: The JCM identifies three critical psychological states: experienced meaningfulness, experienced responsibility and knowledge of actual results. Option A, five, is the number of core job dimensions.

questions.question: In the job characteristics model, autonomy leads to which critical psychological state?

options.b: Knowledge of the actual results of the work

questions.explanation: Autonomy leads to experienced responsibility for outcomes. Option D, experienced meaningfulness, comes from skill variety, task identity and task significance together.

questions.question: In the job characteristics model, the feedback dimension leads to:

options.c: Knowledge of the actual results of the work

questions.explanation: Feedback gives the worker knowledge of the actual results of the work. Option D is produced by autonomy, not feedback.

questions.question: Which three core job dimensions combine to produce experienced meaningfulness of the work?

options.a: Skill variety, task identity and task significance

questions.explanation: Skill variety, task identity and task significance together create experienced meaningfulness. Option C is wrong because autonomy and feedback lead to the other two states.

questions.question: When the three critical psychological states are present, which of the following is NOT an expected outcome?
questions.explanation: The outcomes are high internal motivation, high-quality performance, high satisfaction and low absenteeism and turnover. High absenteeism is the opposite of what the model predicts.

questions.question: The job characteristics model works best for employees who:

options.d: Have a high need for affiliation

questions.explanation: The model works best for people with high growth-need strength, who want to grow on the job. Option D is a McClelland need, not the condition the JCM depends on.

questions.question: Equity theory of motivation was developed by:
questions.explanation: J. Stacy Adams developed equity theory, in which employees compare their input-outcome ratios with others. Option B, Vroom, is the name behind expectancy theory, another process theory.

questions.question: Equity theory proposes that an employee:

options.a: Acts according to the expectation that effort will lead to a valued outcome
options.b: Is motivated by specific and challenging goals
options.c: Moves up a hierarchy once lower needs are satisfied
options.d: Compares their job's input-outcome ratio with that of relevant others and acts to correct any inequity

questions.explanation: Equity theory says employees compare their input-outcome ratio with relevant others and act to correct any unfairness. Option A describes Vroom's expectancy theory.

questions.question: In equity theory, which of the following is an INPUT?
questions.explanation: Inputs are what the employee brings to the job, such as effort, experience, education and skill. Options A, C and D are outcomes the employee receives.

questions.question: In equity theory, which of the following is an OUTCOME?
questions.explanation: Outcomes are what the employee gets from the job, such as pay, recognition and promotion. Options A, B and C are inputs the employee contributes.

questions.question: How many referents do employees use for comparison in equity theory?
questions.explanation: There are three referents: other, system and self. Option A leaves one out, often the system referent of pay policies and procedures.

questions.question: In equity theory, when an employee compares themselves with the organization's pay policies and procedures, the referent being used is:
questions.explanation: The system referent is the organization's pay policies and procedures. Option C, other, refers to people such as colleagues in similar jobs, friends, neighbours or professional associates.

questions.question: A machinist in an Ota factory judges his present pay against what he earned in his own previous job. Which equity referent is he using?
questions.explanation: The self referent is the person's own past experience, such as an earlier job. Option D, other, would mean comparing with another person, such as a co-worker or friend.

questions.question: An accountant at a Lagos bank compares her rewards with those of a friend who does a similar job at another firm. Which referent is she using?
questions.explanation: The other referent includes people in similar jobs in the same organization, plus friends, neighbours or professional associates. Option D, self, would mean comparing with her own past experience.

questions.question: Tunde, a lecturer, believes he puts in the same effort and qualifications as a colleague in his department but receives far lower outcomes. In equity theory, Tunde feels:
questions.explanation: When an employee's input-outcome ratio is lower than a referent's, they feel under-rewarded. Option C applies when the employee gets more outcomes than their inputs justify compared with others.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a likely response to perceived inequity?

options.a: Moving up to the next level of Maslow's hierarchy
options.d: Changing one's own inputs, for example by working less

questions.explanation: Responses to inequity include distorting inputs or outcomes, getting others to change theirs, changing one's own inputs or outcomes, choosing a different referent or quitting. Moving up Maslow's hierarchy belongs to a different theory and is not a response to inequity.

questions.question: The perceived fairness of the amount and allocation of rewards among people is called:
questions.explanation: Distributive justice is about the fairness of the amount and allocation of rewards. Option A, procedural justice, is about the fairness of the process used to decide those rewards.

questions.question: The perceived fairness of the process used to decide how rewards are shared is known as:
questions.explanation: Procedural justice concerns the fairness of the process used to share rewards. Option A, distributive justice, concerns the fairness of the amounts people actually receive.

questions.question: Compared with procedural justice, distributive justice has a greater effect on employees':
questions.explanation: Distributive justice has more effect on satisfaction. Options A, B and C are the things procedural justice affects more: trust in the boss, commitment and intention to quit.

questions.question: Expectancy theory of motivation is associated with:
questions.explanation: Victor Vroom proposed expectancy theory, built on expectancy, instrumentality and valence. Option D, Adams, developed equity theory, which is about fairness comparisons.

questions.question: Expectancy theory states that a person acts in a certain way based on:

options.a: The expectation that the act will be followed by a given outcome and how attractive that outcome is
options.b: The consequences that followed similar behaviour in the past
options.c: The lowest unsatisfied need in a hierarchy
options.d: A comparison of their input-outcome ratio with that of others

questions.explanation: Vroom's theory says behaviour depends on the expectation that an act leads to an outcome and on how attractive that outcome is. Option D describes equity theory instead.

questions.question: In expectancy theory, the effort-performance linkage ('If I work hard, will I perform well?') is called:
questions.explanation: Expectancy is the effort-performance linkage. Option B, instrumentality, is the next link, from performance to reward.

questions.question: In Vroom's theory, the performance-reward linkage ('If I perform well, will I get the reward?') is known as:
questions.explanation: Instrumentality is the belief that good performance will lead to the reward. Option D, expectancy, is the earlier link between effort and performance.

questions.question: In expectancy theory, the attractiveness of a reward to the worker is called:
questions.explanation: Valence is how much the worker values the reward. Option D, instrumentality, is whether performance will actually lead to that reward.

questions.question: Kemi, a teller at a bank in Lagos, believes that working hard will improve her performance, but doubts management will actually pay the promised bonus for good results. Which expectancy linkage is weak?
questions.explanation: Doubting that good performance will bring the reward is a weak instrumentality, the performance-reward link. Option A, expectancy, is fine here because she believes effort will lead to good performance.

questions.question: A manufacturer in Ota offers top performers a free golf club membership, but most of its workers have no interest in golf. In expectancy terms, this reward is low in:
questions.explanation: Valence is how attractive the reward is to the worker, and a reward people do not value has low valence. Option A, instrumentality, is about whether performance actually leads to the reward, which is not in doubt here.

questions.question: According to expectancy theory, when will motivation be low?

options.a: Only when the reward has no cash value
options.b: Only when the worker's referent is the system
options.c: When any one of the three linkages is weak
options.d: Only when all three linkages are weak

questions.explanation: Motivation is low if any one linkage is weak: effort that does not lead to results, results that are not rewarded, or rewards the worker does not value. Option D is wrong because a single weak link is enough to kill effort.

questions.question: In expectancy theory, what matters most in determining a worker's effort?

options.b: The worker's perception of the linkages
options.c: The manager's opinion of the worker
options.d: The actual facts about pay levels

questions.explanation: What counts in expectancy theory is the worker's perception, not the facts. Option D is wrong because even real rewards will not motivate if the worker does not believe in them.

questions.question: When the motivation theories are integrated into one model, which theory forms the base?
questions.explanation: Expectancy theory forms the base of the integrated model, linking effort, performance, rewards and goals. Option B, reinforcement, plays a part by explaining how rewards reinforce behaviour, but it is not the foundation.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly shows the core chain in the integrated model of motivation?

options.a: Individual goals, organizational rewards, individual effort, individual performance
options.b: Individual effort, individual performance, organizational rewards, individual goals
options.c: Individual performance, individual effort, individual goals, organizational rewards
options.d: Organizational rewards, individual effort, individual goals, individual performance

questions.explanation: The integrated model runs from individual effort to individual performance, then to organizational rewards and finally to individual goals. Option A reverses the chain, putting goals and rewards before effort.

questions.question: In the integrated model of motivation, the requirement that rewards must feel fair comes from:
questions.explanation: Equity theory adds the idea that rewards must feel fair compared with others. Option D, reinforcement, contributes the idea that rewards strengthen behaviour, not that they must be fair.

questions.question: In the integrated model, the idea that a well-designed job raises motivation directly comes from:
questions.explanation: The job characteristics model contributes the idea that a well-designed job raises motivation directly. Option C, goal-setting, contributes the idea that goals direct effort.

questions.question: Besides individual effort, what else does the integrated model say affects individual performance?

options.a: The number of hygiene factors present

questions.explanation: The integrated model says that the opportunity to perform also affects performance. Option D, the referent, belongs to equity theory and concerns fairness comparisons, not performance itself.

questions.question: Which pairing of motivation theory and theorist is correct?
questions.explanation: Reinforcement theory is linked to B. F. Skinner. Option D is wrong because equity theory belongs to J. Stacy Adams, while Vroom proposed expectancy theory.

questions.question: Why do most motivation theories face cross-cultural challenges?

options.a: They were mostly developed in the United States, so they do not fit every culture
options.b: They apply only to contingent workers
options.c: They were developed only for low-skilled workers
options.d: They ignore the role of pay entirely

questions.explanation: Most motivation theories were developed in the United States, so they do not fit every culture. Option B is wrong because pay plays a role in several theories, for example as a hygiene factor.

questions.question: In cultures where people strongly avoid uncertainty, which of Maslow's needs may sit at the top of the hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Where people strongly avoid uncertainty, safety needs can sit at the top. Option A, social needs, rise to the top in cultures that value caring and relationships most.

questions.question: In cultures where caring and relationships are valued most, which of Maslow's needs may sit at the top?
questions.explanation: In cultures that value caring and relationships most, social needs can sit at the top. Option A, safety, tends to move to the top where people strongly avoid uncertainty.

questions.question: Which motivating factors appear to be desired across cultures?

options.b: High pay, job security and company policy

questions.explanation: The desire for interesting work, growth and achievement appears across cultures, and these are Herzberg's motivators. Option B lists mainly hygiene factors, which only prevent dissatisfaction.

questions.question: McClelland's high achiever, who accepts moderate risk and cares about performance, fits best in cultures like that of:

options.d: Cultures that value relationships above performance

questions.explanation: McClelland's high achiever fits cultures like the United States. Option A is wrong because this profile does not fit every culture equally, which is exactly the cross-cultural challenge.

questions.question: A work arrangement in which employees work longer hours per day but fewer days per week, such as four 10-hour days, is called:
questions.explanation: A compressed workweek squeezes the week into fewer, longer days. Option A, flextime, keeps a set number of weekly hours but lets workers vary their start and end times around core hours.

questions.question: At a Lagos bank, staff must work 40 hours a week and be present between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m., but each person chooses when to start and finish within limits. This arrangement is:
questions.explanation: Flextime sets a number of hours per week but lets workers vary start and end times within limits, around common core hours. Option D, a compressed workweek, means fewer but longer days.

questions.question: Two part-time administrators at a university department split one full-time position between them. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Job sharing is when two or more people split one full-time job. Option A, job enlargement, means adding more tasks to one person's job, not dividing a job between people.

questions.question: Working from home while linked to the workplace by computer is known as:
questions.explanation: Telecommuting means working from home, connected to the workplace by computer. Option D, flextime, is about choosing start and end times, not working from a different place.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a flexible work arrangement?
questions.explanation: Profit-sharing is a pay-for-performance programme, not a flexible work arrangement. Options A, B and C, together with flextime, are the flexible arrangements used for a diverse workforce.

questions.question: Professionals are typically motivated most by:

options.a: Money and promotion above all else
options.b: Job challenge, keeping up with their field, support and recognition
options.c: Employee recognition programmes alone because pay is limited
options.d: A chance to become permanent employees

questions.explanation: Professionals are motivated by job challenge, keeping up with their field, and support and recognition; money and promotion usually rank low. Option D describes what motivates contingent workers.

questions.question: The loyalty of professional employees is often directed more to:
questions.explanation: Professionals' loyalty is often to their profession more than to their employer, and their work is often a central life interest. Option C reverses this relationship.

questions.question: Contingent workers are most likely to be motivated by:

options.a: Job challenge and keeping up with their field
options.c: A chance to become permanent and training opportunities

questions.explanation: Contingent workers are motivated by the chance to become permanent and by training opportunities. Option A describes what motivates professionals.

questions.question: A hospital in Port Harcourt employs temporary staff who work beside permanent staff earning more and receiving benefits. Which motivation issue should managers watch most closely?
questions.explanation: When contingent workers work beside better-paid permanent staff with benefits, managers must watch for equity problems. Option C is not the main issue, since the concern here is the comparison of rewards between groups.

questions.question: For low-skilled, minimum-wage workers, managers with limited money should rely mainly on:

options.a: Employee recognition programmes and sincere praise
options.d: Long-term career development in their profession

questions.explanation: With money limited, managers lean on employee recognition programmes and sincere praise for low-skilled workers. Option B is wrong because large cash rewards are exactly what limited budgets cannot provide.

questions.question: A reward approach in which an organization's financial statements are shared with all employees, who learn to read them and see how their work affects results, is:
questions.explanation: Open-book management shares the financial statements with all employees so they understand how their work affects results. Option A, a recognition programme, is about personal attention and appreciation for a job well done.

questions.question: Giving personal attention and expressing interest, approval and appreciation for a job well done describes:
questions.explanation: Employee recognition programmes involve personal attention and showing interest, approval and appreciation for good work. Option C, pay-for-performance, ties variable pay to a measure of performance instead.

questions.question: Variable compensation plans that pay employees on the basis of some performance measure are called:
questions.explanation: Pay-for-performance programmes use variable pay based on some measure of performance, such as piece-rate pay or profit-sharing. Option A, recognition programmes, rewards with attention and appreciation rather than pay.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of a pay-for-performance programme?
questions.explanation: Flextime is a flexible work arrangement, not a pay plan. Options B, C and D, together with wage incentive plans, are examples of pay-for-performance.

questions.question: Pay-for-performance programmes are most consistent with which motivation theory?
questions.explanation: Pay-for-performance fits expectancy theory because it ties rewards clearly to performance, strengthening the performance-reward link. Option A is less fitting, because Herzberg treats pay as a hygiene factor rather than a motivator.

questions.question: Which of the following is a NON-financial incentive?
questions.explanation: Praise is a non-financial incentive, like recognition, job enrichment and flexible hours. Options A, C and D are all financial incentives.

questions.question: How many main ways of designing appropriate rewards to motivate employees are there?
questions.explanation: There are three approaches: open-book management, employee recognition programmes and pay-for-performance programmes. Option D is tempting if flexible work arrangements are mistakenly counted, but those are a separate issue.

questions.question: When motivating employees in tough economic times, managers must:

options.a: Rely only on punishment to maintain output
options.b: Stop all forms of recognition until conditions improve
options.c: Replace all permanent staff with contingent workers
options.d: Find creative ways to keep employees' efforts energized, directed and sustained toward goals

questions.explanation: In tough economic times managers must find creative ways to keep employees' efforts energized, directed and sustained toward goals. Option B is wrong because recognition is low-cost and especially useful when money is tight.

questions.question: The leadership style where decisions are made by the manager is:
questions.explanation: Autocratic leaders make decisions on their own and expect others to follow them. Democratic leadership (B) involves employees in decisions, laissez-faire leadership (C) leaves decisions to the group, and collaborative leadership (D) is a shared approach.

questions.question: Democratic leadership involves:

options.b: Encouraging employees to participate in decisions.
options.c: Allowing employees to work without supervision.
options.d: Using strict rules to govern teams.

questions.explanation: Democratic or participative leaders involve employees in decision-making and value their input. Option A describes autocratic leadership, C describes laissez-faire leadership, and D describes a rule-bound, bureaucratic style.

questions.question: Laissez-faire leadership means:

options.a: Managers make all decisions without employee input.
options.b: Employees are given independence to make decisions.

questions.explanation: Laissez-faire leadership gives employees a lot of freedom to make their own decisions with little interference. Option C can be a risk of the style, but it is not what the style means. Option A describes autocratic leadership, and D is close supervision, the opposite of laissez-faire.

questions.question: Leadership is best defined as:

options.b: Guiding and inspiring employees to achieve goals.

questions.explanation: Leadership is an influence process: motivating and inspiring people to work together toward common goals. Option A, delegating tasks, is something leaders do, but it is not leadership itself. Options C and D describe training and planning.

questions.question: An autocratic leadership style works best in:
questions.explanation: An autocratic style works best in a crisis, where one person needs to decide quickly and others need clear direction. Creative teams, independent workers and flexible environments (B, C and D) do better with participative or hands-off styles.

questions.question: Delegation is important for managers because it

options.a: Removes the manager's responsibility for results.

questions.explanation: Delegation gives employees the authority to carry out specific tasks, which develops their skills and raises motivation and performance. Option A is wrong because a manager who delegates still remains accountable for the results. Options C and D are the opposite of what delegation does, since it spreads decision-making and gives employees more independence.

questions.question: A leader who involves employees in decision-making is using:
questions.explanation: Democratic leadership means involving employees in decisions and taking their input seriously. Autocratic leaders (A) decide alone, laissez-faire leaders (B) leave decisions to the group, and bureaucratic leaders (D) rely on rules and procedures.

questions.question: Transformational leadership inspires employees by:
questions.explanation: Transformational leaders inspire people to go beyond their own interests, encouraging innovation, growth and commitment to a shared vision. Options A, C and D describe controlling or narrow task-focused behaviour, which is closer to transactional or autocratic styles.

questions.question: Leaders who delegate decision-making to employees practice:
questions.explanation: Laissez-faire leaders hand decision-making over to employees and give them a lot of freedom. Option D is tempting because transformational leaders also empower people, but they actively inspire and guide them rather than stepping back. Autocratic and directive leaders (A and C) keep decisions to themselves.

questions.question: A manager delegates tasks effectively by:

options.b: Matching tasks with employee skills and abilities.

questions.explanation: Effective delegation matches each task to the person with the right skills and gives them the authority to do it. Option A, giving tasks without instructions, usually leads to mistakes. Options C and D limit the benefits of delegating.

questions.question: Leadership differs from management in that

options.a: Leadership focuses on influencing and inspiring.

questions.explanation: Leadership is about influencing and inspiring people toward a shared goal, while management also includes planning, organizing and controlling. Option B describes the controlling side of management rather than leadership. Options C and D are false, because leaders make decisions and work with others.

questions.question: A manager practicing autocratic leadership will:

options.a: Make all decisions without consulting employees.
options.b: Encourage full employee participation in decision-making.
options.c: Delegate tasks entirely to team members.

questions.explanation: An autocratic manager makes decisions alone without consulting employees. Option B describes democratic leadership and C describes laissez-faire leadership. Option D is not typical, since autocratic leaders usually give very clear directions.

questions.question: Laissez-faire leadership works best when:

options.a: Employees are highly skilled and self-motivated.

questions.explanation: A hands-off, laissez-faire style works best when employees are skilled and self-motivated enough to manage themselves. Options B and C call for more direction and control. Option D describes an autocratic leader, not a laissez-faire one.

questions.question: Charismatic leaders are known for:

options.a: Relying on their personal charm and vision to inspire others.

questions.explanation: Charismatic leaders inspire followers through their personal appeal, confidence and a compelling vision. Options B, C and D describe the opposite: poor communication, a narrow technical focus and rigid rule enforcement.

questions.question: Leadership effectiveness depends on:

options.a: Understanding employee needs and adapting leadership styles.
options.c: Maintaining a single leadership style regardless of context.
options.d: Prioritizing personal goals over organizational objectives.

questions.explanation: Effective leaders read the situation and their people's needs, then adapt their style to fit, which is the core idea of contingency or situational leadership. Option C is the opposite of this idea. Options B and D weaken trust and commitment.

questions.question: What is an example of an informal communication channel?
questions.explanation: The grapevine is the unofficial network that news and rumours travel through between employees. Options B and D are official channels set up by the organization, and C, upward communication, is a formal direction of flow.

questions.question: What is one of the key traits often associated with effective leadership?
questions.explanation: Effective leaders are flexible: they adjust their approach to fit people and situations. Options A, B and D, which are arrogance, isolation and indecisiveness, weaken a leader's influence and are not traits of good leadership.

questions.question: What is the "sandwich" approach in providing feedback?

options.b: Starting with criticism, then praise, and ending with criticism
options.d: Starting with praise, then criticism, and ending with praise

questions.explanation: The sandwich approach puts criticism between two pieces of praise. You start positive, give the critical point, then end positive so the person stays open and motivated. Option B reverses this, and A and C are not the sandwich method.

questions.question: According to situational leadership theory, what does effective leadership depend on?

options.b: Strict adherence to a single leadership style
options.d: The readiness level of followers and task demands

questions.explanation: Situational leadership theory says the best leadership style depends on the followers' readiness, meaning their ability and willingness, and on what the task demands. Options A and C focus on the leader alone, which is trait thinking. B is the opposite of the theory, which is all about changing style.

questions.question: What is a characteristic of transformational leaders?
questions.explanation: Transformational leaders inspire followers to look beyond their own interests and encourage new ideas, innovation and creativity. Option A, contingent rewards, describes transactional leaders, and D, a focus on stability and routine, also fits a transactional style.

questions.question: Which communication channel usually allows the most immediate feedback?
questions.explanation: Face-to-face communication happens in person, so the listener can respond right away and the speaker sees reactions immediately. Options C and D, electronic communication and email, usually involve a delay, and A, the grapevine, is an informal network, not a face-to-face channel as such.

questions.question: ____ refers to overseeing what is being done by subordinates and giving instructions to ensure optimum utilization of resources and achievement of work targets
questions.explanation: Supervision means watching over the work of subordinates and guiding them so that resources are used well and targets are met. Option B, leadership, is about influence and inspiration more broadly, and D, motivation, is about creating the will to work.

questions.question: Which leadership theory emphasizes the importance of adapting leadership style to the situation?
questions.explanation: Contingency theory says there is no one best way to lead: the right style depends on the situation. Option B, behavioural theory, looks for the best behaviours of leaders, while C and D describe particular leadership styles rather than adapting to circumstances.

questions.question: Effective communication in management helps in:
questions.explanation: Clear communication keeps people informed and in step with one another, which makes coordination possible. Options A, C and D, conflicts, waste and lower efficiency, are what poor communication causes.

questions.question: Which management style is most participatory?
questions.explanation: A democratic style involves employees in decisions and encourages them to share ideas, so it is the most participatory. Autocratic leaders (A) decide alone, laissez-faire leaders (C) mostly stay out of the way, and bureaucratic leaders (D) go by the rules.

questions.question: Leadership styles include all except:
questions.explanation: Transformational, autocratic and transactional are all recognised leadership styles. 'Functional' is not a standard leadership style, so it is the exception.

questions.question: An influence process that involves motivating and inspiring people to work together to achieve a common goal is called:
questions.explanation: Leadership is an influence process: it motivates and inspires people so they work together towards a shared goal. Option B is overseeing subordinates' work and giving instructions, and option C is increasing workers' decision-making discretion, so neither is the influence process itself.

questions.question: A leader is best described as someone who:

options.a: Can influence others and who has managerial authority
options.b: Has formal authority only over machines and materials
options.c: Holds a senior position but has no influence over others
options.d: Works alone without directing or influencing anyone

questions.explanation: A leader combines two things: the ability to influence others and managerial authority. Option C fails because a position without influence does not make someone a leader.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the obligations of leadership?

options.a: Preparing the organization's annual financial statements

questions.explanation: The obligations of leadership run from developing a clear vision through motivating, setting expectations, decisions, commitment, a positive environment, delegating and coaching to conflict resolution. Preparing financial statements is an accounting task, not a leadership obligation, while options B, D and C are all on the list.

questions.question: How many obligations of leadership are commonly listed, starting with developing a clear vision and ending with conflict resolution?
questions.explanation: There are nine obligations of leadership, from developing and communicating a clear vision to conflict resolution. Option C is easy to confuse because seven is the number of traits linked with leadership, not the number of obligations.

questions.question: The head of a department at UNILAG calls two lecturers who have been quarrelling over teaching schedules and helps them reach an agreement. Which obligation of leadership is she performing?
questions.explanation: Settling a dispute between team members so they can work together again is conflict resolution, one of the nine obligations of leadership. Option D would involve helping a member build skills, not ending a quarrel.

questions.question: A branch manager at a bank in Lagos meets a new credit officer every week to help him improve how he analyses loan applications. This is an example of which leadership obligation?
questions.explanation: Working with a team member over time to improve his skills is coaching, one of the obligations of leadership. Option B would mean handing a task over to him, not developing how he does it.

questions.question: Which of the following IS one of the obligations of leadership?

options.b: Centralizing all authority in the leader

questions.explanation: Fostering commitment and accountability is one of the nine obligations of leadership. Options B and A describe autocratic behaviour, and option C is the opposite of the obligation to delegate tasks.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a leader from a manager?

options.a: A manager's influence goes beyond formal authority, while a leader's does not
options.b: A leader can be appointed or can emerge from a group, while a manager is appointed to a position
options.c: A leader focuses on planning, organizing and controlling, while a manager inspires
options.d: A manager can emerge from a group, while a leader must be appointed

questions.explanation: Managers are appointed, but leaders may be appointed or may simply emerge from within a group. Option A reverses the truth, because it is the leader whose influence can go beyond formal authority.

questions.question: A manager's influence over subordinates comes mainly from:
questions.explanation: A manager's influence comes from the formal authority of the position he is appointed to. Option D fits a leader better, since a leader's influence can go beyond formal authority.

questions.question: Which of the following is the main focus of a manager rather than a leader?

options.a: Emerging as the voice of an informal group

questions.explanation: Managers focus on planning, organizing and controlling. Option C is the focus of a leader, which is exactly what separates leadership from management.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about managers and leaders is correct?

options.a: A manager and a leader are always the same person
options.b: Ideally all managers should be leaders, but not all leaders have the abilities of a manager
options.c: All leaders automatically have the abilities of a manager
options.d: Managers should avoid acting as leaders

questions.explanation: Ideally every manager should also lead, but a person can lead without having a manager's abilities. Option C reverses this point, since leading others does not guarantee managerial ability.

questions.question: Research that tried to isolate the characteristics that set leaders apart from non-leaders is known as:
questions.explanation: Trait theories looked for the personal characteristics that set leaders apart from non-leaders. Option D studied what leaders do rather than what they are like.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven traits linked with leadership?
questions.explanation: Initiating structure is a leader behaviour dimension from the Ohio State studies, not a personal trait. Options B, D and A are all among the seven traits linked with leadership.

questions.question: Which of the following IS one of the seven traits linked with leadership?
questions.explanation: Desire to lead is one of the seven leadership traits. Option C is an Ohio State behaviour dimension, option B is one of Fiedler's situational factors and option A comes from Situational Leadership Theory.

questions.question: Some later lists add an eighth trait to the seven traits linked with leadership. This trait is:
questions.explanation: Later lists add proneness to guilt, meaning a strong sense of responsibility to others. Option B is a behaviour dimension from the Ohio State studies, not a trait.

questions.question: As a leadership trait, proneness to guilt refers to:

options.a: A tendency to blame subordinates for failure
options.b: A habit of avoiding criticism from superiors
options.c: A strong sense of responsibility to others

questions.explanation: Proneness to guilt describes a leader who feels a strong sense of responsibility to others. Option A describes the opposite, because blaming subordinates shows a lack of responsibility to them.

questions.question: Staff of a hospital in Ibadan admire their medical director because she always tells the truth and keeps her promises. Which leadership trait does she show most clearly?
questions.explanation: Telling the truth and keeping promises reflect honesty and integrity, one of the seven leadership traits. Option A is about being outgoing and sociable, which says nothing about truthfulness.

questions.question: Apart from the traits identified in trait research, which two qualities are also described as marks of an effective leader?

options.d: Formal authority and a high job title

questions.explanation: Flexibility and strong communication skills are also marks of an effective leader. Option D describes things a manager gets from his position, not personal qualities that make a leader effective.

questions.question: What was the main weakness of trait theories of leadership?

options.a: They focused only on what leaders do rather than who they are
options.b: They studied followers' readiness instead of the leader
options.c: They insisted that a leader's style can never change
options.d: They ignored the situation and the interaction between leader and group

questions.explanation: Traits alone could not explain leadership, because trait theories ignored the situation and how the leader and group interact. Option A describes behavioural theories, which came after trait theories.

questions.question: What do trait theories conclude about a person who has the traits linked with leadership?

options.a: The person is only more likely to be an effective leader
options.b: The person no longer needs managerial authority
options.c: The person is certain to become an effective leader
options.d: The person will be effective in every situation

questions.explanation: Having the traits only makes a person more likely to be an effective leader. It does not guarantee success, so options C and D claim too much, since the situation also matters.

questions.question: The failure of trait theories to fully explain leadership pushed researchers to study:

options.b: The power that comes from a leader's position
options.d: The communication networks of the organization

questions.explanation: Since traits alone could not explain leadership, researchers turned to what leaders actually do, which gave rise to behavioural theories. Option A came later, in contingency thinking such as Situational Leadership Theory.

questions.question: Theories that identify the behaviours separating effective leaders from ineffective ones are called:
questions.explanation: Behavioural theories focus on what effective leaders do that ineffective leaders do not. Option B looks at personal characteristics rather than behaviour.

questions.question: The University of Iowa leadership studies are associated with:
questions.explanation: Kurt Lewin led the University of Iowa studies that identified the autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire styles. Option C developed the Managerial Grid instead.

questions.question: The Managerial Grid was developed by:
questions.explanation: Blake and Mouton developed the Managerial Grid, built on concern for people and concern for production. Option B developed Situational Leadership Theory, which is a contingency theory.

questions.question: The three leadership styles identified by the University of Iowa studies are:
questions.explanation: The Iowa studies identified the autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire styles. Option B lists Hersey and Blanchard styles, and option D lists path-goal behaviours.

questions.question: What was the main finding of the University of Iowa studies?

options.a: Employee-oriented leaders had the lowest productivity
options.b: High-high leaders always produced the best results
options.c: Group members were more satisfied under democratic leaders
options.d: Laissez-faire leaders produced the highest satisfaction

questions.explanation: The Iowa studies found that group members were more satisfied under democratic leaders. Option B misstates the Ohio State finding, which said high-high leaders often but not always got good results.

questions.question: The two dimensions of leader behaviour identified in the Ohio State studies are:

options.c: Concern for people and concern for production

questions.explanation: Ohio State described leader behaviour in terms of initiating structure and consideration. Option B is the Michigan pair, and option C is the basis of the Managerial Grid.

questions.question: The two dimensions of leader behaviour identified in the University of Michigan studies are:
questions.explanation: The Michigan studies described leaders as employee-oriented or production-oriented. Option B is the Ohio State pair, which is easy to mix up with Michigan.

questions.question: The University of Michigan studies concluded that:

options.a: Group members were most satisfied under autocratic leaders
options.b: Leaders who were high on both dimensions always succeeded
options.c: Production-oriented leaders had higher productivity and satisfaction
options.d: Employee-oriented leaders had higher productivity and satisfaction

questions.explanation: Michigan found that employee-oriented leaders were linked with higher productivity and higher satisfaction. Option C reverses this, since production-oriented leaders were not the ones favoured.

questions.question: What did the Ohio State studies find about leaders who were high in both initiating structure and consideration?

options.a: They consistently produced the lowest satisfaction
options.b: They always achieved the best results
options.c: They were found to be ineffective in all situations
options.d: They often got good results, but not always

questions.explanation: Ohio State found that high-high leaders often achieved good results, but there were exceptions. Option B overstates the finding, and those exceptions are part of why researchers later turned to the situation.

questions.question: The two dimensions of the Managerial Grid are:

options.b: Concern for people and concern for production

questions.explanation: The Managerial Grid plots concern for people against concern for production. Option D belongs to the Ohio State studies, and option C is the meaning of readiness in Situational Leadership Theory.

questions.question: On the Managerial Grid, which style is considered the best?
questions.explanation: The 9,9 position, team management, is high on both concern for production and concern for people and is seen as the best style. Option C is only medium on both dimensions.

questions.question: How many positions are there on the Managerial Grid?
questions.explanation: The grid has 9 points on each of its two dimensions, giving 9 x 9 = 81 positions. Option B is the number of points on just one dimension.

questions.question: On the Managerial Grid, the first number in a position such as 9,1 stands for:
questions.explanation: The first number is concern for production and the second is concern for people. Option B is the second number, so 9,1 means high production and low people.

questions.question: On the Managerial Grid, 'impoverished' management is found at which position?
questions.explanation: Impoverished management, at 1,1, shows little concern for either people or production. Option B is country club management, which is high on people.

questions.question: On the Managerial Grid, country club management (1,9) means:

options.a: High concern for production and low concern for people
options.b: Medium concern for both people and production
options.c: Little concern for either people or production
options.d: High concern for people and low concern for production

questions.explanation: Country club management sits at 1,9, which means low production but high concern for people. Option A is task management at 9,1.

questions.question: The production manager of a manufacturing firm in Ota pushes hard for output targets but shows little interest in his workers' needs or feelings. On the Managerial Grid, his style is closest to:
questions.explanation: High concern for production with low concern for people is task management, placed at 9,1. Option D is the reverse, with high concern for people and low concern for production.

questions.question: On the Managerial Grid, 'middle of the road' management describes a leader who is:

options.a: High on people but low on production
options.b: Medium on both concern for people and concern for production
options.c: High on both concern for people and concern for production
options.d: Low on both concern for people and concern for production

questions.explanation: Middle of the road management sits at 5,5, with medium concern for both people and production. Option C describes team management at 9,9.

questions.question: The medical director of a hospital in Lagos sets the theatre roster alone, tells each nurse exactly how to do the work and does not invite suggestions. Which Iowa leadership style is this?
questions.explanation: An autocratic leader centralizes authority, dictates work methods, makes decisions alone and limits participation. Option C would involve staff in decisions, which this director does not do.

questions.question: Which behaviour is typical of a democratic leader in the Iowa studies?

options.a: Giving the group complete freedom to work as it sees fit
options.b: Making decisions alone and limiting participation
options.d: Using feedback as an opportunity to coach employees

questions.explanation: A democratic leader involves employees in decisions, delegates authority and uses feedback to coach. Option A describes laissez-faire leadership, where the leader stays out of the decision entirely.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a democratic leader and a laissez-faire leader?

options.a: The laissez-faire leader dictates work methods, while the democratic leader does not
options.b: The democratic leader still takes part in the decision, while the laissez-faire leader hands it over entirely
options.c: There is no difference, as both give the group complete freedom
options.d: The democratic leader makes all decisions alone, while the laissez-faire leader consults

questions.explanation: Both styles involve employees, but a democratic leader still takes part in the decision, while a laissez-faire leader gives the group complete freedom. Option C is the common mistake of treating the two styles as the same.

questions.question: The head of a university department wants to redesign a course and knows that his lecturers' ideas will make the final plan better. Which Iowa style suits this situation best?
questions.explanation: Democratic leadership suits a team whose ideas improve the decision, because the leader involves members while still taking part. Option B fits a crisis needing quick decisions, which this is not.

questions.question: Lewin's early finding about democratic leadership was that it produced:

options.a: Poor quantity and poor quality of work
options.b: Both good quantity and good quality of work
options.c: Good quality only when the leader was absent
options.d: High quantity but very poor quality of work

questions.explanation: Lewin's early finding was that democratic leadership gave both good quantity and good quality of work. Later studies were more mixed on performance, but option D does not describe his early finding.

questions.question: What did later studies of the Iowa styles find?

options.a: Results on performance were mixed, but satisfaction stayed higher under democratic leaders
options.b: Autocratic leaders always produced the highest satisfaction
options.c: Laissez-faire leaders consistently produced the best performance
options.d: Democratic leaders produced lower satisfaction than autocratic leaders

questions.explanation: Later studies gave mixed results on performance, but group members stayed more satisfied under democratic leaders. Options B and D contradict the steady finding on satisfaction.

questions.question: In the Ohio State studies, the extent to which a leader defines his role and group members' roles to reach goals, including organizing work, work relationships and goals, is called:
questions.explanation: Initiating structure is how far a leader defines his own role and members' roles in reaching goals. Option D is one of Fiedler's situational factors, describing how structured the job tasks are, not a leader behaviour.

questions.question: In the Ohio State studies, the extent to which a leader has work relationships marked by mutual trust and respect for members' ideas and feelings is called:
questions.explanation: Consideration is the Ohio State dimension about mutual trust and respect for members' ideas and feelings. Option A is the similar people-side dimension, but it belongs to the Michigan studies.

questions.question: Which pair of leader behaviour dimensions both represent the 'people side' of leadership?
questions.explanation: Consideration (Ohio State) and employee-oriented (Michigan) are both about people. Option C is the task-side pair, and options D and A mix one people dimension with one task dimension.

questions.question: In the Michigan studies, a production-oriented leader is one who stresses:

options.b: Mutual trust and respect for members' feelings
options.c: The technical or task side of the job

questions.explanation: A production-oriented leader stresses the technical or task side of the job. Option D describes the employee-oriented leader, the other Michigan dimension.

questions.question: 'Initiating structure' as a dimension of leader behaviour comes from which study?
questions.explanation: Initiating structure, together with consideration, comes from the Ohio State studies. Option C used employee-oriented and production-oriented instead.

questions.question: What weakness of behavioural theories led to the development of contingency theories?

options.a: They focused too much on personal traits
options.c: They did not consider the situation
options.d: They claimed leadership style is fixed

questions.explanation: Behavioural theories looked at what leaders do but ignored the situation, which led to contingency theories. Option B is wrong because behaviour was exactly what these theories studied.

questions.question: The central idea of contingency theories of leadership is that:

options.a: Effective leaders are born with a fixed set of traits
options.b: The 9,9 style works best in every organization
options.c: There is no one best leadership style, so the leader must adapt to the situation
options.d: The democratic style is the best in every situation

questions.explanation: Contingency theories hold that no single style is best, and the right style depends on the situation. Option B reflects the Managerial Grid's single best style, which is exactly the kind of universal answer contingency theories reject.

questions.question: Which contingency theory holds that a leader's style is fixed and cannot easily change?
questions.explanation: The Fiedler model treats a leader's style as fixed, so the match between leader and situation is what matters. Option C says the opposite, because the style changes with the readiness of followers.

questions.question: According to the Fiedler model, group performance depends on:

options.a: The readiness of followers to do a task
options.b: Matching the leader's style to how much the situation lets the leader control and influence
options.c: The leader helping followers reach their own goals
options.d: Forming an in-group and an out-group of followers

questions.explanation: Fiedler argued that performance depends on the right match between the leader's fixed style and how much control and influence the situation gives. Option A is the basis of Situational Leadership Theory instead.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of Fiedler's three situational factors?
questions.explanation: Fiedler's three situational factors are leader-member relations, task structure and position power. Follower readiness belongs to Hersey and Blanchard's Situational Leadership Theory, not the Fiedler model.

questions.question: In the Fiedler model, the degree of confidence, trust and respect followers have for their leader is called:
questions.explanation: Leader-member relations measures the confidence, trust and respect followers have for the leader. Option A sounds similar but is an Ohio State behaviour dimension, not one of Fiedler's situational factors.

questions.question: In the Fiedler model, the degree to which job tasks are formal and structured is called:
questions.explanation: Task structure describes how formal and structured job tasks are. Option A is a trap because it is a leader behaviour from the Ohio State studies, not a feature of the situation.

questions.question: The new plant manager at a manufacturer in Ota has full power to hire, fire, discipline, promote and set the pay of his staff. In the Fiedler model, this situational factor is:
questions.explanation: Position power is the leader's power over hiring, firing, discipline, promotions and pay. Option D is one of the five types of power, which comes from personal traits people admire, not from control over pay and discipline.

questions.question: Combining Fiedler's three situational factors produces how many possible situations?
questions.explanation: Mixing the three factors gives eight situations, ranging from very favourable to very unfavourable. Option C is the number of factors, not the number of situations they produce.

questions.question: In the Fiedler model, the LPC questionnaire stands for:
questions.explanation: LPC means least-preferred co-worker: the leader describes the co-worker he liked least using pairs of opposite adjectives. Options D, C and A are invented expansions.

questions.question: On Fiedler's LPC questionnaire, a supervisor describes the co-worker he liked least in kind and favourable terms. Fiedler would classify him as:
questions.explanation: A high LPC score, from describing the least-preferred co-worker kindly, shows a relationship-oriented leader. Option B is the low-LPC leader, who describes that co-worker in harsh terms.

questions.question: A leader who gets a low score on Fiedler's LPC questionnaire is classified as:
questions.explanation: A low LPC score marks a task-oriented leader in the Fiedler model. Option A is the high-LPC leader.

questions.question: According to the Fiedler model, task-oriented leaders perform best in situations that are:

options.d: Highly structured but with weak leader-member relations only

questions.explanation: Fiedler found that task-oriented leaders do best at the two extremes, very favourable or very unfavourable situations. Option B is where relationship-oriented leaders do best.

questions.question: According to the Fiedler model, relationship-oriented leaders perform best in situations that are:

options.b: Either very favourable or very unfavourable

questions.explanation: Relationship-oriented leaders do best in moderately favourable situations. Option B describes where task-oriented leaders do best.

questions.question: Because the Fiedler model treats leadership style as fixed, how can a mismatch between leader and situation be corrected?

options.a: Change the leader or change the situation
options.b: Ask the leader to become laissez-faire
options.c: Let followers choose a new style for the leader
options.d: Train the leader to switch styles as followers mature

questions.explanation: If style cannot change, the only options are to replace the leader or change the situation to fit him. Option D assumes style can change, which is the view of Situational Leadership Theory, not Fiedler.

questions.question: Situational Leadership Theory was developed by:
questions.explanation: Hersey and Blanchard developed Situational Leadership Theory, which ties style to the readiness of followers. Option D developed the Managerial Grid, a behavioural theory.

questions.question: In Situational Leadership Theory, 'readiness' refers to:

options.a: How far people have the ability and willingness to do a task
options.b: How much power the leader has over pay and promotion
options.c: How much followers like and respect the leader
options.d: How structured and formal the job tasks are

questions.explanation: Readiness is the extent to which followers have both the ability and the willingness to do a task. Option C is closer to Fiedler's leader-member relations, not readiness.

questions.question: In Situational Leadership Theory, which style fits followers who are unable and unwilling to do a task (R1)?
questions.explanation: Followers at R1 are unable and unwilling, so the leader uses telling: high task and low relationship behaviour. Option D is for followers who are unable but willing.

questions.question: A new team of graduate trainees at a bank in Lagos is very eager to work but does not yet have the skills for the job. Under Situational Leadership Theory, the manager should use:
questions.explanation: Followers who are unable but willing (R2) need selling, which is high task and high relationship. Option B suits followers who are both unable and unwilling, but these trainees are eager.

questions.question: Experienced engineers at a firm in Ota have all the skills needed for a project but are unwilling to commit to it. Under Situational Leadership Theory, which style should their manager use?
questions.explanation: Followers who are able but unwilling (R3) call for participating: low task and high relationship behaviour. Option D suits followers who are both able and willing.

questions.question: In Situational Leadership Theory, which style combines high task behaviour with high relationship behaviour?
questions.explanation: Selling is high task and high relationship, used with followers who are unable but willing. Option D is high task but low relationship.

questions.question: In Situational Leadership Theory, the delegating style is described as:

options.a: Low task and high relationship behaviour
options.b: Low task and low relationship behaviour
options.c: High task and high relationship behaviour
options.d: High task and low relationship behaviour

questions.explanation: Delegating is low task and low relationship, used when followers are able and willing (R4). Option A describes participating.

questions.question: According to Situational Leadership Theory, as followers become more ready, the leader should:

options.a: Increase both control and relationship behaviour
options.b: Cut back on both control and relationship behaviour
options.c: Keep the same style regardless of readiness
options.d: Increase control but reduce relationship behaviour

questions.explanation: As readiness grows, the leader cuts back on both control and relationship behaviour, moving towards delegating. Option C reflects Fiedler's fixed style, not Situational Leadership Theory.

questions.question: How does Situational Leadership Theory differ from the Fiedler model on leadership style?

options.a: Situational Leadership Theory says style can change, while Fiedler says style is fixed
options.b: Situational Leadership Theory says style is fixed, while Fiedler says style can change
options.c: Both say performance depends only on the leader's traits
options.d: Both say the leader's style can never change

questions.explanation: Hersey and Blanchard allow the leader to change style as follower readiness changes, while Fiedler treats style as fixed. Option B reverses the two theories.

questions.question: Path-goal theory of leadership was proposed by:
questions.explanation: Robert House proposed path-goal theory, in which the leader helps followers reach their goals. Option B is linked to the model with a fixed leadership style.

questions.question: Path-goal theory states that the leader's job is to:

options.a: Help followers reach their goals by giving direction and support
options.b: Match a fixed style to the favourableness of the situation
options.c: Hand all decisions to followers who are able and willing
options.d: Form an in-group and an out-group among followers

questions.explanation: In path-goal theory the leader helps followers reach their goals and provides the direction and support they need. Option B describes the Fiedler model.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four path-goal leader behaviours?
questions.explanation: The four path-goal behaviours are directive, supportive, participative and achievement-oriented. Delegating is one of Hersey and Blanchard's styles, not a path-goal behaviour.

questions.question: In path-goal theory, a leader who tells followers what is expected of them, schedules work and gives specific direction is showing which behaviour?
questions.explanation: Directive leadership tells followers what is expected, schedules work and directs how to do it. Option B consults followers and uses their suggestions instead.

questions.question: A ward sister at a hospital in Enugu is friendly with her nurses and shows real concern for their needs. In path-goal theory, this is which leader behaviour?
questions.explanation: A supportive leader is friendly and shows concern for followers' needs. Option A would involve consulting the nurses and using their suggestions in decisions.

questions.question: A sales manager at a telecom company in Lagos sets very challenging targets for her team and makes clear she expects top performance. In path-goal theory, this is which behaviour?
questions.explanation: Setting challenging goals and expecting top performance is achievement-oriented leadership. Option C is about telling followers what to do and scheduling work, not setting stretching goals.

questions.question: In path-goal theory, a leader who consults followers and uses their suggestions is showing which behaviour?
questions.explanation: A participative leader consults followers and uses their suggestions. Option C is a Situational Leadership style and not one of the path-goal behaviours.

questions.question: In path-goal theory, which of the following is NOT a follower characteristic that affects the right leader behaviour?
questions.explanation: Follower characteristics are locus of control, experience and perceived ability. Task structure is part of the environment, the other group of factors in path-goal theory.

questions.question: Leader-member exchange (LMX) theory states that leaders:

options.a: Form an in-group and an out-group, and in-group members get more trust and attention
options.b: Should give every follower exactly the same treatment
options.c: Change style only according to the task structure
options.d: Must keep one fixed style for all followers

questions.explanation: LMX theory says leaders create an in-group and an out-group, and in-group members receive more trust and attention and tend to perform better. Option B is the opposite of what LMX describes.

questions.question: A leader who motivates followers mainly by exchanging rewards for productivity is called a:
questions.explanation: A transactional leader works through clear goals and exchanges rewards for productivity. Option A goes further by stimulating and inspiring followers to achieve extraordinary outcomes.

questions.question: A leader who stimulates and inspires followers to achieve extraordinary outcomes is known as a:
questions.explanation: Transformational leaders stimulate and inspire followers to achieve extraordinary outcomes. Option C relies on exchanging rewards for productivity rather than inspiring beyond normal results.

questions.question: The manager of a bottling plant in Ota tells workers exactly what output is expected and pays a bonus to every worker who meets the weekly target. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Setting clear goals and exchanging rewards for productivity is transactional leadership. Option D would involve inspiring workers towards extraordinary outcomes, innovation and personal growth, not just a bonus for meeting targets.

questions.question: How is transformational leadership related to transactional leadership?

options.a: Transactional leadership is built on top of transformational leadership
options.b: Transformational leadership is built on top of transactional leadership
options.c: The two have no connection with each other
options.d: Transformational leadership is the exact opposite of transactional leadership

questions.explanation: Transformational leadership builds on top of transactional leadership rather than replacing it. Option D is the common mistake of treating them as opposites.

questions.question: An enthusiastic, self-confident leader whose personality and actions influence people to behave in certain ways is called a:
questions.explanation: A charismatic leader is enthusiastic and self-confident, and his personality and actions shape how people behave. Option B influences people through rewards rather than personality.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of charismatic leaders?

options.b: They avoid taking risks to achieve their vision
options.c: They behave in ways that are out of the ordinary

questions.explanation: Charismatic leaders are willing to take risks to achieve their vision, so avoiding risk does not fit them. Options D, A and C are all among the five characteristics of charismatic leaders.

questions.question: How many characteristics of charismatic leaders are commonly identified?
questions.explanation: Five characteristics are identified: having a vision, expressing it, taking risks for it, being sensitive to the environment and followers' needs, and behaving out of the ordinary. Option B is the number of traits linked with leadership.

questions.question: Which of the following IS a characteristic of charismatic leaders?

options.b: Keeping a fixed style regardless of the situation
options.c: Strict reliance on exchanging rewards for output
options.d: Sensitivity to limits in the environment and to followers' needs

questions.explanation: Charismatic leaders are sensitive to environmental limits and to followers' needs. Option A is wrong because charismatic leaders behave in ways that are out of the ordinary.

questions.question: The ability to create and express a realistic, credible and attractive vision of the future that improves on the present is called:
questions.explanation: Visionary leadership is creating and expressing a realistic, credible and attractive vision of a better future. Option C is about defining roles and organizing work, not painting a picture of the future.

questions.question: The two priorities of team leadership are:

options.b: Hiring team members and setting their pay
options.c: Managing the team's external boundary and helping the team process
options.d: Planning the budget and controlling costs

questions.explanation: Team leadership has two priorities: managing the team's external boundary and helping the team process. Option A describes a communication barrier and autocratic behaviour, not team leadership.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four roles of a team leader?
questions.explanation: The four roles of a team leader are liaison with outsiders, troubleshooter, conflict manager and coach. Acting as the sole decision maker is not one of them, while options A, C and B are.

questions.question: The leader of a project team at a Lagos fintech firm represents the team in meetings with other departments and outside partners. Which team leader role is this?
questions.explanation: Representing the team to people outside it is the liaison with outsiders role. Option C would mean settling disagreements inside the team.

questions.question: How many sources of power can a leader draw on?
questions.explanation: A leader can draw on five types of power: legitimate, coercive, reward, expert and referent. Option D adds one too many, while options C and B leave some out.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the five sources of power?
questions.explanation: The five types are legitimate, coercive, reward, expert and referent power. Situational power is not one of them, while options A, D and B are on the list.

questions.question: A new head of department at a federal ministry in Abuja is obeyed mainly because of the official post she holds. Which type of power is she using?
questions.explanation: Legitimate power comes from the leader's position in the organization. Option D would mean people obey because they admire her and want to be like her, not because of her post.

questions.question: A supervisor in a factory in Ota threatens to suspend workers who arrive late. Which type of power is he using?
questions.explanation: Coercive power is the power to punish or control, as with the threat of suspension. Option A works the other way, through positive rewards.

questions.question: A bank manager in Lagos influences her staff by giving bonuses, praise and recommendations for promotion to those who perform well. Which type of power is this?
questions.explanation: Reward power is the power to give positive rewards such as bonuses and praise. Option B is the power to punish, the opposite approach.

questions.question: Colleagues at a hospital in Ibadan follow the advice of a junior doctor on a rare condition because she has special knowledge of it. Which type of power does she have?
questions.explanation: Expert power comes from expertise, special skills or knowledge, so even a junior doctor can have it. Option B would depend on a senior position, which she does not hold.

questions.question: Power that comes from a person's desirable resources or personal traits, so that others admire him and want to be like him, is called:
