questions.question: Total asset turnover (sales divided by total assets) belongs to which group of ratios?
questions.explanation: Total asset turnover shows how efficiently the firm uses all its assets to generate sales, so it is an activity ratio. Option B is wrong because profitability ratios use net profit, not sales, in the numerator.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Return on investment is calculated as:

options.a: Net profit after taxes divided by total assets
options.b: Total debt divided by total assets
options.c: Net profit after taxes divided by total sales

questions.explanation: Return on investment is a profitability ratio that divides net profit after taxes by total assets. Option C is the profit margin on sales, a different profitability ratio.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Profit margin on sales is calculated as:

options.a: Net profit after taxes divided by total sales
options.c: Current assets divided by current liabilities
options.d: Net profit after taxes divided by total assets

questions.explanation: Profit margin on sales divides net profit after taxes by total sales and is a profitability ratio. Option D is return on investment, which uses total assets rather than total sales.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: How many groups of financial ratios are commonly used as control tools?
questions.explanation: The four groups are liquidity, leverage, activity and profitability ratios. Option B is wrong because it leaves out one of these groups.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four groups of financial ratios used for control?
questions.explanation: The four groups are liquidity, leverage, activity and profitability. Growth ratios are not one of them, while options C, D and A are all part of the list.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The finance manager of a manufacturing company in Ikeja wants to know whether the company can pay the suppliers whose bills are due next month. Which group of ratios should she examine?
questions.explanation: Bills due next month are short-term debts, and liquidity ratios test the ability to meet current debts. Option D is about the use of debt to finance assets and paying interest, a longer-term concern.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: A budget is best described as:

options.a: Neither a planning nor a control tool
options.d: Both a planning tool and a control tool

questions.explanation: A budget is used in planning to allocate resources and in control to provide quantitative standards against which resource use can be compared. Options B and C each describe only half of its role.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: When used as a control tool, a budget mainly provides managers with:

options.b: Quantitative standards to compare resource use against
options.d: A list of best practices from competitors

questions.explanation: In control, a budget gives quantitative standards, so managers can compare how resources are actually used with what was planned. Option D describes benchmarking, not budgeting.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: A system that gives managers needed information on a regular basis is called a:
questions.explanation: A management information system provides managers with the information they need on a regular basis, turning raw data into information. Option C is a performance measurement tool covering four areas, not a regular information supply system.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Raw, unanalysed facts are referred to as:
questions.explanation: Data are raw, unanalysed facts, while information is data that has been analysed and processed. Option C is the common confusion, since an MIS turns data into information.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Information controls work in two ways. Which pair correctly identifies them?

options.a: As a liquidity ratio and as a leverage ratio
options.b: As a tool to control other activities and as an area to be controlled
options.c: As a planning tool and as a leading tool
options.d: As a feedforward control and as a strategic control

questions.explanation: Information is a tool for controlling other activities, giving managers the right information at the right time, and it is also something that must itself be controlled and protected. Option D names types of control, not the two roles of information controls.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: When information is treated as an area to be controlled, which tools are used to protect it?
questions.explanation: As an area to control, information must be protected with tools such as encryption, firewalls and data back-ups. Option A lists control tools for other activities, not protections for the information itself.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The balanced scorecard measures performance in four areas. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: The four areas of the balanced scorecard are financial, customer, internal processes, and people/innovation/growth assets. Supplier relations is not one of them, while options B, A and C are.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The balanced scorecard was developed by:
questions.explanation: Robert Kaplan and David Norton developed the balanced scorecard as a way of measuring performance beyond finance. Option A, Deming, is linked with quality and the 14 points, not the balanced scorecard.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Why do organizations use the balanced scorecard instead of relying on financial results alone?

options.b: Financial results alone can hide weak customer service or poor staff development
options.c: The balanced scorecard measures only profit
options.d: The balanced scorecard replaces the need for goals

questions.explanation: The balanced scorecard looks at more than finance, because good financial figures can hide problems in customer service or staff development. Option C is wrong because the whole point of the tool is to go beyond financial measures.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The search for the best practices among competitors or noncompetitors that lead to superior performance is known as:
questions.explanation: Benchmarking is the search for best practices, from competitors or noncompetitors, that lead to superior performance. Option D is a multi-area performance measurement tool and does not involve searching outside for best practices.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: In benchmarking, a benchmark is:

options.b: The acceptable limits of variance around a standard
options.d: The standard of excellence used for comparison

questions.explanation: A benchmark is the standard of excellence against which an organization compares itself. Option B describes the range of variation, which belongs to the comparing step of control.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which company is credited with the first major benchmarking effort in the United States?
questions.explanation: Xerox is credited with the first major benchmarking effort in the United States. The other companies named are well known, but none of them is credited with this first effort.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: A Nigerian bank identifies the best practices of its top-performing branch in Victoria Island and introduces them in all its other branches. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Benchmarking can be done inside the organization by copying the best practices of one unit in others, which is what the bank is doing. Option B is a tool for measuring performance in four areas, not for spreading best practices between branches.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four contemporary control issues?

options.a: Workplace concerns such as privacy and employee theft

questions.explanation: The four contemporary control issues are cross-cultural differences and global turmoil, workplace concerns, controlling customer interactions and corporate governance. Writing a mission statement is a planning task, not a control issue.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Why do controls in an organization's distant global units tend to be more formal?

options.c: Managers cannot observe work directly in distant units
options.d: Global units have no standards to meet

questions.explanation: In distant global units managers cannot watch work directly, so they rely on more formal controls. Option A is wrong and unfair; the reason is physical distance, not the employees themselves.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The unauthorised taking of company property by employees for their own use is called:
questions.explanation: Employee theft is the unauthorised taking of company property by employees for their own personal use. Option A concerns employers monitoring email and internet use, not employees taking property.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: To prevent theft from its drug store, a hospital in Enugu screens job applicants carefully and publishes a clear policy on who may enter the store. Which type of control is the hospital using against employee theft?
questions.explanation: Careful hiring and clear policies act before any theft happens, so they are feedforward controls. Option A would involve fair treatment and supervision while work is under way, and option B would be investigation after theft has occurred.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: A supermarket in Port Harcourt investigates a stock loss and follows up with the staff involved after the theft has occurred. Which type of control against employee theft is this?
questions.explanation: Investigation and follow-up after a theft deal with the problem once it has happened, so they are feedback controls. Option A would mean steps like careful hiring and clear policies taken before any theft.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The sequence from employees to customers to profit is known as the:
questions.explanation: The service profit chain links satisfied, productive employees to better service, customer satisfaction and loyalty, and then to revenue and profit. Option B is the series of work activities that add value from raw inputs to finished product.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: According to the service profit chain, what is the correct order of links?

options.a: Customer loyalty, profit, better service, satisfied employees
options.b: Better service, profit, satisfied employees, customer loyalty
options.c: Profit, customer loyalty, satisfied employees, better service
options.d: Satisfied employees, better service, customer loyalty, profit

questions.explanation: The chain starts with satisfied, productive employees, who give better service, which builds customer satisfaction and loyalty, which brings revenue and profit. Option C reverses the chain by putting profit first.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The system used to govern a corporation so that the interests of its owners are protected is called:
questions.explanation: Corporate governance is the system used to govern a corporation in a way that protects the owners' interests. Option C supplies managers with regular information but does not govern the corporation on behalf of owners.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the two areas of corporate governance reform?

options.b: The role of boards of directors

questions.explanation: The two areas of reform are the role of boards of directors, who should be independent and actually oversee management, and financial reporting. The other options are control concepts from elsewhere and are not governance reforms.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002) in the United States, which raised disclosure and reporting requirements, is associated with which contemporary control issue?
questions.explanation: Sarbanes-Oxley is part of the financial reporting area of corporate governance, requiring accurate and honest financial information. Option C deals with employers monitoring employees, which this law is not about.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The part of the organization that produces goods or services, where resources are transformed into goods and services, is the:
questions.explanation: The operations function is where the organization's resources are transformed into goods and services. Option D deals with selling and promoting output, not producing it.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Operations management is defined as:

options.a: The management of employees' welfare and pensions
options.b: The system used to protect the interests of a corporation's owners
options.c: The administration of business structure, practices and processes to enhance efficiency and maximise profit
options.d: The search for best practices among competitors

questions.explanation: Operations management is the administration of business structure, practices and processes to improve efficiency and maximise profit. Option D describes benchmarking and option B describes corporate governance.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The process that converts resources into finished goods and services is known as the:
questions.explanation: Operations management is also defined as the transformation process, which turns inputs such as people, equipment and information into finished goods and services. Option C is the sequence from employees to customers to profit, and option B is the measure-compare-act cycle of controlling, neither of which converts resources into output.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The goals of operations management focus on several areas. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.c: Increasing the number of management levels

questions.explanation: Operations management goals focus on controlling costs, maximising profitability and properly allocating available resources. Adding management levels is not one of these goals; options D, A and B are.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Effective operations management begins and ends with:
questions.explanation: Effective operations management begins and ends with the customer, whose needs shape what is produced and how. Option C matters for incoming supplies, but it is the customer, not the supplier, at both ends.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: In operations management, every member of an organization is said to have customers:

options.a: Only at the top of the hierarchy
options.d: At the next process, where one's work goes next

questions.explanation: Every member of an organization has customers at the next process, meaning whoever receives their work next. Option C is wrong because internal colleagues who receive one's work also count as customers.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the main functions of operations management?
questions.explanation: The main functions of operations management are planning, scheduling, purchasing, controlling, quality control and inventory control. Recruiting is a staffing activity, not one of these functions.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: How many types of operations management are there?
questions.explanation: The four types are manufacturing, service, logistics and project management. Option A is the number of main functions of operations management, not the number of types.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: A company in Apapa manages warehouses and a fleet of trucks that move and store goods for other firms. Which type of operations management does this represent?
questions.explanation: Logistics is the type of operations management concerned with the movement and storage of goods. Option B is about producing goods, which this company does not do.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: A university in Lagos appoints a team to manage the building of a new hostel, from planning through to completion. Which type of operations management is this?
questions.explanation: Project management manages a specific one-off project from planning to completion, on time, within budget and to specification. Option A deals with moving and storing goods, not delivering a single project.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four types of operations management?
questions.explanation: The four types are manufacturing, service, logistics and project management. Marketing is a separate business function, while options B, C and D are all types of operations management.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: In the transformation process, which of the following is an input?
questions.explanation: Inputs include people, technology, capital, equipment and information, among others. Options D and A are outputs, and option C is part of the transformation process itself.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which of the following belongs to the transformation stage of the transformation process?
questions.explanation: The transformation stage consists of work activities, operations methods and management activities. Options B and A are inputs, and option D is an output.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: A bakery in Ota produces 1,200 loaves of bread using 300 labour-hours. Using productivity = outputs divided by inputs, what is its labour productivity?
questions.explanation: Productivity is outputs divided by inputs, so 1,200 loaves divided by 300 labour-hours gives 4 loaves per labour-hour. Option C divides the wrong way round, inputs by outputs.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which characteristic distinguishes service organizations from manufacturing organizations?

options.a: They include car makers and steel firms
options.b: Their output is used as it is produced

questions.explanation: Service organizations produce nonphysical outputs that are used as they are produced. Options D, C and A all describe manufacturing organizations.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a service organization?

options.c: A food processing factory in Kano
options.d: A car assembly plant in Lagos

questions.explanation: Hospitals, like banks, airlines and schools, produce nonphysical outputs, so they are service organizations. Options D, A and C produce physical goods and are manufacturing organizations.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which of the following trends has made operations vital to every organization's success?

options.b: A reduced need for efficient delivery
options.d: The rise of the service economy

questions.explanation: Global competition, the rise of the service economy and the need for efficient procurement, production and delivery have made operations vital. Options A, C and B state the opposite of these trends.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Who gave 14 points for improving management's productivity?
questions.explanation: W. Edwards Deming proposed 14 points for improving management's productivity and is closely linked with quality and TQM. Option C developed the balanced scorecard, not the 14 points.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: How many points did W. Edwards Deming propose for improving management's productivity?
questions.explanation: Deming gave 14 points for improving management's productivity. Option A is the number of main functions of operations management, a different list.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the themes of Deming's 14 points?
questions.explanation: Deming's points stress planning for the long term, not the short term. Options D, C and B are all genuine themes of his points, along with training workers and constant improvement.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Much of W. Edwards Deming's early influence on quality was in:
questions.explanation: Deming is linked with quality and TQM, and much of his early influence was in Japan. The other countries are not where his early influence was felt.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Productivity in an organization improves through:

options.a: Both people and operations variables working together

questions.explanation: Productivity improves through both people and operations variables; machines alone are not enough because the whole system must work together. Option B is the tempting but wrong idea that technology by itself is sufficient.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The performance features, attributes and other aspects of goods and services that customers are willing to give up resources (usually money) for are known as:
questions.explanation: Value is whatever features and attributes of a product or service customers are willing to pay for with their resources, usually money. Option C is the ability of a product to reliably do what it should and satisfy customers, which is related but not the same.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The entire series of work activities that add value at each step, from raw materials to finished product, is called the:
questions.explanation: The value chain is the whole series of work activities that add value at each step from raw inputs to finished product. Option C links employees to customers to profit, not the steps in producing a product.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Value chain management is the process of:

options.a: Managing the sequence of activities and information along the entire value chain
options.b: Monitoring employees' email and internet use
options.c: Managing only the flow of incoming materials

questions.explanation: Value chain management manages the sequence of activities and information along the entire value chain. Option C describes the narrower supply chain management, which focuses on incoming supplies.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which statement correctly compares value chain management with supply chain management?

options.a: Both are internally focused and aim at cutting costs
options.b: Value chain management covers only incoming materials
options.c: Value chain management is internally focused and aims at efficiency
options.d: Value chain management is externally focused and aims at effectiveness

questions.explanation: Value chain management has an external focus, covers both incoming supplies and outgoing products and aims at effectiveness, creating the most value for customers. Option C describes supply chain management instead, the swap that exams often test.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The goal of supply chain management is:

options.a: Effectiveness, creating the most value for customers

questions.explanation: Supply chain management is internally focused on the efficient flow of incoming supplies, with the goal of efficiency and cutting costs. Option A is the goal of value chain management.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: A food processor in Kano focuses only on getting its incoming raw materials delivered efficiently and at the lowest possible cost. This narrow internal focus is best described as:
questions.explanation: An internal focus on the efficient flow of incoming supplies to cut costs is supply chain management. Option D would also cover outgoing products and services and aim at creating the most value for customers.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The goal of value chain management is to create a value chain strategy that:

options.a: Cuts the cost of incoming materials only
options.b: Measures performance only in financial terms
options.c: Meets and exceeds customer needs and allows full and seamless integration of all members of the chain
options.d: Keeps information private from all partners

questions.explanation: Value chain management aims for a strategy that meets and exceeds customer needs and fully, seamlessly integrates all members of the chain. Option A is the narrower cost focus of supply chain management.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: How many requirements are there for successful value chain management?
questions.explanation: The six requirements are coordination and collaboration, technology investment, organizational processes, leadership, employees and organizational culture and attitudes. Option B is the number of obstacles, not requirements.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for successful value chain management?
questions.explanation: Organizational barriers are an obstacle to value chain management, not a requirement. Options B, C and D are genuine requirements, along with organizational processes, employees and culture.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an obstacle to value chain management?
questions.explanation: Technology investment is one of the six requirements for value chain management, not an obstacle. The four obstacles are organizational barriers, cultural attitudes, required capabilities and people.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: How many obstacles to value chain management are commonly identified?
questions.explanation: The four obstacles are organizational barriers, cultural attitudes, required capabilities and people. Option B is the number of requirements for value chain management.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Refusal to share information, reluctance to change the status quo and security worries are examples of which obstacle to value chain management?
questions.explanation: These are organizational barriers, which block the information sharing and change that value chain management needs. Option C refers instead to lack of trust and fear of losing intellectual property.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: A Lagos manufacturer refuses to work closely with its distributors because it does not trust them and fears they will copy its product designs. This is an example of which obstacle to value chain management?
questions.explanation: Lack of trust and fear of losing intellectual property to partners are cultural attitudes. Option C is tempting, but organizational barriers refer to refusal to share information, reluctance to change and security worries.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Unwillingness to change, lack of commitment and the time and energy needed are examples of which obstacle to value chain management?
questions.explanation: These problems come from the people involved, so they are the people obstacle. Option D is about partners lacking the skills or systems needed, not about willingness or commitment.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: A firm in Ota wants to link up with its suppliers in a value chain, but several suppliers do not have the skills or computer systems needed to take part. Which obstacle is this?
questions.explanation: When partners lack the skills or systems needed, the obstacle is required capabilities. Option C would concern unwillingness to change or lack of commitment, not missing skills or systems.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: In a value chain, who has the power to decide what value is and when it is delivered?
questions.explanation: In a value chain the customer has the power, deciding what value is and when it is delivered. Option D is tempting because the manufacturer makes the product, but it must respond to what customers value.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the benefits of value chain management?
questions.explanation: Value chain management brings improved procurement, logistics and product development and enhanced customer order management. It cannot eliminate competitors, so that option is the odd one out.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The ability of a product or service to reliably do what it is supposed to do and satisfy customer expectations is called:
questions.explanation: Quality is the ability of a product or service to reliably do what it is supposed to do and satisfy customer expectations. Option D is what customers are willing to give up resources for, which is a different idea.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: A philosophy of management driven by continuous improvement and responsiveness to customer needs and expectations is:
questions.explanation: TQM is a management philosophy built on continuous improvement and responsiveness to customer needs and expectations. Option A is a series of international quality standards, and option B is a defect-reduction programme.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: A series of international quality management standards that set uniform guidelines for processes, so that products conform to customer requirements, is known as:
questions.explanation: ISO 9000 is a series of international quality management standards that set uniform rules for processes. Option D is a programme aimed at reducing defects to no more than 3.4 per million.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: The goal of the Six Sigma quality programme is no more than:

options.a: 6 defects per million units or procedures
options.b: 3.4 defects per thousand units or procedures
options.c: 34 defects per million units or procedures
options.d: 3.4 defects per million units or procedures

questions.explanation: Six Sigma aims for no more than 3.4 defects per million units or procedures. Option B gets the number right but the scale wrong, which would allow a thousand times more defects.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: A quality programme designed to reduce defects, lower costs, save time and improve customer satisfaction is:
questions.explanation: Six Sigma is a quality programme to reduce defects, lower costs, save time and improve customer satisfaction. Option D is a set of international standards and certification, not a defect-reduction programme.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Total quality management (TQM) is most closely linked with which management thinker?
questions.explanation: TQM is linked with W. Edwards Deming, who also gave 14 points for improving productivity. Option D co-developed the balanced scorecard, a performance measurement tool rather than a quality philosophy.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: A paint manufacturer in Ota seeks certification from the International Organization for Standardization to show export customers that it has proper quality processes. Which quality standard is it pursuing?
questions.explanation: ISO 9000 is set by the International Organization for Standardization, and certification tells customers a firm has proper quality processes. Option C is an internal programme with a defect target, not a certification from that body.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Giving customers a product when, where and how they want it is called:
questions.explanation: Mass customisation means providing customers with a product when, where and how they want it. Option B is the opposite idea of producing large volumes of a standard product.

questions.topic: Foundations of Control and Operations Management
questions.question: Which of the following is a focus of total quality management (TQM)?

options.d: Reducing the number of customers served

questions.explanation: TQM focuses on the customer, continuous improvement, accurate measurement and employee involvement. Option A is wrong because TQM is about ongoing improvement rather than a single check.
